A standard trapezoid is called a *colorful trapezoid* if the three small triangles it contains are all of different colors. Find the maximum number of *non-overlapping* colorful trapezoids.

positive_text:
Let $\beta = \alpha$ be an irrational number with $\beta > 1$, and let $M$ be a positive integer such that $M > \frac{\beta^2}{\beta - 1}$. Given an integer $y_1 > M$, define a sequence $\{y_n\}$ by the rule:
$$
\quad y_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \lfloor \beta y_n \rfloor, & \text{if } y_n \le M, \\
\lfloor \frac{y_n}{\beta} \rfloor, & \text{if } y_n > M. 
\end{cases}
$$
(1) Show that $\{y_n\}$ is eventually periodic.
(2) Show that the smallest such period is an odd integer not depending on $y_1$.

negatives.text:
Fix an irrational number $\alpha > 1$ and a positive integer $L$ such that $L > \frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha - 1}$. Given an integer $x_1 > L$, define a sequence $\{x_n\}$ as follows: for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$$
\quad x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \lfloor \alpha x_n \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n \le L, \\
\lfloor \alpha x_n \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n > L. 
\end{cases}
$$
(1) Prove that the sequence $\{x_n\}$ is eventually periodic.
(2) Prove that the smallest period is independent of $x_1$.

Fix an irrational number $\alpha > 1$ and a positive integer $L$ such that $L > \frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha - 1}$. Given an integer $x_1 > L$, define a sequence $\{x_n\}$ as follows: for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$$
\quad x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \lfloor \alpha x_n \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n \le L, \\
\lfloor \alpha + x_n \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n > L. 
\end{cases}
$$
(1) Prove that the sequence $\{x_n\}$ is eventually periodic.
(2) Prove that the smallest period is independent of $x_1$.

Fix an irrational number $\alpha > 1$ and a positive integer $L$ such that $L > \frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha - 1}$. Given an integer $x_1 > L$, define a sequence $\{x_n\}$ as follows: for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$$
\quad x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \lfloor \alpha x_n \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n \le L, \\
\lfloor x_n^\alpha \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n > L. 
\end{cases}
$$
(1) Prove that the sequence $\{x_n\}$ is eventually periodic.
(2) Prove that the smallest period is independent of $x_1$.

positive_text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $L$, $M$, and $N$ be the midpoints of segments $AI$, $AC$, and $CI$, respectively. Suppose a point $D$ lies strictly inside segment $AM$ such that $BD = BC$. The incircle of triangle $ABD$ is tangent to $AD$ and $BD$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $J$ be the circumcenter of triangle $AIC$, and let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $DMJ$. If line $MN$ intersects $\omega$ at $P(\neq M)$ and line $JL$ intersects $\omega$ at $Q(\neq J)$, show that lines $EF$, $PQ$, and $LN$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Write $L$, $M$, and $N$ for the midpoints of $AI$, $AC$, and $CI$, respectively. Suppose there is a point $D$ in the interior of segment $AM$ such that $BD = CD$. The incircle of triangle $ABD$ touches $AD$ and $BD$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $J$ be the circumcenter of triangle $AIC$, and $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $DMJ$. The line $MN$ intersects $\omega$ at point $P(\neq M)$, and the line $JL$ intersects $\omega$ at point $Q(\neq J)$. Prove that the three lines $EF$, $PQ$, and $LN$ pass through a common point.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Write $L$, $M$, and $N$ for the midpoints of $AI$, $AC$, and $CI$, respectively. Suppose there is a point $D$ in the interior of segment $AM$ such that $BD > BC$. The incircle of triangle $ABD$ touches $AD$ and $BD$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $J$ be the circumcenter of triangle $AIC$, and $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $DMJ$. The line $MN$ intersects $\omega$ at point $P(\neq M)$, and the line $JL$ intersects $\omega$ at point $Q(\neq J)$. Prove that the three lines $EF$, $PQ$, and $LN$ pass through a common point.

positive_text:
Find the minimal real number $\mu$ such that for all positive integers $a$, $b$, and $n$ with $a + b \not\equiv 0 \pmod{n}$, there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfying $1 \le k < n$ and
$$
\left\{ \frac{ak}{n} \right\} + \left\{ \frac{bk}{n} \right\} \le \mu.
$$

negatives.text:
Find the smallest real number $\mu$ such that for all positive integers $a$, $b$, and $n$ with $a + b$ divisible by $n$, there exists a positive integer $k < n$ with
$$
\left\{ \frac{ak}{n} \right\} + \left\{ \frac{bk}{n} \right\} \le \mu.
$$

Find the smallest real number $\mu$ such that for all positive integers $a$, $b$, and $n$ with $a + b$ not divisible by $n$, there exists a positive integer $k < n$ with
$$
\left\lfloor \frac{ak}{n} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{bk}{n} \right\rfloor \le \mu.
$$

Find the smallest real number $\mu$ such that for all positive integers $a$, $b$, and $n$ with $a + b$ not divisible by $n$, there exists a positive integer $k < n$ with
$$
\left\{ \frac{ak}{n} \right\}^2 + \left\{ \frac{bk}{n} \right\}^2 \le \mu.
$$

positive_text: Let $a_1 > a_2 > \dots > a_n > 1$ be positive integers with $M$ as the least common multiple of $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$. For a finite set $X$ of integers, define $$ f(X) = \min_{1 \le i \le n} \sum_{x \in X} \left(\frac{x}{a_i} - \left\lfloor \frac{x}{a_i} \right\rfloor\right). $$ Put $f(\emptyset) = 0$. A set $X$ is *minimal* if every proper subset $Y$ of $X$ satisfies $f(Y) < f(X)$. Prove that, if $X$ is minimal and $f(X) \ge \frac{2}{a_n}$, then $$ |X| \le f(X) \cdot M. $$

negatives.text: Let $a_1 > a_2 > \dots > a_n > 1$ be positive integers with $M$ as the least common multiple of $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$. For a finite set of integers $X$, define $$ f(X) = \min_{1 \le i \le n} \sum_{x \in X} \left\{ \frac{x}{a_i} \right\}. $$ Put $f(\emptyset) = 0$. A set $X$ is *minimal* if for any proper subset $Y$ of $X$, $f(Y) < f(X)$. Prove that, if $X$ is minimal and $f(X) \ge \frac{2}{a_1}$, then $$ |X| \le f(X) \cdot M. $$

Let $a_1 > a_2 > \dots > a_n > 1$ be positive integers with $M$ as the least common multiple of $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$. For a finite set of integers $X$, define $$ f(X) = \min_{1 \le i \le n} \sum_{x \in X} \left\{ \frac{x}{a_i} \right\}. $$ Put $f(\emptyset) = 0$. A set $X$ is *minimal* if for any proper subset $Y$ of $X$, $f(Y) < f(X)$. Prove that, if $X$ is minimal and $f(X) \ge \frac{1}{a_n}$, then $$ |X| \le f(X) \cdot M. $$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be a point such that $AD \parallel BC$ and $DB > DC$. Let $E$ be a point on the arc $\widearc{BC}$ of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ not containing $A$ with $EB < EC$. Let $F$ be on the extension of $BC$ such that $\angle ADE = \angle DFE$. If the line $FD$ meets the extension of $BA$ at $X$ and the extension of $CA$ at $Y$, show that $\angle XEY$ remains constant.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be a point such that $AD \parallel BC$ and $DB > DC$. Let $E$ be on the arc $\widearc{BC}$ of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ that does not contain $A$, with $EB > EC$. Let $F$ be on the extension of $BC$ such that $\angle DFE = \angle ADE$. The line $FD$ intersects the extension of $BA$ at $X$ and the extension of $CA$ at $Y$. Prove that $\angle XEY$ is constant.

positive_text:
Given a positive integer $n \ge 4$, prove that the equation
$$
(2^x - 1)(5^x - 1) = z^{n}
$$
has no positive integer solutions $(x, z)$.

negatives.text:
Given a positive integer $n \ge 4$, prove that the equation
$$
(2^x + 1)(5^x + 1) = y^n
$$
has no positive integer solutions $(x, y)$.

Given a positive integer $n \ge 4$, prove that the equation
$$
(2^x - 1)(5^x - 1) = y^n
$$
has no positive integer solutions $(x, y)$ for all $x$ even.

Given a positive integer $n \ge 4$, prove that the equation
$$
(2^x - 1)(5^x - 1) = y^{n+1}
$$
has no positive integer solutions $(x, y)$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Alice and Bob play a game on the complete graph $K_n$, where each edge starts uncolored. On their turn, a player may color either one or two uncolored edges red. The rule is that after each move, there must be no triangle (i.e., three vertices with all three connecting edges) with all edges colored red. The game ends when no further move is possible. Show that there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for all $n \ge 2$, Alice can always force the total number of red edges to be at most $\left(\frac{1}{4} - \varepsilon\right)n^2 + n$, regardless of Bob's strategy.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Two players, Alice and Bob, play a game on the complete graph $K_n$, where they alternately color edges red, with Alice starting first. On each turn, a player may color one or two edges red, but the game ends when the number of red edges exceeds $\left(\frac{1}{4} + \varepsilon\right)n^2 - n$. Prove that Alice can always force the game to end with at least $\left(\frac{1}{4} + \varepsilon\right)n^2 - n$ red edges, regardless of Bob's strategy.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Two players, Alice and Bob, play a game on the complete graph $K_n$, where they alternately color edges red, with Alice starting first. On each turn, a player may color one or two edges red, with the constraint that no four vertices can form a complete red subgraph $K_4$. The game ends when no more moves are possible. Prove that there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that Alice can ensure the number of red edges is at most $\left(\frac{1}{4} - \varepsilon\right)n^2 + n$, regardless of Bob's strategy.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Two players, Alice and Bob, play a game on the complete graph $K_n$, where they alternately color edges red, with Alice starting first. On each turn, a player may color one or two edges red, with the constraint that after each move, no two adjacent edges are colored red. The game ends when no more moves are possible. Prove that there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that Alice can ensure the number of red edges is at most $\left(\frac{1}{4} - \varepsilon\right)n^2 + n$, regardless of Bob's strategy.

positive_text: Let $A(x)$ and $B(x)$ be non-constant real polynomials such that for each positive integer $k$, there exists a positive integer $l$ satisfying $A(k) = B(l)$.\n(a) Show that if $\deg(B)$ divides $\deg(A)$, then there exists a real polynomial $f(x)$ with $A(x) = B(f(x))$.\n(b) Prove that $\deg(B)$ divides $\deg(A)$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ be non-constant real polynomials such that for every positive integer $m$, there exists a positive integer $n$ with $P(m) = Q(n)$.\n(1) Prove that if $\deg(Q)$ divides $\deg(P)$, then there exists a real polynomial $h(x)$ such that $P(x) = Q(h(x))$.\n(2) Prove that $\deg(P)$ divides $\deg(Q)$.

Let $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ be non-constant real polynomials such that for every positive integer $m$, there exists a positive integer $n$ with $P(m) = Q(n)$.\n(1) Prove that if $\deg(Q)$ divides $\deg(P)$, then there exists a real polynomial $h(x)$ such that $P(x) = Q(h(x)) + 1$.\n(2) Prove that $\deg(Q)$ divides $\deg(P)$.

Let $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ be non-constant real polynomials such that for every positive integer $m$, there exists a positive integer $n$ with $P(m) = Q(n)$.\n(1) Prove that if $\deg(Q)$ divides $\deg(P)$, then there exists a real polynomial $h(x)$ such that $P(x) = Q(h(x))$.\n(2) Prove that $\deg(Q)$ is strictly less than $\deg(P)$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be isosceles with $|AB| = |AC|$. The bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\overline{AC}$ at point $D$. Given that $|BC| = |BD| + |AD|$, determine the measures of all the angles in the triangle.

positive_text:

$$

Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ with $b \ge 0$ satisfying
$$
a^2 + 2ab + b! = 131.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ with $b \ge 0$ such that
$$
a^2 + 2ab - b! = 131.
$$

Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ with $b \ge 0$ such that
$$
a^2 + 2ab + b! = 132.
$$

Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ with $b \ge 0$ such that
$$
a^2 - 2ab + b! = 131.
$$

positive_text: Determine all real pairs $(x, y)$ satisfying $x^2 + y^2 = 25$, for which the expression $xy + x + y$ is minimized.

negatives.text: Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of real numbers such that $a^2 + b^2 = 25$, for which $ab - a - b$ attains the smallest possible value.
Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of real numbers such that $a^2 + b^2 = 25$, for which $ab + a + b$ attains the largest possible value.
Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of real numbers such that $a^2 + b^2 = 25$, for which $ab + a + b^2$ attains the smallest possible value.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{N}$ be the set of positive integers. Suppose $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is a *multiplicative* function such that $f(2^2) = 2^2$ and
$$
\quad f(a^2 + b^2) = f(a^2) + f(b^2)
$$
for all $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that $f(k^2) = k^2$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

negatives.text:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a *multiplicative* function such that $f(4) = 4$ and
$$
\quad f(m^2 + n^2) = f(m^2) + f(n^2) + 1
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that $f(m^2) = m^2$ for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a *multiplicative* function such that $f(4) = 4$ and
$$
\quad f(m^2 + n^2) = f(m^2) + f(n^2)
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that $f(m^3) = m^3$ for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a *multiplicative* function such that $f(4) = 4$ and
$$
\quad f(m^2 + n^2) = f(m^2) + f(n^2)
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that $f(m^2) = 2m^2$ for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$.

positive_text:
Let $m$ be a positive integer, and $p$ be a prime number such that $p > m$. Prove that the number of positive integers $n$ such that
$$
(n - m - p)^2
$$
is a perfect square, is independent of the value of $p$. (Bulgaria 2013)

negatives.text:
Let $m$ be a positive integer, and $p$ be a prime number such that $p > m$. Prove that the number of positive integers $n$ for which
$$
m^2 + n^2 + p^2 + 2mn - 2mp - 2np
$$
is a square of some positive integer, does not depend on $p$. (Bulgaria 2013)

Let $m$ be a positive integer, and $p$ be a prime number such that $p > m$. Prove that the number of positive integers $n$ for which
$$
m^2 + n^2 + p^2 - 2mn - 2mp - 2np
$$
is a cube of some positive integer, does not depend on $p$. (Bulgaria 2013)

Let $m$ be a positive integer, and $p$ be a prime number such that $p > m$. Prove that the number of positive integers $n$ for which
$$
m^2 + n^2 + p^2 - 2mn - 2mp - 2np
$$
is a square of some positive integer, depends on $p$. (Bulgaria 2013)

positive_text: \text{Find all real solutions } (x, y, z) \text{ such that } \frac{1}{xy} - \frac{x}{z} = 1, \quad \frac{1}{yz} - \frac{y}{x} = 1, \quad \frac{1}{zx} - \frac{z}{y} = 1.

negatives.text: \text{Solve the system } \frac{1}{xy} = \frac{x}{z} - 1, \quad \frac{1}{yz} = \frac{y}{x} - 1, \quad \frac{1}{zx} = \frac{z}{y} - 1 \text{ in the real numbers.}
\text{Solve the system } \frac{1}{xy} = \frac{x^2}{z} + 1, \quad \frac{1}{yz} = \frac{y^2}{x} + 1, \quad \frac{1}{zx} = \frac{z^2}{y} + 1 \text{ in the real numbers.}
\text{Solve the system } \frac{1}{xy} = \frac{x}{z}, \quad \frac{1}{yz} = \frac{y}{x}, \quad \frac{1}{zx} = \frac{z}{y} \text{ in the real numbers.}

positive_text: Given $k$ heaps with $1, 2, \dots, k$ stones respectively, where $k \ge 3$, in each step $i$ we select any three heaps whose total number of stones exceeds $i$, merge them, and remove $i$ stones from the resulting heap. When only one heap remains, it contains $p$ stones. Prove that $p$ is a perfect square if and only if $2k+2$ and $3k+1$ are perfect squares, and determine the smallest $k$ for which $p$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text: Let $k$ heaps have $1, 2, \dots, k$ stones, with $k \ge 3$. At step $i$, choose any three heaps whose total is greater than $i$, merge them, and remove $i+1$ stones from the new heap. After some steps, one heap remains with $p$ stones. Prove that $p$ is a perfect square if and only if $2k+2$ and $3k+1$ are perfect squares. Find the minimal $k$ for which this occurs.

Given $k$ heaps with $1, 2, \dots, k$ stones, with $k \ge 3$, at step $i$, choose any three heaps whose total is greater than $i$, merge them, and remove $i$ stones from the new heap. After some steps, one heap remains with $p$ stones. Prove that $p$ is a perfect square if and only if $2k+2$ and $3k-1$ are perfect squares. Find the minimal $k$ for which this occurs.

Suppose $k$ heaps contain $1, 2, \dots, k$ stones, with $k \ge 3$. At step $i$, choose any three heaps whose total is greater than $i$, merge them, and remove $i$ stones from the new heap. After some steps, one heap remains with $p$ stones. Prove that $p$ is a perfect square if and only if $2k+2$ and $3k+1$ are perfect cubes. Find the minimal $k$ for which this occurs.

positive_text:
Two circles, $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$, are located inside rectangle $ABCD$, where $AB = 9$ and $BC = 8$. Circle $k_1$ is tangent to sides $AD$ and $CD$, and circle $k_2$ is tangent to $AB$ and $BC$. The circles are tangent to each other.

a) Show that $r_1 + r_2 = 5$.

b) Determine the minimum and maximum possible values for the area of triangle $AS_1S_2$.

Two circles, $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$, are located inside rectangle $ABCD$, where $AB = 9$ and $BC = 8$. Circle $k_1$ is tangent to sides $AD$ and $CD$, and circle $k_2$ is tangent to $AB$ and $BC$. The circles are tangent to each other.

a) Show that $r_1 + r_2 = 5$.

b) Determine the minimum and maximum possible values for the area of triangle $AS_1S_2$.

negatives.text:
Two circles, $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$, are located inside rectangle $ABCD$ with $AB = 9$ and $BC = 8$. Circle $k_1$ is tangent to sides $AD$ and $CD$, and circle $k_2$ is tangent to $AB$ and $BC$. The circles are tangent to each other.

a) Prove $r_1 + r_2 = 5$.

b) What is the least and what is the greatest possible area of triangle $S_1S_2D$?

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be any positive real numbers. Prove the inequality
$$
(a + b + c) \left( \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} \right) \le k^2, \quad \text{where } k = \min \left( \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{a}, \frac{b}{a} + \frac{c}{b} + \frac{a}{c} \right) \right).
$$
Determine the condition for equality.

negatives.text:
Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be positive real numbers. Prove the inequality
$$
(x + y + z) \left( \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z} \right) \le m^2, \quad \text{where } m = \max \left( \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{x}, \frac{y}{x} + \frac{z}{y} + \frac{x}{z} \right) \right).
$$
Find when equality holds.

Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be positive real numbers. Prove the inequality
$$
(x + y + z) \left( \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z} \right) \le m^2, \quad \text{where } m = \min \left( \frac{x^2}{y} + \frac{y^2}{z} + \frac{z^2}{x}, \frac{y^2}{x} + \frac{z^2}{y} + \frac{x^2}{z} \right) \right).
$$
Determine when equality occurs.

Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be positive real numbers. Prove the inequality
$$
(x + y + z) \left( \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z} \right) \ge m^2, \quad \text{where } m = \min \left( \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{x}, \frac{y}{x} + \frac{z}{y} + \frac{x}{z} \right) \right).
$$
Find when equality holds.

positive_text: \text{Let } k_1(S_1, r_1) \text{ and } k_2(S_2, r_2) \text{ be circles tangent to the sides of right triangle } ABC, \text{ where } AC = 4, BC = 3, AB = 5. \text{ Circle } k_1 \text{ is tangent to } AB \text{ and } AC, \text{ while } k_2 \text{ is tangent to } AB \text{ and } BC. \text{ The circles touch each other externally, and it is given that } 4r_1 = 9r_2. \text{ Find } r_1 \text{ and } r_2.

negatives.text: \text{Touching circles } k_1(S_1, r_1) \text{ and } k_2(S_2, r_2) \text{ lie in a right-angled triangle } ABC \text{ with legs } AC = 4 \text{ and } BC = 3. \text{ The circle } k_1 \text{ is tangent to } AB \text{ and } AC, \text{ while } k_2 \text{ is tangent to } AB \text{ and } BC. \text{ Find radii } r_1 \text{ and } r_2, \text{ if } 9r_1 = 4r_2.

\text{Two circles } k_1(S_1, r_1) \text{ and } k_2(S_2, r_2) \text{ are placed in a right-angled triangle } ABC \text{ with } AC = 4 \text{ and } BC = 3. \text{ Circle } k_1 \text{ is tangent to } AB \text{ and } AC, \text{ and circle } k_2 \text{ is tangent to } AB \text{ and } BC. \text{ The circles are internally tangent instead of externally tangent. Find radii } r_1 \text{ and } r_2, \text{ if } 4r_1 = 9r_2.

\text{Two circles } k_1(S_1, r_1) \text{ and } k_2(S_2, r_2) \text{ are inscribed in a right-angled triangle } ABC \text{ with } AC = 4 \text{ and } BC = 3. \text{ The circle } k_1 \text{ is tangent to } AB \text{ and } AC, \text{ and } k_2 \text{ is tangent to } AB \text{ and } BC. \text{ It is given that } r_1^2 + r_2^2 = 1. \text{ Find the values of } r_1 \text{ and } r_2, \text{ given that } 4r_1 = 9r_2.

positive_text: Two circles $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$ lie in the plane with $|S_1S_2| > r_1 + r_2$. Determine the set of points $X$ not on the line $S_1S_2$ such that the segments $S_1X$ and $S_2X$ meet the circles $k_1$ and $k_2$ respectively at points whose perpendicular distances to $S_1S_2$ are equal.

negatives.text: Given two circles $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$ with $|S_1S_2| > r_1 + r_2$, find the locus of points $X$ not on the line $S_1S_2$ such that the segments $S_1X$ and $S_2X$ intersect $k_1$ and $k_2$ at points whose perpendicular distances to $S_1S_2$ are negative of each other.

Two circles $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$ lie in the plane with $|S_1S_2| > r_1 + r_2$. Determine the set of points $X$ not on the line $S_1S_2$ such that the segments $S_1X$ and $S_2X$ intersect $k_1$ and $k_2$ at points whose squared distances to the line $S_1S_2$ are equal.

Let $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$ be two circles with $|S_1S_2| > r_1 + r_2$. Find the locus of points $X$ not on the line $S_1S_2$ such that the segments $S_1X$ and $S_2X$ intersect $k_1$ and $k_2$ at points whose distances to the line $S_1S_2$ are in a fixed ratio $k 
eq 1$.

positive_text: In a cinema with 234 attendees, they are seated in $n$ rows, $n \ge 4$, such that every person in row $i$ has exactly $j$ friends in row $j$, for all $i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}, i \neq j$. Determine all possible values of $n$, given that the friendship relation is symmetric.

negatives.text: In a cinema with 234 individuals seated in $n$ rows, $n \ge 4$, each individual in the $i$-th row has at least $j$ friends in the $j$-th row for all $i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}, i \neq j$. Find all possible values of $n$, assuming the friendship is symmetric.

In a cinema with 234 individuals seated in $n$ rows, $n \ge 4$, each individual in the $i$-th row has exactly $j$ friends in the $j$-th row for all $i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}, i \neq j$. However, friendship is not symmetric. Find all possible values of $n$.

In a cinema with 234 individuals seated in $n$ rows, $n \ge 4$, each individual in the $i$-th row has exactly $j$ friends in the $j$-th row for all $i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}, i \neq j$. Find all possible values of $n$, assuming that the total number of friendships is maximized.

positive_text:
Find the minimal real $ m $ such that there exist real numbers $ a $ and $ b $ satisfying
$$
\left|\frac{x^2 + a x + b}{1}\right| \le m
$$
for every $ x $ in the open interval $ (0, 2) $.

negatives.text:
Find the least real $ m $ such that there exist reals $ a $ and $ b $ for which the inequality
$$
|x^2 + a x + b| \le m
$$
holds for all $ x \in (0, 2) $, and $ x^2 + a x + b $ is non-negative on the interval.

Find the least real $ m $ such that there exist reals $ a $ and $ b $ for which the inequality
$$
|x^2 + a x + b| \le m
$$
holds for all $ x \in (0, 2) $, and the function $ x^2 + a x + b $ is increasing on the interval.

positive_text: A family of sets $\mathcal{F}$ is called *perfect* if for any three sets $A, B, C \in \mathcal{F}$, it holds that either $(A \setminus B) \cap C = \emptyset$ or $(B \setminus A) \cap C = \emptyset$. Prove that if $\mathcal{F}$ is a perfect family of subsets of a finite set $S$, then $|\mathcal{F}| \leq |S| + 1$.

negatives.text: A family of sets $\mathcal{F}$ is called *perfect* if for every triple of sets $X_1, X_2, X_3 \in \mathcal{F}$, at least one of the sets $(X_1 \setminus X_2) \cup X_3$, $(X_2 \setminus X_1) \cup X_3$ is empty. Show that if $\mathcal{F}$ is a perfect family consisting of subsets of a finite set $U$, then $|\mathcal{F}| \le |U| + 1$.

A family of sets $\mathcal{F}$ is called *perfect* if for every triple of sets $X_1, X_2, X_3 \in \mathcal{F}$, at least one of the sets $(X_1 \setminus X_2) \cap X_3$, $(X_2 \setminus X_1) \cap X_3$ is non-empty. Show that if $\mathcal{F}$ is a perfect family consisting of subsets of a finite set $U$, then $|\mathcal{F}| \le |U| + 1$.

A family of sets $\mathcal{F}$ is called *perfect* if for every triple of sets $X_1, X_2, X_3 \in \mathcal{F}$, both of the sets $(X_1 \setminus X_2) \cap X_3$, $(X_2 \setminus X_1) \cap X_3$ are empty. Show that if $\mathcal{F}$ is a perfect family consisting of subsets of a finite set $U$, then $|\mathcal{F}| \le |U| + 1$.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be positive real numbers such that
$$xy + yz + zx = 16, \quad x \ge 3.$$
Minimize the expression $2x + y + z$.

negatives.text: Given positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ such that $ab + bc + ca = 16$ and $a \ge 3$, minimize $2a^2 + b + c$.
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers satisfying $ab + bc + ca = 16$ and $a \ge 3$. Find the minimum value of $2a + b^2 + c^2$.

positive_text: Determine all integers $k \ge 2$ for which a $k$-element set $M$ of positive integers exists such that the product of all elements in $M$ is divisible by the sum of any pair of distinct elements in $M$.

negatives.text: Find all integers $k \ge 2$ for which there exists a $k$-element set $M$ of positive integers such that the product of all numbers in $M$ is divisible by the difference of any two (different) numbers from $M$.

Find all integers $k \ge 2$ for which there exists a $k$-element set $M$ of positive integers such that the product of all numbers in $M$ is divisible by the product of any two (different) numbers from $M$.

Find all integers $k \ge 2$ for which there exists a $k$-element set $M$ of positive integers such that the product of all numbers in $M$ is divisible by the sum of any two (different) numbers from $M$, excluding the smallest element in $M$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a right triangle with right angle at $C$, and let $AB$ be the hypotenuse. Suppose $BC > AC$. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. A circle centered at $D$ with radius $DC$ intersects $BC$ at a point $Q$ and $AB$ at two points $E$ and $F$ ($E \neq F$), with $F$ lying on segment $AB$. The segment $QE$ meets $AC$ at a point $P$. Prove that $PE = QF$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $C$, and let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$. A circle centered at $D$ with radius $CD$ intersects $BC$ at a point $Q$ and $AB$ at points $E$ and $F$ ($E \neq F$), with $F$ on $AB$. If segment $QE$ intersects $AC$ at $P$, prove that $PF = QF$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $C$, and let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$. A circle centered at $D$ with radius $CD$ intersects $BC$ at a point $Q$ and $AB$ at points $E$ and $F$ ($E \neq F$), with $F$ on $AB$. If segment $QE$ intersects $AC$ at $P$, prove that $PE = DF$.

positive_text:
Given a trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel CD$ and $BC = AB + CD$, show that
(i) the leg $AD$ contains a point lying on the circle with diameter $BC$,
(ii) the leg $BC$ contains a point lying on the circle with diameter $AD$.

negatives.text:
Given a trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel CD$ and $BC = AB - CD$, prove that
(i) there is a point of a circle with diameter $BC$ on the leg $AD$,
(ii) there is a point of a circle with diameter $AD$ on the leg $BC$.

Given a trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel CD$ and $BC^2 = AB^2 + CD^2$, prove that
(i) there is a point of a circle with diameter $BC$ on the leg $AD$,
(ii) there is a point of a circle with diameter $AD$ on the leg $BC$.

Given a trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel CD$ and $BC = AB + CD + 1$, prove that
(i) there is a point of a circle with diameter $BC$ on the leg $AD$,
(ii) there is a point of a circle with diameter $AD$ on the leg $BC$.

positive_text:
Let $r$ and $r_a$ denote the inradius and the exradius opposite $A$ in triangle $ABC$. Prove that if
$$
 r + r_a = c,
$$
where $c = |BC|$, then triangle $ABC$ is a right triangle.

negatives.text:
Let $r$ and $r_a$ be the inradius and the exradius opposite $A$ in triangle $ABC$. Show that if
$$
 r + r_a = |AB|,
$$
then the triangle is right-angled.

Let $r$ and $r_a$ be the inradius and the exradius opposite $A$ in triangle $ABC$. Show that if
$$
 r - r_a = |BC|,
$$
then the triangle is right-angled.

Let $r$ and $r_a$ be the inradius and the exradius opposite $A$ in triangle $ABC$. Show that if
$$
 r + r_a =  rac{1}{2}|BC|,
$$
then the triangle is right-angled.

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers satisfying
$$
(a + c)(b^2 + a c) = 4a.
$$
Determine the maximum value of $b + c$ and all such triples $(a, b, c)$ that achieve this maximum.

negatives.text:
For positive $a$, $b$, $c$ it holds
$$
(a + c)(b^2 + ac) = 4a.
$$
Find the minimal possible value of $b + c$ and all triples $(a, b, c)$, for which the value is attained.

For positive $a$, $b$, $c$ it holds
$$
(a + c)(b^2 + ac) = 4a^2.
$$
Find the maximal possible value of $b + c$ and all triples $(a, b, c)$, for which the value is attained.

For positive $a$, $b$, $c$ it holds
$$
(a + c)(b^2 + ac) = 4a.
$$
Find the maximal possible value of $b - c$ and all triples $(a, b, c)$, for which the value is attained.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $|BC| = 1$, and suppose there exists a unique point $D$ on segment $BC$ such that $|DA|^2 = |DB| \cdot |DC|$. Determine all possible values of the perimeter of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Suppose triangle $ABC$ has $|BC| = 1$ and a unique point $D$ on $BC$ such that $|DA|^2 = |DB|^2 + |DC|^2$. Find all possible values of the perimeter of triangle $ABC$.
Let triangle $ABC$ have $|BC| = 1$ and a unique point $D$ on $BC$ such that $|DA| = |DB| \cdot |DC|$. Find all possible values of the perimeter of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with base $AB$. Let $D$ lie anywhere on segment $AB$, and let $E$ be a point such that $ADEC$ is a parallelogram. Let $F$ lie on the extension of $ED$ beyond $D$ such that $EF = EB$. Show that the chord formed by the intersection of line $BE$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABF$ is equal to $2AC$.

negatives.text: Let $D$ be an arbitrary point on the base $AB$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$. Let $E$ be such that $ADEC$ is a parallelogram. Point $F$ on the ray opposite to $ED$ satisfies $EF = AE$. Prove that the length of a chord cut by line $BE$ in the circumcircle of triangle $ABF$ is twice the length of $AC$.

Let $D$ be an arbitrary point on the base $AB$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$. Let $E$ be such that $ADEC$ is a parallelogram. Point $F$ lies on the ray opposite to $ED$ such that $EF = EB$. Prove that the length of a chord cut by line $EF$ in the circumcircle of triangle $ABF$ is twice the length of $AC$.

Let $D$ be an arbitrary point on the base $AB$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$. Let $E$ be such that $ADEC$ is a parallelogram. Point $F$ on the ray opposite to $ED$ satisfies $EF = EB$. Prove that the length of a chord cut by line $BE$ in the circumcircle of triangle $ABF$ is equal to $AC$.

positive_text:
Let $p$ be a circle centered at $K$ and passing through $M$, and let $q$ be a semicircle with diameter $KM$. Let $L$ lie strictly between $K$ and $M$. A line through $L$ perpendicular to $KM$ intersects $q$ at $Q$ and $p$ at two points $P_1, P_2$ such that $P_1$ lies farther from $Q$ than $P_2$. If the line $MQ$ intersects $p$ again at $R$, show that the areas $S_1, S_2$ of triangles $MP_1Q$ and $P_2RQ$ satisfy
$$
1 < \frac{S_1}{S_2} < 3 + \sqrt{8}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $p$ be a circle with center $K$ passing through $M$, $q$ a semicircle with diameter $KM$ and $L$ a point inside the segment $KM$. A line through $L$ perpendicular to $KM$ intersects $q$ at point $Q$ and $p$ at points $P_1, P_2$ such that $P_1Q > P_2Q$. Line $MQ$ intersects $p$ for the second time at $R 
e M$. Prove that areas $S_1, S_2$ of triangles $MP_1Q, P_2RQ$ satisfy
$$
1 < \frac{S_1}{S_2} < 3 - \sqrt{8}.
$$

Let $p$ be a circle with center $K$ passing through $M$, $q$ a semicircle with diameter $KM$ and $L$ a point inside the segment $KM$. A line through $L$ perpendicular to $KM$ intersects $q$ at point $Q$ and $p$ at points $P_1, P_2$ such that $P_1Q > P_2Q$. Line $MQ$ intersects $p$ for the second time at $R 
e M$. Prove that areas $S_1, S_2$ of triangles $MP_1Q, P_2RQ$ satisfy
$$
\frac{S_1}{S_2} < 1.
$$

Let $p$ be a circle with center $K$ passing through $M$, $q$ a semicircle with diameter $KM$ and $L$ a point inside the segment $KM$. A line through $L$ perpendicular to $KM$ intersects $q$ at point $Q$ and $p$ at points $P_1, P_2$ such that $P_1Q > P_2Q$. Line $MQ$ intersects $p$ for the second time at $R 
e M$. Prove that areas $S_1, S_2$ of triangles $MP_1Q, P_2RQ$ satisfy
$$
1 < \frac{S_1}{S_2} < 3 + \sqrt{3}.
$$

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $S_b$ and $S_c$ be the midpoints of $AC$ and $AB$, respectively. Show that the inequality $AB < AC$ implies $\angle B S_c C < \angle B S_b C$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with midpoints $S_b, S_c$ of $AC$, $AB$, respectively. Prove that if $AB > AC$ then $\angle B S_c C < \angle B S_b C$.
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $S_b, S_c$ the midpoints of $AC$, $AB$, respectively. Prove that if $AB < AC$ then $\angle B S_c C = \angle B S_b C$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle. Points $D$ and $E$ lie on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $AB - AD = AC - AE$. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABE$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $ABC$, $ADE$, and $AO_1O_2$ intersect at a common point other than $A$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$ such that $BD = -CE$. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABE$ and $ACD$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $ABC$, $ADE$, and $AO_1O_2$ have a common point different from $A$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle. Points $D$ and $E$ lie on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $BD = CE^2$. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABE$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $ABC$, $ADE$, and $AO_1O_2$ have a common point different from $A$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with points $D$ and $E$ on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $BD = CE$. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the incenters of triangles $ABE$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $ABC$, $ADE$, and $AO_1O_2$ have a common point different from $A$.

positive_text: Determine all integers $n > 2$ such that there exists an integer $k$ with $n^{n-2} = k^n$.

negatives.text: Find all integers $n > 2$ such that $n^{n-1}$ is an $n$th power of some integer.
Find all integers $n > 2$ such that $n^{n-2} + 1$ is an $n$th power of some integer.

positive_text:
Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
f\left(f(a) + \frac{b+1}{f(b)}\right) = \frac{1}{f(b)} + a + 1
$$
for all $a, b > 0$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
f\left(f(x) - \frac{y+1}{f(y)}\right) = \frac{1}{f(y)} + x + 1
$$
for all $x, y > 0$.

Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
f\left(f(x) + \frac{y^2 + 1}{f(y)}\right) = \frac{1}{f(y)} + x + 1
$$
for all $x, y > 0$.

Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
f\left(f(x) + \frac{y+1}{f(y)}\right) = \frac{1}{f(y)} - x + 1
$$
for all $x, y > 0$.

positive_text: Two circles $\omega$ and $\gamma$ of different radii intersect at two points, one of which is $P$. A line $\ell$ through $P$ intersects the arc of $\omega$ outside $\gamma$ at $X_1$ and the arc of $\gamma$ outside $\omega$ at $X_2$. Let $R$ lie on segment $X_1X_2$ such that $X_1P = RX_2$. Let $T$ be the intersection of the tangents to $\omega$ at $X_1$ and to $\gamma$ at $X_2$. Show that line $RT$ is tangent to a fixed circle, regardless of the choice of $\ell$.

negatives.text: Two circles $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$ with different radii intersect at two points, one of which is $P$. A line $\ell$ through $P$ intersects the arc of $\Omega_1$ outside $\Omega_2$ at $X_1$, and the arc of $\Omega_2$ outside $\Omega_1$ at $X_2$. Let $R$ be the point on segment $X_1X_2$ such that $X_1P = R X_2$. The tangent to $\Omega_1$ through $X_1$ and the tangent to $\Omega_2$ through $X_2$ intersect at $T$. Prove that line $RT$ is perpendicular to a fixed line, independent of the choice of $\ell$.

Two circles $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$ with different radii intersect at two points, one of which is $P$. A line $\ell$ through $P$ intersects the arc of $\Omega_1$ outside $\Omega_2$ at $X_1$, and the arc of $\Omega_2$ outside $\Omega_1$ at $X_2$. Let $R$ be the point on segment $X_1X_2$ such that $X_1P = RX_2$. The tangent to $\Omega_1$ through $X_1$ meets the tangent to $\Omega_2$ through $X_2$ at $T$. Prove that line $RT$ is tangent to a fixed circle, independent of the choice of $\ell$, assuming the line $\ell$ is fixed.

Two circles $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$ with different radii intersect at two points, one of which is $P$. A line $\ell$ through $P$ intersects the arc of $\Omega_1$ outside $\Omega_2$ at $X_1$, and the arc of $\Omega_2$ outside $\Omega_1$ at $X_2$. Let $R$ be the point on segment $X_1X_2$ such that $X_1R = RX_2$. The tangent to $\Omega_1$ through $X_1$ meets the tangent to $\Omega_2$ through $X_2$ at $T$. Prove that line $RT$ is tangent to a fixed circle, independent of the choice of $\ell$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. On the rays extending beyond $A$ from $C$ and $B$, respectively, define points $B'$ and $C'$ such that $B'C = AB$ and $C'B = AC$. Prove that the circumcenter of triangle $AB'C'$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. (Patrik Bak)

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute. Define points $B'$ and $C'$ such that $|B'C| = |AB|$ and $|C'B| = |AC|$, with $B'$ and $C'$ lying on the rays $AC$ and $AB$, respectively. Prove that the circumcenter of triangle $AB'C'$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. (Patrik Bak)

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute. Define points $B'$ and $C'$ such that $|B'C| = |AB|$ and $|C'B| = |AC|$, with $B'$ and $C'$ lying on the rays $CA$ and $AB$, respectively. Prove that the circumcenter of triangle $AB'C'$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. (Patrik Bak)

positive_text:
Suppose there are 10 male and 10 female participants at a gathering. Each female has a preference list of exactly $k$ males, and each male has a preference list of exactly $k$ females. Determine whether there necessarily exists a pair of individuals who mutually like each other. Consider the cases: 

a) $k = 5$, 

b) $k = 6$.

negatives.text:
There are 10 boys and 10 girls at a party. Each girl likes exactly $k$ boys, and each boy dislikes exactly $k$ girls. Is it always possible to find a couple where both the partners like each other? Consider the cases: 

a) $k = 5$, 

b) $k = 6$.

There are 10 boys and 10 girls at a party. Each girl likes at most $k$ boys and each boy likes at most $k$ girls. Is it always possible to find a couple where both the partners like each other? Consider the cases: 

a) $k = 5$, 

b) $k = 6$.

There are 10 boys and 10 girls at a party. Each girl likes exactly $k$ boys, and each boy likes exactly $k$ girls. Is it always possible to find at least two couples where both the partners like each other? Consider the cases: 

a) $k = 5$, 

b) $k = 6$.

positive_text: Let $AB$ be the diameter of a semicircle with center $O$, and let $X$ lie inside the semicircle. Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $XOB$, and let $Y$ be the second point of intersection of line $AX$ with the semicircle. Prove that the segment $YG$ is equal in length to the segment $GB$.

negatives.text: Let $AB$ be the diameter of a semicircle with center $O$, and let $X$ be a point in the interior of the semicircle. Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $XOA$, and let $Y$ be the second point where the line $AX$ intersects the semicircle. Prove that $YG = GB$.

Let $AB$ be the diameter of a semicircle with center $O$, and let $X$ be a point in the interior of the semicircle. Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $XOB$, and let $Y$ be the second point where the line $AX$ intersects the semicircle. Prove that $YG = OG$.

Let $AB$ be the diameter of a semicircle with center $O$, and let $X$ be a point in the interior of the semicircle. Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $XOB$, and let $Y$ be the second point where the line $BX$ intersects the semicircle. Prove that $YG = GB$.

positive_text: Suppose triangle $ABC$ has side lengths $AB = 13$, $BC = 14$, and $CA = 15$. If triangle $A'B'C'$ is obtained by translating triangle $ABC$ along a unit vector, determine the maximum possible area of the overlap between $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = 13$, $BC = 14$, and $CA = 15$. Let triangle $A'B'C'$ be a reflection of $ABC$ across a line of unit length. Find the largest possible area of the intersection of triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = 13$, $BC = 14$, and $CA = 15$. Let triangle $A'B'C'$ be a translate of $ABC$ by a unit vector. Find the smallest possible area of the intersection of triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = 13$, $BC = 14$, and $CA = 15$. Let triangle $A'B'C'$ be a translate of $ABC$ by a unit vector. Find the largest possible area of the union of triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$.

positive_text:
Find all integers $n \ge 3$ such that the polynomial
$$
W(x) = x^n - 3x^{n-1} + 2x^{n-2} + 6
$$
is reducible over $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.

negatives.text:
Find all integers $n \ge 3$ such that the polynomial
$$
W(x) = x^n - 3x^{n-1} + 2x^{n-2} - 6
$$
can be expressed as a product of two polynomials with positive degrees and integer coefficients.

Find all integers $n \ge 3$ such that the polynomial
$$
W(x) = x^n - 3x^{n-1} + 2x^{n-2} + 6
$$
can be expressed as a product of two polynomials with positive degrees and real coefficients.

Find all integers $n \ge 3$ such that the polynomial
$$
W(x) = x^n - 3x^{n-1} + 2x^{n-2} + 6
$$
has a root in $\mathbb{Z}$.

positive_text: Determine the number of ways to distribute $n \ge 1$ distinct balls to nine individuals $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, $I$ such that the number of balls given to $A$ is equal to the total number of balls received by $B$, $C$, $D$, and $E$ combined.

negatives.text: We distribute $n \ge 1$ labelled balls among nine persons $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, $I$. Determine in how many ways it is possible to distribute the balls under the condition that $A$ gets twice the number of balls as the persons $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ together.

We distribute $n \ge 1$ labelled balls among nine persons $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, $I$. Determine in how many ways it is possible to distribute the balls under the condition that $A$ gets the same number of balls as the persons $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ together, with the added condition that each person receives at least one ball.

We distribute $n \ge 1$ labelled balls among nine persons $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, $I$. Determine in how many ways it is possible to distribute the balls under the condition that $A$ gets the same number of balls as the persons $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ together, but only if $n$ is even.

positive_text: There are $n$ children seated in a circle. One child, let's call her Erika, has $n$ candies, and all others have none. The process proceeds in rounds: in each round, any child with at least two candies is allowed to act. Erika selects one such child, and that child gives one candy to each of their two immediate neighbors. The process continues until each child has exactly one candy. For which values of $n \geq 3$ is this possible?

negatives.text: There are $n$ children seated in a circle. Erika starts with $n$ candies, and the others have none. In each round, any child with at least two candies gives one candy to each of their two neighbors. The process ends when all children have at least one candy. For which $n \geq 3$ is this process possible in finite time?

There are $n$ children seated in a circle. Erika has $n$ candies, and all others have none. In each round, any child with at least two candies gives one candy to each of their two neighbors. The process ends when all children have exactly one candy. However, in each round, all such eligible children act simultaneously. For which $n \geq 3$ is this process possible in finite time?

positive_text: Show that for each natural number $k$, there exists some positive integer $n$ such that the decimal expansion of $2^n$ contains a substring consisting of exactly $k$ consecutive zeros, flanked by nonzero digits on both sides.

negatives.text:
Prove, that for every integer $k \ge 1$ there is a positive integer $n$ with the following property: in decimal representation of $2^n$ one can find a block of at least $k$ consecutive zeros, i.e.
$$
2^n = \dots a \overline{00\dots0} b\dots, \quad \text{ $\ge k$ zeros }
$$
where $a$, $b$ are nonzero digits.

Prove, that for every integer $k \ge 1$ there is a positive integer $n$ with the following property: in decimal representation of $3^n$ one can find a block of exactly $k$ consecutive zeros, i.e.
$$
3^n = \dots a \overline{00\dots0} b\dots, \quad \text{ $k$ zeros }
$$
where $a$, $b$ are nonzero digits.

Prove, that for every integer $k \ge 1$ there is a positive integer $n$ with the following property: in decimal representation of $2^n$ one can find a block of exactly $k$ consecutive zeros, i.e.
$$
2^n = \dots a \overline{00\dots0} b\dots, \quad \text{ $k$ zeros }
$$
where $a$, $b$ are digits with $a \le 9$, $b \le 9$.

positive_text: Does there exist a convex pentagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ such that for each $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$, the lines $A_iA_{i+3}$ and $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ intersect at a point $B_i$, and the set $\{B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5\}$ lies on a single straight line? (Indices are cyclic with $A_6 = A_1$, etc.)

negatives.text: Does there exist a convex pentagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ such that for $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$, the lines $A_iA_{i+3}$ and $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ intersect at a point $B_i$, and the points $B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5$ are non-collinear? (Assume $A_6 = A_1$, $A_7 = A_2$, $A_8 = A_3$.)

Does there exist a convex pentagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ such that for $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$, the lines $A_iA_{i+3}$ and $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ intersect at a point $B_i$, and the points $B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5$ are coplanar? (Assume $A_6 = A_1$, $A_7 = A_2$, $A_8 = A_3$.)

Does there exist a convex pentagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ such that for $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$, the lines $A_iA_{i+3}$ and $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ are parallel, and the points $B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5$ are collinear? (Assume $A_6 = A_1$, $A_7 = A_2$, $A_8 = A_3$.)

positive_text: Let $ k $ be the circumcircle of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, where the extensions of $DA$ and $CB$ intersect at a point $E$ such that $|CD|^2 = |AD| \cdot |ED|$. Let $F$ ($F \neq A$) be the second intersection of the circle $k$ with the line perpendicular to $ED$ at $A$. Prove that $AD = CF$ if and only if the circumcenter of triangle $ABE$ lies on $ED$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $DA$ and $CB$ intersecting at a point $E$ such that $|CD|^2 = |AD| \cdot |ED|$. Let $F$ ($F \neq A$) be the second intersection of the circle $k$ with the perpendicular to $ED$ at $A$. Prove that $AD = CF$ if and only if the circumcenter of triangle $ABE$ lies on $EC$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $DA$ and $CB$ intersecting at a point $E$ such that $|CD|^2 = |AD| \cdot |ED|$. Let $F$ ($F \neq A$) be the second intersection of the circle $k$ with the perpendicular to $ED$ at $A$. Prove that $AD = CF$ if and only if the centroid of triangle $ABE$ lies on $ED$.

positive_text: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with equal angles at $A$, $C$, and $E$, and with adjacent sides equal: $AB = BC$, $CD = DE$, $EF = FA$. Show that the lines $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Given a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$, such that $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$ and $AB = BC$, $CD = DE$, $EF = FA$. Prove that the lines $BD$, $CE$, and $FA$ have a common point.
Given a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$, such that $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$ and $AB = BC$, $CD = DE$, $EF = FA$. Prove that the lines $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are parallel.
Given a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$, such that $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$ and $AB = BC$, $CD = DE$, $EF = FA$. Prove that the lines $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ intersect pairwise at three distinct points.

positive_text:
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ be a sequence of positive integers with $1 \le a_i \le 50$. Suppose that for all $n$-tuples of positive integers $b_1, \dots, b_n$, there exists some positive integer $m$ and integers $c_1, \dots, c_n$ such that
$$
 m b_i \equiv c_i^{a_i} \pmod{\mathbb{Z}^+} \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, n.
$$
Prove $n \le 16$ and determine the number of such sequences when $n = 16$.

negatives.text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers with $1 \le a_i \le 50$. Suppose that for all $n$-tuples $b_1, \dots, b_n$ of positive integers, there exists a positive integer $m$ and integers $c_1, \dots, c_n$ such that
$$
 m b_i \equiv c_i^{a_i} \pmod{2} \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, n.
$$
Prove that $n \le 16$ and count the number of such sequences when $n = 16$.

Let $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ be a sequence of positive integers with $1 \le a_i \le 50$. Suppose that for all $n$-tuples $b_1, \dots, b_n$ of positive integers, there exist a positive integer $m$ and integers $c_1, \dots, c_n$ such that
$$
 m b_i \equiv c_i^{a_i} + 1 \pmod{\mathbb{Z}^+} \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, n.
$$
Prove that $n \le 16$ and find the number of such sequences when $n = 16$.

positive_text: The city of Mar del Plata is structured as a square $WSEN$. For an even integer $n$, the city is divided by $2(n + 1)$ one-way streets into a grid of $n \times n$ blocks, each of size 100 m $\times$ 100 m. Adjacent parallel streets are oppositely directed. The $WS$ street runs from $W$ to $S$, and the $WN$ street from $W$ to $N$. A street cleaning car starts at $W$ and aims to reach $E$. What is the longest possible route the car can take, ensuring no 100 m segment is traversed more than once?

negatives.text: The city of Mar del Plata is a square $WSEN$ with $n \times n$ blocks (100 m $\times$ 100 m), for even $n$, divided by $2(n + 1)$ streets. All streets are one-way, with adjacent parallel streets having the same direction. The $WS$ street runs from $W$ to $S$, and the $WN$ street from $W$ to $N$. A cleaning car starts at $W$ and must reach $E$, cleaning roads along the way. What is the maximum route length if no 100 m segment is traversed more than once?

The city of Mar del Plata is a square $WSEN$ with $n \times n$ blocks (100 m $\times$ 100 m), for even $n$, divided by $2(n + 1)$ one-way streets. Adjacent parallel streets have opposite directions. The $WS$ street runs from $W$ to $S$, and the $WN$ street from $W$ to $N$. A cleaning car starts at $W$ and must reach $E$, but now it can traverse each 100 m segment up to two times. What is the maximum route length?

The city of Mar del Plata is a square $WSEN$ with $n \times n$ blocks (100 m $\times$ 100 m), for even $n$, divided by $2(n + 1)$ one-way streets. Adjacent parallel streets have opposite directions. The $WS$ street runs from $W$ to $S$, and the $WN$ street from $W$ to $N$. A cleaning car starts at $W$ and must return to $W$, cleaning roads along the way. What is the maximum route length if no 100 m segment is traversed more than once?

positive_text: Let $x, y, z, w$ be positive real numbers such that $xyzw = 4$ and $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2 = 10$. Find the maximum value of $xy + yz + zw + wx$.

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c, d$ be positive real numbers such that $abcd = 4$ and $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 10$. Find the maximum value of $ab + bc + cd + da + ac + bd$.
Let $a, b, c, d$ be positive real numbers such that $abcd = 4$ and $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 10$. Determine the minimum value of $ab + bc + cd + da$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral such that $CD = BC$, and let $\omega$ be a circle centered at $C$ that is tangent to diagonal $BD$. If $I$ is the incenter of triangle $ABD$, prove that the line through $I$ parallel to side $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$, let $\omega$ be the circle centered at $C$ tangent to $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Show that the line through $I$ parallel to $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$, let $\omega$ be the circle centered at $C$ tangent to $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABD$. Show that the line through $I$ perpendicular to $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$, let $\omega$ be the circle centered at $C$ tangent to $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABD$. Show that the line through $I$ parallel to $AC$ is tangent to $\omega$.

positive_text: An equilateral triangle of side length $n$ is subdivided into a triangular lattice of $n^2$ smaller triangular cells (Fig. 1). Initially, some cells are infected. A cell becomes infected if it has at least two infected neighbors sharing a side. Find the smallest number of initially infected cells needed to ensure all cells become infected for $n = 12$.

negatives.text: An equilateral triangle of side length $n = 12$ is divided into $n^2$ triangular cells via a triangular lattice (Fig. 1). Some cells are infected. A cell becomes infected if it has at least one infected neighbor. Determine the smallest number of initially infected cells such that all cells will eventually be infection.

An equilateral triangle of side length $n = 12$ is divided into $n^2$ triangular cells via a triangular lattice (Fig. 1). Some cells are infected. A cell becomes infected if it is adjacent to at least two infected cells, but only if it is on the boundary of the triangle. Determine the smallest number of initially infected cells such that all cells will eventually be infected.

An equilateral triangle of side length $n = 12$ is divided into $n^2$ triangular cells via a triangular lattice (Fig. 1). Some cells are infected. A cell becomes infected if it is adjacent to at least two infected cells, but only if it is in the interior of the triangle. Determine the smallest number of initially infected cells such that all interior cells will eventually be infected.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be a point on side $BC$. Let $E$ and $F$ be points on the extensions of $AB$ and $AC$ beyond $B$ and $C$ respectively, with $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. Suppose $P$ is a point such that triangle $PEF$ has $D$ as its incenter. Prove that $P$ lies on or inside the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have a point $D$ on side $BC$. Points $E$ and $F$ lie on the lines $AB$ and $AC$ such that $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. If $P$ is such that $D$ is the excenter of triangle $PEF$, prove that $P$ lies inside or on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have a point $D$ on side $BC$. Points $E$ and $F$ lie on the lines $AB$ and $AC$ beyond $B$ and $C$ such that $BE = 2BD$ and $CF = 2CD$. If $P$ is such that $D$ is the incenter of triangle $PEF$, prove that $P$ lies inside or on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have a point $D$ on side $BC$. Points $E$ and $F$ lie on the lines $AB$ and $AC$ beyond $B$ and $C$ such that $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. If $P$ is such that $D$ is the incenter of triangle $PEF$, prove that $P$ lies outside or on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let quadrilateral $ABCD$ satisfy $AB = BC = CD$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on the rays $CA$ and $BD$, respectively, such that $BX = CY$. Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of $BX, CY, XD$, and $YA$, respectively. Show that $P, Q, R, S$ are concyclic.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB = BC = CD$. There are points $X, Y$ on rays $CA, BD$, respectively, such that $BX = CY$. Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of $BX, CY, DX, YA$, respectively. Prove that points $P, Q, R, S$ lie on a circle.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB = BC = CD$. Points $X, Y$ lie on rays $CA, BD$ such that $BX = CY$. Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of $BX, CY, XD, YA$, respectively. Prove that the points $P, Q, R, S$ are collinear.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ satisfying the condition
$$
 f(x + y f(x)) = f(x) f(x + y)
$$
for every $x, y > 0$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ such that for all $x, y > 0$,
$$
 f(x + y f(x)) = f(x) + f(x + y).
$$

Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ such that for all $x, y > 0$,
$$
 f(x + y f(x)) = f(x)^2 f(x + y).
$$

positive_text: Consider a system of $n$ identical spheres arranged between two coaxial cylinders. Each sphere touches both cylinders and its two nearest neighbors. Let $r$ denote the radius of each sphere, and $R$ the radius of the outer cylinder. Show that the ratio $r/R$ is strictly less than $\frac{\pi}{n+\frac{\pi}{n}}$.

negatives.text: A ball bearing consists of two cylinders with the same axis and $n$ equal balls between them. Each ball touches both cylinders and two adjacent balls. Let $r$ be the radius of the balls and $R$ the radius of the outer cylinder. Prove that $r/R < \frac{\pi}{n-\frac{\pi}{n}}$.

A ball bearing consists of two cylinders with the same axis and $n$ equal balls between them. Each ball touches both cylinders and two adjacent balls. Let $r$ be the radius of the balls and $R$ the radius of the outer cylinder. Prove that $r/R > \frac{\pi}{n+\frac{\pi}{n}}$.

A ball bearing consists of two cylinders with the same axis and $n$ equal balls between them. Each ball touches both cylinders and two adjacent balls. Let $r$ be the radius of the balls and $R$ the radius of the outer cylinder. Prove that $r/R < \frac{\pi^2}{n+\frac{\pi}{n}}$.

positive_text: Let the side lengths of a quadrilateral be $x$, $y$, $z$, and $w$, with area $A$. Show that $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2 \ge 4A$. Determine when equality occurs.

negatives.text: Let the sides of a quadrilateral be $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$, and its area be $S$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \le 4S$. When does equality occur?
Let a quadrilateral have side lengths $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$, and area $S$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \ge 4\sqrt{S}$. For which quadrilaterals does equality hold?
Suppose the sides of a quadrilateral are $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$, and its area is $S$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \ge 4S + 1$. When does equality occur?

positive_text: Consider $n \ge 3$ trams in a city, each on a separate line parallel to the $x$-axis. Each tram runs between $x = 0$ and $x = n$ and has length $1$. The first tram moves at speed $1$, the second at speed $2$, ..., the $n$th at speed $n$. Upon reaching either end of its line, a tram immediately reverses direction without changing orientation. At time $t = 0$, the back end of each tram is at $x = 0$. Prove that at no point in time do the trams collectively project to the entire interval $[0, n]$ on the $x$-axis.

negatives.text: In a coordinate city there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines parallel to the $x$-axis such that each line begins from $x$-coordinate $0$ and ends at $x$-coordinate $n$. Exactly one tram of length $1$ is moving on each line: on the first line with speed $1$, on the second line with speed $2$ etc, until on the last line with the speed $n$. When a tram reaches the end of its line it instantly starts moving back without turning around. In the morning all trams start moving at the same time from the starting position where the $x$-coordinate of the back end of the tram is $0$. Prove that the trams' projections onto the $x$-axis always cover the entire interval from $0$ to $n$.

In a coordinate city there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines parallel to the $x$-axis such that each line begins from $x$-coordinate $0$ and ends at $x$-coordinate $n$. Exactly one tram of length $1$ is moving on each line: on the first line with speed $1$, on the second line with speed $2$ etc, until on the last line with the speed $n^2$. When a tram reaches the end of its line it instantly starts moving back without turning around. In the morning all trams start moving at the same time from the starting position where the $x$-coordinate of the back end of the tram is $0$. Prove that the trams' projections onto the $x$-axis never cover the whole interval from $0$ to $n$.

In a coordinate city there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines parallel to the $x$-axis such that each line begins from $x$-coordinate $0$ and ends at $x$-coordinate $n$. Exactly one tram of length $2$ is moving on each line: on the first line with speed $1$, on the second line with speed $2$ etc, until on the last line with the speed $n$. When a tram reaches the end of its line it instantly starts moving back without turning around. In the morning all trams start moving at the same time from the starting position where the $x$-coordinate of the back end of the tram is $0$. Prove that the trams' projections onto the $x$-axis never cover the whole interval from $0$ to $n$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$. Suppose $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ are positive integers such that $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i$ is even and $b_i \le i$ for all $i$. Prove there exists a choice of signs in the expression $b_1 \pm b_2 \pm \dots \pm b_n$ so that the result is $0$.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$. Positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ whose sum is odd and which satisfy $a_i \le i$ for every $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, are given. Prove that it is possible to choose signs in the expression $a_1 \pm a_2 \pm \dots \pm a_n$ in such a way that its value becomes $0$.

Let $n \ge 2$. Positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ whose product is even and which satisfy $a_i \le i$ for every $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, are given. Prove that it is possible to choose signs in the expression $a_1 \pm a_2 \pm \dots \pm a_n$ in such a way that its value becomes $0$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle with side lengths $AB = a$ and $BC = b$, where $a \ge b$. Let $E$ be a point on segment $AB$, not coinciding with $A$ or $B$, such that there is a unique way to select points $F, G, H$ on $BC, CD, DA$ respectively so that $EFGH$ forms a rectangle. Determine the ratio of the area of $EFGH$ to that of $ABCD$.

negatives.text: In a rectangle $ABCD$ with $|AB| = a$ and $|BC| = b$, where $a > b$, let $E$ be a point on side $AB$ such that there are exactly two ways to choose points $F, G, H$ on sides $BC, CD, DA$, respectively, so that $EFGH$ is a rectangle. Find the ratio of the areas of rectangles $EFGH$ and $ABCD$.

In a rectangle $ABCD$ with $|AB| = a$ and $|BC| = b$, where $a \ge b$, let $E$ be a point in the interior of side $AB$ such that there is exactly one possibility to choose points $F, G, H$ on sides $BC, CD, DA$, respectively, so that $EFGH$ is a square. Find the ratio of the areas of rectangles $EFGH$ and $ABCD$.

positive_text: \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{a^2 + bc}{b + c} \geq a + b + c \text{ for all } a, b, c > 0.

negatives.text: \frac{a^2 + bc}{b + c} + \frac{b^2 + ca}{c + a} + \frac{c^2 + ab}{a + b} \leq a + b + c \text{ for all } a, b, c > 0.
\frac{a^2 + bc}{b + c} + \frac{b^2 + ca}{c + a} + \frac{c^2 + ab}{a + b} \geq a + b + c + 1 \text{ for all } a, b, c > 0.
\frac{a^2 + bc}{b + c} + \frac{b^2 + ca}{c + a} + \frac{c^2 + ab}{a + b} \geq ab + bc + ca \text{ for all } a, b, c > 0.

positive_text: Let $\angle ABC$ in a right triangle $ABC$ be an integer number of degrees. Suppose there exists a positive integer $n$ such that one can select points $K_0 = A$, $K_2, \dots, K_{2n}$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ and points $K_1 = C$, $K_3, \dots, K_{2n+1} = B$ on the leg $CB$ so that for each $i = 1, \dots, 2n$, triangle $K_{i-1}K_iK_{i+1}$ is isosceles with base $K_{i-1}K_{i+1}$. Determine all possible values for $\angle ABC$.

negatives.text: Suppose $\angle ABC$ is an integer in a right triangle $ABC$. For some positive integer $n$, points $K_0 = A$, $K_2, \dots, K_{2n}$ lie on the hypotenuse $AB$, and $K_1 = C$, $K_3, \dots, K_{2n+1} = B$ lie on the leg $CB$. If every triangle $K_{i-1}K_iK_{i+1}$, for $i = 1, \dots, 2n$, is isosceles with base $K_{i-1}K_i$, determine all possible values for $\angle ABC$.

Let $\angle ABC$ be an integer in a right triangle $ABC$. Suppose there exists a positive integer $n$ such that points $K_0 = A$, $K_2, \dots, K_{2n}$ lie on the hypotenuse $AB$, and points $K_1 = C$, $K_3, \dots, K_{2n+1} = B$ lie on the leg $CB$. If each triangle $K_{i-1}K_iK_{i+1}$, for $i = 1, \dots, 2n$, is right-angled at $K_i$, determine all possible values of $\angle ABC$.

Let $\angle ABC$ be an integer in a right triangle $ABC$. Suppose there exists a positive integer $n$ such that points $K_0 = A$, $K_2, \dots, K_{2n}$ lie on the hypotenuse $AB$, and points $K_1 = C$, $K_3, \dots, K_{2n+1} = B$ lie on the leg $CB$. If each triangle $K_{i-1}K_iK_{i+1}$, for $i = 1, \dots, 2n$, is equilateral, determine all possible values of $\angle ABC$.

positive_text: Let square $ABCD$ be embedded in the coordinate plane with vertex $A$ on the $x$-axis and vertex $C$ on the $y$-axis. Show that either $B$ or $D$ lies on the line $y = x$ and the remaining one lies on $y = -x$.

negatives.text: A square $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with its vertices $A$ and $C$ lying on the same coordinate axis. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ or $D$ lies on the line $y = x$ and the other one on $y = -x$.

A square $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with its vertices $A$ and $C$ lying on different coordinate axes. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ or $D$ lies on the line $y = x$ and the other one on $y = x$.

A square $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with its vertices $A$ and $C$ lying on different coordinate axes. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ or $D$ lies on the line $y = 2x$ and the other one on $y = -2x$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with circumcircle $\omega$. Suppose point $D$ lies on the arc $AB$ of $\omega$ not containing $C$, and let $A_1$ and $B_1$ be the feet of perpendiculars from $C$ onto $DA$ and $DB$, respectively. Prove that the length of segment $AB$ is greater than or equal to the length of segment $A_1B_1$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with circumcircle $\omega$. Let $D$ be a point on the arc $AB$ not containing $C$, and let $A_1$ and $B_1$ be points on $DA$ and $DB$ such that $CA_1 \parallel DA$ and $CB_1 \parallel DB$. Prove that $AB \ge A_1B_1$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with circumcircle $\omega$. Let $D$ be a point on arc $AB$ not containing $C$, and let $A_1$ and $B_1$ be points on $DA$ and $DB$ such that $CA_1 \perp DA$ and $CB_1 \perp DB$. Prove that $AB^2 \ge A_1B_1^2 + 1$.

positive_text:
Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers such that $2x^2 + y^2 = 9z^2$. Prove that
$$
\frac{2z}{x} + \frac{z}{y} \ge \sqrt{3}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $2a^2 + b^2 = 9c^2$. Prove that
$$
\frac{2c}{a} + \frac{c}{b} \le \sqrt{3}.
$$

Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $2a^2 + b^2 = 9c^2$. Prove that
$$
\frac{2c^2}{a} + \frac{c^2}{b} \ge \sqrt{3}.
$$

Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $a^2 + b^2 = 9c^2$. Prove that
$$
\frac{2c}{a} + \frac{c}{b} \ge \sqrt{3}.
$$

positive_text: Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix with entries from $\{0,1\}$, where $m \le n$, and each row is distinct. Determine the largest integer $k$ such that in any such matrix, it is possible to set $k$ columns entirely to 1 (i.e., color them red) while ensuring all rows remain distinct.

negatives.text: On a square board with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, where $m \le n$, some squares are colored black such that no two rows are alike. Find the biggest integer $k$ such that for every possible coloring to start with one can always color $k$ columns entirely red or black in such a way that no two rows are still alike.

On a square board with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, where $m \le n$, some squares are colored black such that no two rows are alike. Find the biggest integer $k$ such that for every possible coloring to start with one can always color $k$ columns entirely red in such a way that all rows become identical.

On a square board with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, where $m \le n$, some squares are colored black such that no two rows are alike. Find the biggest integer $k$ such that for every possible coloring to start with one can always color $k$ columns entirely red in such a way that the number of distinct rows is at most $m-1$.

positive_text:
Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $|AB| = |AC|$, and let the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersect $AC$ at point $D$.

a) Does the isosceles nature of triangle $BCD$ imply that triangle $ABD$ is also isosceles?

b) Does the isosceles nature of triangle $ABD$ imply that triangle $BCD$ is also isosceles?

negatives.text:
Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $|AB| = |BC|$, and the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $AC$ at $D$.

a) Is triangle $ABD$ isosceles whenever triangle $BCD$ is isosceles?

b) Is triangle $BCD$ isosceles whenever triangle $ABD$ is isosceles?

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $|AB| = |AC|$, and the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects $BC$ at $D$.

a) Is triangle $ABD$ isosceles whenever triangle $BCD$ is isosceles?

b) Is triangle $BCD$ isosceles whenever triangle $ABD$ is isosceles?

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $|AB| = |AC|$, and the bisector of angle $\angle BCA$ intersects $AB$ at $D$.

a) Is triangle $ABD$ isosceles whenever triangle $BCD$ is isosceles?

b) Is triangle $BCD$ isosceles whenever triangle $ABD$ is isosceles?

positive_text:
Jüri wants to construct $n$ circles and several lines in the plane such that all lines pass through a single point, and for any pair of circles, there are two lines that are tangent to both. 

a) Can this construction be achieved for all $n \ge 2$?

b) What values of $n$ allow this to be done if all circles have equal radii?

negatives.text:
Jüri wishes to draw $n$ circles and any number of lines on the plane such that all the lines meet at one point, and for every two circles there exists one line that touches both of these circles.

a) Is it possible for Jüri to solve this problem for any $n \ge 2$?

b) For which natural numbers $n$ is it possible to solve this problem if in addition all the circles must have the same radius?

Jüri wishes to draw $n$ circles and any number of lines on the plane such that all the lines meet at one point, and for every two circles there exist two lines that intersect both of these circles.

a) Is it possible for Jüri to solve this problem for any $n \ge 2$?

b) For which natural numbers $n$ is it possible to solve this problem if in addition all the circles must have the same radius?

Jüri wishes to draw $n$ circles and any number of lines on the plane such that all the lines meet at one point, and for every two circles there exist two lines that intersect both of these circles at least once.

a) Is it possible for Jüri to solve this problem for any $n \ge 2$?

b) For which natural numbers $n$ is it possible to solve this problem if in addition all the circles must have the same radius?

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ lie in the plane, and let the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersect $BC$ at point $P$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$, and let the line $MP$ intersect $AB$ at point $K$. If $\frac{|PC|}{|BP|} = 2$, prove that $AP$ is perpendicular to $CK$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle on the plane. The angle bisector from the vertex $A$ meets the side $BC$ at $P$, and the median from the vertex $B$ meets the side $AC$ at $M$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ meet at the point $K$. Prove that if $\frac{|PC|}{|BP|} = 1$, then $AP$ and $CK$ are perpendicular.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle on the plane. The angle bisector from the vertex $A$ meets the side $BC$ at $P$, and the median from the vertex $B$ meets the side $AC$ at $M$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ meet at the point $K$. Prove that if $\frac{|BP|}{|PC|} = 2$, then $AP$ and $CK$ are perpendicular.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle on the plane. The angle bisector from the vertex $A$ meets the side $BC$ at $P$, and the median from the vertex $B$ meets the side $AC$ at $M$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ meet at the point $K$. Prove that if $\frac{|PC|}{|BP|} = 2$, then $AP$ and $MK$ are perpendicular.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be points on $AB$ and $AC$ (not at the vertices). Show that the circle passing through $A$, $P$, and $Q$ also passes through the circumcenter $O$ of triangle $ABC$ if and only if the segment $AP$ is congruent to the segment $CQ$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, and are not the vertices. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ passes through the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ if and only if $|AP| = |AQ|$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, and are not the vertices. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ passes through the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ if and only if $|AP| = |BQ|$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, and are not the vertices. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ passes through the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ if and only if $|AP| = |AQ| + |CQ|$.

positive_text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Denote by $R_A$, $R_B$, and $R_C$ the circumradii of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$, and $AIB$, respectively, and by $R$ the circumradius of triangle $ABC$. Show that $R_A + R_B + R_C \le 3R$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $R_A$, $R_B$, and $R_C$ be the radii of the circumcircles of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$, and $AIB$, respectively, and $R$ be the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $R_A + R_B + R_C \ge 3R$.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $R_A$, $R_B$, and $R_C$ be the radii of the circumcircles of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$, and $AIB$, respectively, and $R$ be the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $R_A^2 + R_B^2 + R_C^2 \le 3R^2$.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $R_A$, $R_B$, and $R_C$ be the radii of the circumcircles of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$, and $AIB$, respectively, and $R$ be the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $\frac{1}{R_A} + \frac{1}{R_B} + \frac{1}{R_C} \le \frac{3}{R}$.

positive_text: In trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB$ and $CD$, the diagonals intersect at point $P$. Prove that the trapezoid is isosceles if $\frac{|PA|}{|PB|} = \frac{|PD|}{|PC|}$.

negatives.text: In trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB$ and $CD$, the diagonals intersect at point $P$. Prove that if $\frac{|PA|}{|PD|} = \frac{|PC|}{|PB|}$ then the trapezoid is isosceles.
Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with bases $AB$ and $CD$, and diagonals intersecting at point $P$. If $\frac{|PA|}{|PD|} = \frac{|PB|}{|PD|}$, prove that the trapezoid is isosceles.

positive_text: Determine all possible values of $n \mod 6$ such that there exists an integer $m$ with $n^3 - m^2 - m = 1$.

negatives.text: Find all remainders which one can get when dividing by $6$ an integer $n$ which satisfies $n^3 = m^2 - m + 1$ for some integer $m$.
Find all remainders which one can get when dividing by $6$ an integer $n$ which satisfies $n^2 = m^2 + m + 1$ for some integer $m$.
Find all remainders which one can get when dividing by $6$ an integer $n$ which satisfies $n^3 = m^2 + m - 1$ for some integer $m$.

positive_text: Let $x$ and $y$ be positive integers such that $y$ is a multiple of $x$ and concatenating $x$ and $y$ in this order results in $(x + y)^2$. Prove that $\frac{y}{x} = 6$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $b$ is divisible by $a$ and writing $a$ and $b$ one after another in this order gives $(a + b)^3$. Prove that $\frac{b}{a} = 6$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $b$ is divisible by $a$ and writing $b$ and $a$ one after another in this order gives $(a + b)^2$. Prove that $\frac{b}{a} = 6$.
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $b$ is divisible by $a$ and writing $a$ and $b$ one after another in this order gives $a^2 + b^2$. Prove that $\frac{b}{a} = 6$.

positive_text: On a blackboard, the numbers $1$ through $200$ are listed. Juku must assign a plus or minus sign to each number. For every $n$ such that $1 \le n \le 100$, the number $n$ and one of its multiples must be assigned opposite signs. What is the set of numbers to assign minus signs to in order to maximize the final expression's value?

negatives.text: Numbers $1, \dots, 200$ are written on a blackboard in one line. Juku has to write in front of each number plus or minus sign so that for any positive integer $n \le 100$, the number itself and one of its multiples have the same sign. Which numbers must he assign a minus sign in order to get the maximal possible value of the expression?

Numbers $1, \dots, 200$ are written on a blackboard in one line. Juku has to write in front of each number plus or minus sign so that for any positive integer $n \le 100$, the number itself and one of its multiples have different signs. Which numbers must he assign a plus sign in order to get the maximal possible value of the expression?

Numbers $1, \dots, 200$ are written on a blackboard in one line. Juku has to write in front of each number plus or minus sign so that for any positive integer $n \le 100$, the number itself and one of its squares have different signs. Which numbers must he assign a minus sign in order to get the maximal possible value of the expression?

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with altitudes from $A$ and $B$ meeting $BC$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. If the line $CM$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $CDE$ at another point $P$ and the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at another point $Q$, prove that
$$
|MP| = |MQ|.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $D$ and $E$ as the feet of the altitudes from $A$ and $B$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$, and suppose that line $CM$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $CDE$ at point $P$ and the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at point $Q$. Prove that
$$
|MP| = |PQ|.
$$

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $D$ and $E$ as the feet of the altitudes from $A$ and $B$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$, and suppose that line $CM$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $CDE$ at point $P$ and the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at point $Q$. Prove that
$$
|MP| = 2|MQ|.
$$

positive_text: Let $D$ be the point different from $B$ on the hypotenuse $AB$ of a right triangle $ABC$ with $CB = CD$. Let $O$ be the center of the circle passing through $A$, $C$, and $D$. If ray $OD$ meets $CB$ at $P$ and the line through $O$ perpendicular to $AB$ intersects ray $CD$ at $Q$, and $A$, $C$, $P$, $Q$ lie on a circle, does this necessarily mean that $ACPQ$ is a square?
