negatives.text: There is a set of $n$ binary sequences of length 200. Every pair of sequences differ in at least 99 positions. Is it possible that $n \ge 101$?
There is a set of $n$ binary sequences of length 200. Every pair of sequences differ in at most 101 positions. Is it possible that $n \ge 101$?

positive_text: Let $P_1P_2\dots P_n$ be a convex polygon with $n \ge 4$. For each index $i$, define $g(i)$ as the largest angle formed at a vertex $P_j$ such that $\angle P_iP_jP_{i+1}$ is defined and $j \ne i, i+1$ (with $P_{n+1} = P_1$). Determine the minimal total $g(1) + g(2) + \dots + g(n)$ for any such polygon.

negatives.text: Let $A_1A_2\dots A_n$ be a convex polygon with $n \ge 4$. For each $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, define $f(i)$ as the minimum of the angles $\angle A_iA_jA_{i+1}$ where $A_j$ can be any vertex different from $A_i$ and $A_{i+1}$ (with $A_{n+1} = A_1$). Find the maximum possible value of $f(1) + f(2) + \dots + f(n)$.

Let $A_1A_2\dots A_n$ be a convex polygon with $n \ge 4$. For each $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, define $f(i)$ as the maximum of the angles $\angle A_iA_jA_{i+1}$ where $A_j$ is any vertex adjacent to $A_i$ (with $A_{n+1} = A_1$). Find the smallest possible value of $f(1) + f(2) + \dots + f(n)$.

positive_text: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ in acute triangle $\triangle ABC$, and let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AM$. The circumcircle of triangle $\triangle ABD$ meets $BC$ again at a point $E$ distinct from $B$. Let $F$ be a point on segment $AE$ such that $FB = FC$. Show that $F$ lies at the midpoint of $AE$.

negatives.text: Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ of acute triangle $\triangle ABC$, and let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AM$. The circumcircle of triangle $\triangle ABD$ intersects $BC$ again at $E \neq B$. Suppose $F$ is a point on segment $AE$ such that $FB > FC$. Prove that $F$ is the midpoint of $AE$.

Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ of acute triangle $\triangle ABC$, and let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AM$. The circumcircle of triangle $\triangle ABD$ intersects $BC$ again at $E \neq B$. Suppose $F$ is a point on segment $AE$ such that $\angle FBC = \angle FBA$. Prove that $F$ is the midpoint of $AE$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium with $AD \parallel BC$ and $AD > BC$. The side lengths satisfy $AB = CD$. A point $P$ exists in the plane such that the distances from $P$ to $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ are $1$, $2$, $3$, and $4$ respectively. Determine the ratio $AD : BC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium with $AD \parallel BC$, $AD > BC$, and $AB = CD$. A point $P$ in the plane satisfies $PA = 1$, $PB = 2$, $PC = 3$, and $PD = 4$. Suppose $AB = 2CD$ instead of $AB = CD$. Find $AD : BC$.

Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium with $AD \parallel BC$, $AD > BC$, and $AB = CD$. A point $P$ in the plane satisfies $PA = 1$, $PB = 2$, $PC = 3$, and $PD = 4$. Find $AD : BC$ if $AD$ is not parallel to $BC$.

positive_text: \text{Let square } ABCD \text{ contain a point } P \text{ where } \angle APD + \angle BPC = 180^\circ \text{ and } \angle BPC < 90^\circ. \text{ If } PB = 3 \text{ and } PC = 4, \text{ determine the length of side } BC.

negatives.text: \text{ABCD is a square. A point } P \text{ inside } ABCD \text{ satisfies } \angle APD + \angle BPC = 180^\circ \text{ and } \angle BPC > 90^\circ. \text{ If } PB = 3 \text{ and } PC = 4, \text{ find } BC.

\text{ABCD is a square. A point } P \text{ inside } ABCD \text{ satisfies } \angle APD + \angle BPC = 180^\circ \text{ and } \angle BPC \text{ is acute. If } PB = 3 \text{ and } PD = 4, \text{ find } BC.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle BAC = 75^\circ$ and $\angle BCA = 45^\circ$. Extend $BC$ to a point $T$ such that $CT = BC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AT$. Determine $\angle BMC$.

negatives.text: Given $\triangle ABC$, $\angle CAB = 75^\circ$ and $\angle ACB = 45^\circ$. $BC$ is extended to $T$ so that $BC = CT$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the segment $BT$. Find $\angle BMC$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $I$ be the incenter of the triangle. Drop a perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$, meeting it at $D$. Let $E$ be the second intersection point of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $BC$ with the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$. If $\angle MID = \angle C - \angle B$, show that $DE = DI$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $I$ be its incenter. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The line through $A$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersects the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at a point $E$ different from $A$. If $\angle MID = \angle ACB + \angle ABC$, prove that $DE = DI$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $I$ be its incenter. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The line through $A$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersects the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at a point $E$ different from $A$. If $\angle MID = \angle ABC - \angle ACB$, prove that $DE = DI$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $I$ be its incenter. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The line through $A$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersects the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at a point $E$ different from $A$. If $\angle MID = 2(\angle ACB - \angle ABC)$, prove that $DE = DI$.

positive_text: Let $a, b, c$ be positive integers, with $b$ and $c$ not exceeding $2023$, such that $a - b = 2c$ and $(a^2 + c^2)(b^2 + c^2)$ is divisible by $17^2$. How many ordered triples $(a, b, c)$ satisfy these conditions?

negatives.text: Let $u, v, w$ be positive integers, with $v$ and $w$ not exceeding $2023$, such that $u - v = 2w$ and $(u^2 - w^2)(v^2 + w^2)$ is divisible by $289$. How many sets of possible values of $(u, v, w)$ are there?

Let $u, v, w$ be positive integers, with $v$ and $w$ not exceeding $2023$, such that $u + v = 2w$ and $(u^2 + w^2)(v^2 + w^2)$ is divisible by $289$. How many sets of possible values of $(u, v, w)$ are there?

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, where $AB < AC$, let $AD$ be the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meeting $BC$ at $D$. Let $\Gamma$ be a circle passing through $A$ and $D$ that is tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Let $E$ be the second intersection of $\Gamma$ with $AB$, and let $F$ be the second point of intersection of the tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle BDE$ at $D$ with $\Gamma$. If $P$ is the intersection of $EF$ and $AC$, show that $PD$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ with $AB < AC$, let $AD$ be the bisector of $\angle BAC$ with $D$ on $BC$. Let $\Gamma$ be a circle passing through $A$ and $D$ which is tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Suppose $\Gamma$ cuts the side $AB$ again at $E \neq A$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle BDE$ at $D$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F \neq D$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the segments $EF$ and $AB$. Prove that $PD$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ with $AB < AC$, let $AD$ be the bisector of $\angle BAC$ with $D$ on $BC$. Let $\Gamma$ be a circle passing through $A$ and $D$ which is tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Suppose $\Gamma$ cuts the side $AB$ again at $E \neq A$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle BDE$ at $D$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F \neq D$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the segments $EF$ and $AC$. Prove that $PF$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ with $AB < AC$, let $AD$ be the bisector of $\angle BAC$ with $D$ on $BC$. Let $\Gamma$ be a circle passing through $A$ and $D$ which is tangent to $BC$ at $D$. Suppose $\Gamma$ cuts the side $AB$ again at $E \neq A$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle BDE$ at $E$ intersects $\Gamma$ again at $F \neq E$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the segments $EF$ and $AC$. Prove that $PD$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

positive_text: Given an equilateral triangle $ABC$ and a point $P$ inside it such that $AP = 15$ and $BP = 8$, determine the maximum possible value of the total area of triangles $ABP$ and $BCP$.

negatives.text: A point $P$ lies inside an equilateral triangle $ABC$ such that $AP = 15$ and $BP = 8$. Find the maximum possible value of the product of the areas of triangles $ABP$ and $BCP$.
A point $P$ lies outside an equilateral triangle $ABC$ such that $AP = 15$ and $BP = 8$. Find the maximum possible value of the sum of the areas of triangles $ABP$ and $BCP$.
A point $P$ lies inside an equilateral triangle $ABC$ such that $AP = 15$ and $BP = 8$. Find the maximum possible value of the sum of the perimeters of triangles $ABP$ and $BCP$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = 5$, $AD = 17$, and $CD = 6$. Suppose the internal angle bisectors of $\angle DAB$ and $\angle CDA$ meet at the center point of segment $BC$. Determine the area of quadrilateral $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = 5$, $AD = 17$, and $CD = 6$. If the angle bisectors of $\angle BAD$ and $\angle ADC$ intersect at the midpoint of $BD$, find the area of $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = 5$, $AD = 17$, and $CD = 6$. If the external angle bisectors of $\angle BAD$ and $\angle ADC$ intersect at the midpoint of $BC$, find the area of $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = 5$, $AD = 17$, and $CD = 6$. If the angle bisectors of $\angle BAD$ and $\angle ADC$ intersect at the centroid of triangle $ABC$, find the area of $ABCD$.

positive_text: How many solutions exist for $\frac{\ln x}{\ln 3} = 3 \sin(3\pi x)$?

negatives.text: How many solutions are there to the equation $\log_3 x = 3 \cos(3\pi x)$?
How many solutions are there to the equation $\log_3 x = 3 \sin(\pi x)$?
How many solutions are there to the equation $\log_3 x = 3 \sin^2(3\pi x)$?

positive_text: Let $b_{0}$ be an arbitrary real number and define $b_{i+1} = \left\lfloor b_{i} \right\rfloor \cdot (b_{i} - \left\lfloor b_{i} \right\rfloor)$ for all $i \geq 0$. Show that $b_{i} = b_{i+2}$ for sufficiently large $i$.

negatives.text: Let $e_{0}$ be a real number, and define $e_{i+1} = \left\lfloor e_{i} \right\rfloor + (e_{i} - \left\lfloor e_{i} \right\rfloor)$ for $i \geq 0$. Prove that $e_{i} = e_{i+2}$ for sufficiently large $i$.

Let $f_{0}$ be a real number, and define $f_{i+1} = \left\lfloor f_{i} \right\rfloor \cdot (f_{i} - \left\lfloor f_{i} \right\rfloor)^2$ for $i \geq 0$. Prove that $f_{i} = f_{i+2}$ for sufficiently large $i$.

Let $g_{0}$ be a real number, and define $g_{i+1} = \left\lfloor g_{i} \right\rfloor \cdot (\left\lfloor g_{i} \right\rfloor + 1)$ for $i \geq 0$. Prove that $g_{i} = g_{i+2}$ for sufficiently large $i$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB > CD$. Let points $K$ and $L$ be on $AB$ and $CD$ such that $\frac{AK}{KB} = \frac{DL}{LC}$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be points on $KL$ such that $\angle APB = \angle BCD$ and $\angle CQD = \angle ABC$. Show that $P$, $Q$, $B$, and $C$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB > CD$. Points $K$ and $L$ lie on $AB$ and $CD$ such that $\frac{AK}{KB} = \frac{DL}{LC}$. Suppose that there are points $P$ and $Q$ on $KL$ satisfying $\angle APB = \angle BCD$ and $\angle CQD = \angle BAC$. Prove that points $P$, $Q$, $B$, and $C$ are concyclic.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle A < 90^\circ$ and $\angle C < \angle A$. A point $D$ lies on side $AC$ such that $BD = BA$. Suppose the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $AB$ and $AC$ at $K$ and $L$, respectively. If $J$ is the incenter of triangle $BCD$, prove that the line $KL$ intersects $AJ$ at its midpoint.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $\angle A < 90^\circ$ and $\angle C < \angle A$. Place point $D$ on side $AC$ such that $BD = BC$. Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch $AB$ and $AC$ at $K$ and $L$, and let $J$ be the incenter of triangle $BCD$. Prove that the line $KL$ intersects segment $AJ$ at its midpoint.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $\angle A < 90^\circ$ and $\angle C < \angle A$. Place point $D$ on side $AC$ such that $BD = BA$. Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch $AB$ and $AC$ at $K$ and $L$, and let $J$ be the incenter of triangle $BCD$. Prove that the line $KL$ intersects segment $BJ$ at its midpoint.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $\angle A < 90^\circ$ and $\angle C < \angle A$. Place point $D$ on side $AC$ such that $BD = BA$. Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch $AB$ and $AC$ at $K$ and $L$, and let $J$ be the incenter of triangle $BCD$. Prove that the line $KL$ intersects segment $AJ$ at a point one-third of the way from $A$ to $J$.

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. Two circles, one passing through $A$ and $D$, and the other passing through $B$ and $C$, are externally tangent at a point $P$ located inside $ABCD$. If
$$
\angle PAB + \angle PDC \leq 90^\circ \quad \text{ and } \quad \angle PBA + \angle PCD \leq 90^\circ,
$$
show that $AB + CD \geq BC + AD$.

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. A circle passing through the points $A$ and $D$ and a circle passing through the points $B$ and $C$ are internally tangent at a point $P$ inside the quadrilateral. Suppose that
$$
\angle PAB + \angle PDC \leq 90^\circ \quad \text{ and } \quad \angle PBA + \angle PCD \leq 90^\circ.
$$
Prove that $AB + CD \geq BC + AD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. A circle passing through the points $A$ and $D$ and a circle passing through the points $B$ and $C$ are externally tangent at a point $P$ inside the quadrilateral. Suppose that
$$
\angle PAB + \angle PDC \leq 90^\circ \quad \text{ and } \quad \angle PBA + \angle PCD \leq 90^\circ.
$$
Prove that $AB + CD > BC + AD$.

positive_text:
Let $p > q > 1$ be relatively prime positive integers. Define the weight of an integer $c$, denoted by $w(c)$, to be the minimal value of $|x| + |y|$ such that there exist integers $x$ and $y$ satisfying $p x + q y = c$.
An integer $c$ is said to be a local champion if $w(c) \geq w(c \pm p)$ and $w(c) \geq w(c \pm q)$.
Determine all such local champions and the total number of them.

negatives.text:
Let $a > b > 1$ be relatively prime positive integers. Define the weight of an integer $c$, denoted by $w(c)$, to be the minimal possible value of $|x| + |y|$ taken over all pairs of integers $x$ and $y$ such that
$$
a x + b y = c.
$$
An integer $c$ is called a local champion if $w(c) > w(c \pm a)$ and $w(c) > w(c \pm b)$.
Find all local champions and determine their number.

Let $a > b > 1$ be relatively prime positive integers. Define the weight of an integer $c$, denoted by $w(c)$, to be the minimal possible value of $|x| + |y|$ taken over all pairs of integers $x$ and $y$ such that
$$
a x - b y = c.
$$
An integer $c$ is called a local champion if $w(c) \geq w(c \pm a)$ and $w(c) \geq w(c \pm b)$.
Find all local champions and determine their number.

Let $a > b > 1$ be relatively prime positive integers. Define the weight of an integer $c$, denoted by $w(c)$, to be the minimal possible value of $|x| + |y|$ taken over all pairs of integers $x$ and $y$ such that
$$
2a x + 2b y = c.
$$
An integer $c$ is called a local champion if $w(c) \geq w(c \pm a)$ and $w(c) \geq w(c \pm b)$.
Find all local champions and determine their number.

positive_text:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be such that for all $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$, the inequality
$$
 f(a+b) \geq f(a) + f(f(b)) - 1
$$
holds. Determine all possible values of $f(2007)$.

negatives.text:
Find all possible values of $f(2007)$ for functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ satisfying the condition
$$
 f(m+n) \leq f(m) + f(f(n)) - 1
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be such that for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, the inequality
$$
 f(m+n) \geq f(m) + f(f(n)) + 1
$$
holds. Determine all possible values of $f(2007)$.

Find all possible values of $f(2007)$ for functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ satisfying the condition
$$
 f(m+n) \geq f(m) + f(n)^2 - 1
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$.

positive_text: Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Find all binary sequences $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n^{2}+n}$ such that the sum of any $n$ consecutive terms in the first $n^{2}-n+1$ blocks is strictly less than the sum of the next $n$ consecutive terms in that block.

negatives.text: Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Find all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n^{2}+n}$ such that $a_{i} \in \{0,1\}$ for all $i$ and $a_{i+1}+a_{i+2}+\ldots+a_{i+n} > a_{i+n+1}+a_{i+n+2}+\ldots+a_{i+2n}$ for all $0 \leq i \leq n^{2}-n$.

Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Find all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n^{2}+n}$ such that $a_{i} \in \{0,1\}$ for all $i$ and $a_{i+1}^{2}+a_{i+2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{i+n}^{2} < a_{i+n+1}^{2}+a_{i+n+2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{i+2n}^{2}$ for all $0 \leq i \leq n^{2}-n$.

positive_text: Given a unit square partitioned into $n>1$ rectangles with sides parallel to the square’s sides, suppose every line parallel to a side of the square that intersects the square’s interior also intersects the interior of one of the rectangles. Show that at least one rectangle lies entirely in the interior of the square.

negatives.text: A unit square is dissected into $n>1$ rectangles with sides parallel to the square’s sides. Any line parallel to a side of the square and intersecting its interior also intersects the interior of some rectangle. Prove that in this dissection, there exists a rectangle with at least one point on the boundary of the square.

A unit square is dissected into $n>1$ rectangles with sides parallel to the square’s sides. Any line parallel to a side of the square and intersecting its interior also intersects the interior of some rectangle. Prove that in this dissection, there exists a rectangle with all sides on the boundary of the square.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $X$ be a variable point on the shorter arc $AM$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABM$. Let $T$ be a point in the interior of $\angle BMA$ such that $TX = BX$ and $\angle TMX = 90^\circ$. Prove that the difference $\angle MTB - \angle CTM$ is constant with respect to the position of $X$.

negatives.text: In isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $X$ be a point on the shorter arc $MA$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABM$. Define $T$ such that $TX = BX$ and $\angle TMX = 80^\circ$, with $T$ located in the domain of $\angle BMA$. Prove that $\angle MTB - \angle CTM$ does not depend on the position of $X$.

positive_text: Find the minimal positive real number $k$ such that the following condition holds for any convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}, D_{1}$ on $AB, BC, CD, DA$ respectively. Let $S$ denote the sum of the two smallest areas among $\triangle AA_{1}D_{1}, \triangle BB_{1}A_{1}, \triangle CC_{1}B_{1}, \triangle DD_{1}C_{1}$, and let $S_{1}$ be the area of quadrilateral $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}D_{1}$. Then the inequality $k S_{1} \geq S$ always holds.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral, and let points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}, D_{1}$ lie on sides $AB, BC, CD, DA$, respectively. Consider the areas of triangles $\triangle AA_{1}D_{1}, \triangle BB_{1}A_{1}, \triangle CC_{1}B_{1}, \triangle DD_{1}C_{1}$; let $S$ be the sum of the two largest ones, and let $S_{1}$ be the area of quadrilateral $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}D_{1}$. Find the smallest positive real number $k$ such that $k S_{1} \geq S$.

positive_text:
Let $w$, $x$, $y$, $z$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
wx y z = 1 \quad \text{ and } \quad w + x + y + z > \frac{w}{x} + \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{w}
$$
Prove that
$$
w + x + y + z < \frac{x}{w} + \frac{y}{x} + \frac{z}{y} + \frac{w}{z}
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
abcd = 1 \quad \text{ and } \quad a + b + c + d > \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} + \frac{d}{a}
$$
Prove that
$$
a + b + c + d < \frac{b}{a^2} + \frac{c}{b^2} + \frac{d}{c^2} + \frac{a}{d^2}
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
abcd = 1 \quad \text{ and } \quad a + b + c + d > \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} + \frac{d}{a}
$$
Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} + \frac{1}{d} < \frac{b}{a} + \frac{c}{b} + \frac{d}{c} + \frac{a}{d}
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
abcd = 1 \quad \text{ and } \quad a + b + c + d > \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{d} + \frac{d}{a}
$$
Prove that
$$
a + b + c + d < \frac{b}{a} + \frac{c}{b} + \frac{d}{c} + \frac{a}{d} + 1
$$

positive_text: \text{Let } a, b, c, d > 0. \text{ Show that} \quad \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{a+b+c} \geq 0 \quad \text{and characterize when equality holds.}

negatives.text: \text{For positive real numbers } a, b, c, d, \text{ prove or disprove} \quad \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{a+b-c} + \frac{(b-c)(b-d)}{b+c-d} + \frac{(c-d)(c-a)}{c+d-a} + \frac{(d-a)(d-b)}{d+a-b} \geq 0.

\text{For positive real numbers } a, b, c, d, \text{ show that} \quad \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{a+b+c} + \frac{(b-c)(b-d)}{b+c+d} + \frac{(c-d)(c-a)}{c+d+a} + \frac{(d-a)(d-b)}{d+a+b} \leq 0 \quad \text{and determine when equality holds.}

\text{Given positive real numbers } a, b, c, d, \text{ prove} \quad \frac{(a-b)^2(a-c)}{a+b+c} + \frac{(b-c)^2(b-d)}{b+c+d} + \frac{(c-d)^2(c-a)}{c+d+a} + \frac{(d-a)^2(d-b)}{d+a+b} \geq 0 \quad \text{and find when equality occurs.}

positive_text:
Find all functions $f$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, the identity
$$
\ f(a f(a + b)) = f(b f(a)) + a^2
$$
holds.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying for all real $x, y$ the identity
$$
\ f(x f(x + y)) = f(y f(x)) - x^2 .
$$

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying for all real $x, y$ the identity
$$
\ f(x f(x + y)) = f(y f(x)) + y^2 .
$$

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying for all real $x, y$ the identity
$$
\ f(x f(x + y)) = f(y f(x)) + x^3 .
$$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have an incircle touching $AB$ at $Z$ and $AC$ at $Y$. Let $G$ be the intersection point of lines $BY$ and $CZ$. Define points $R$ and $S$ such that $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are parallelograms. Show that $GR = GS$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have an incircle touching $AB$ at $Z$ and $AC$ at $Y$. Let $G$ be the intersection of $BY$ and $CZ$, and let $R$ and $S$ be points such that $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are rectangles. Prove that $GR = GS$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have an incircle touching $AB$ at $Z$ and $AC$ at $Y$. Let $G$ be the intersection of $BY$ and $CZ$, and let $R$ and $S$ be points such that $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are parallelograms. Prove that $GR > GS$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have an incircle touching $AB$ at $Z$ and $AC$ at $Y$. Let $G$ be the intersection of $BY$ and $CZ$, and let $R$ and $S$ be points such that $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are parallelograms. Prove that $GR = GS$ in the case where $ABC$ is equilateral.

positive_text:
Suppose $P$ is a convex polygon with a point $O$ such that $P$ is centrally symmetric about $O$. Show that there exists a parallelogram $R$ containing $P$ such that
$$
\frac{\text{Area}(R)}{\text{Area}(P)} \leq \sqrt{2}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $P$ be a convex polygon symmetric to some point $O$. Prove that for some parallelogram $R$ satisfying $P \subset R$ we have
$$
\frac{|R|}{|P|} \leq \sqrt{3}.
$$

Let $P$ be a convex polygon symmetric to some point $O$. Prove that for some parallelogram $R$ satisfying $P \subset R$ we have
$$
\frac{|R|}{|P|} < \sqrt{2}.
$$

Let $P$ be a convex polygon symmetric to some point $O$. Prove that for some parallelogram $R$ satisfying $P \subset R$ we have
$$
\frac{|R|}{|P|} \leq 2.
$$

positive_text: \text{In a round-robin tennis tournament with } n \geq 4 \text{ players, each pair plays once with no ties. A group of four players is termed bad if one is defeated by the other three, and each of the three has one win and one loss among themselves. If no bad groups exist, and } w_i, \ell_i \text{ are the number of wins and losses for player } i, \text{ prove that} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(w_i - \ell_i\right)^3 \geq 0

negatives.text: \text{In a tennis tournament with } n \geq 4 \text{ players, each pair plays once with no ties. A set of four players is called bad if one player is defeated by the other three, and each of the three has one win and one loss among themselves. If there are no bad companies, let } w_i, \ell_i \text{ be the win and loss counts for player } i. \text{ Prove that} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(w_i - \ell_i\right)^3 \leq 0

\text{In a tennis tournament with } n \geq 4 \text{ players, each pair plays once with no ties. A set of four players is called bad if one player is defeated by the other three, and each of the three has one win and one loss among themselves. If there are no bad companies, let } w_i, \ell_i \text{ be the win and loss counts for player } i. \text{ Prove that} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(w_i + \ell_i\right)^3 \geq 0

\text{In a tennis tournament with } n \geq 4 \text{ players, each pair plays once with no ties. A set of four players is called bad if one player is defeated by the other three, and each of the three has one win and one loss among themselves. If there are no bad companies, let } w_i, \ell_i \text{ be the win and loss counts for player } i. \text{ Prove that} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(w_i - \ell_i\right)^2 \geq 0

positive_text:
Let $\mathcal{P}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{P}_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers, satisfying:
(1) every integer lies in at least one of them;
(2) for each $i$, there exists an integer in $\mathcal{P}_{i}$ that is not in any other $\mathcal{P}_{j}$, $j \neq i$.
Let $n$ be the least common multiple of the steps of these progressions, with prime factorization $n = p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \cdots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$. Prove that
$$
 s \geq 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}(p_{i} - 1)
$$

negatives.text:
Let $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers, the following conditions being satisfied:
(i) each integer belongs to at least one of them;
(ii) each progression contains a number which does not belong to other progressions.
Denote by $n$ the least common multiple of steps of these progressions; let $n=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$ be its prime factorization. Prove that
$$
 s \leq 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}(p_{i} - 1)
$$

Let $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers, the following conditions being satisfied:
(i) each integer belongs to at least one of them;
(ii) each progression contains a number which does not belong to other progressions.
Denote by $n$ the least common multiple of steps of these progressions; let $n=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$ be its prime factorization. Prove that
$$
 s \geq 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}(p_{i} + 1)
$$

Let $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers, the following conditions being satisfied:
(i) each integer belongs to at least one of them;
(ii) each progression contains a number which does not belong to other progressions.
Denote by $n$ the least common multiple of steps of these progressions; let $n=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$ be its prime factorization. Prove that
$$
 s \geq 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} (\alpha_{i} + 1)(p_{i} - 1)
$$

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$. The internal bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets the circumcircle of triangle $DBC$ at a point $E$ distinct from $B$ and $C$. The line $BD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $AEB$ at a point $F$ distinct from $B$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ intersect at a point $I$, and the lines $CI$ and $BD$ intersect at a point $K$. Prove that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$. The external bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects the circle through $D$, $B$, and $C$ in a point $E$ outside the triangle $ABC$. The line $BD$ intersects the circle through $A$, $E$, and $B$ in two points $B$ and $F$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ meet at a point $I$, and the lines $CI$ and $BD$ meet at a point $K$. Show that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects the circle through $D$, $B$, and $C$ in a point $E$ inside the triangle $ABC$. The line $CD$ intersects the circle through $A$, $E$, and $B$ in two points $B$ and $F$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ meet at a point $I$, and the lines $CI$ and $BD$ meet at a point $K$. Show that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects the circle through $D$, $B$, and $C$ in a point $E$ inside the triangle $ABC$. The line $BD$ intersects the circle through $A$, $E$, and $B$ in two points $B$ and $F$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ meet at a point $I$, and the lines $BI$ and $CD$ meet at a point $K$. Show that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

positive_text: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with all sides tangent to a circle $\omega$ centered at $O$. Suppose the circumcircle of triangle $ACE$ coincides in center with $\omega$. Let $J$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $CD$. Suppose that the perpendicular from $B$ to $DF$ intersects the line $EO$ at a point $K$. Let $L$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $K$ to $DE$. Prove that the lengths $DJ$ and $DL$ are equal.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with all sides tangent to a circle $\omega$ centered at $O$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $ACE$ has the same center as $\omega$. Let $J$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $CD$. Suppose that the perpendicular from $B$ to $DF$ intersects the line $EO$ at a point $K$. Let $L$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $K$ to $EF$. Prove that $DJ = DL$.

Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with all sides tangent to a circle $\omega$ centered at $O$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $ACE$ has the same center as $\omega$. Let $J$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $CD$. Suppose that the perpendicular from $B$ to $DF$ intersects the line $EO$ at a point $K$. Let $L$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $K$ to $DE$. Prove that $DJ < DL$.

Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with all sides tangent to a circle $\omega$ centered at $O$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $ACE$ has the same center as $\omega$. Let $J$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $CD$. Suppose that the perpendicular from $B$ to $DF$ intersects the line $EO$ at a point $K$. Let $L$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $K$ to $DE$. Prove that $DJ + DL = 2DO$.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive integer and define $n = 2^{k} + 1$. Show that $n$ is prime if and only if there exists a sequence $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n-1}$ containing each integer from $1$ to $n-1$ exactly once, and a sequence $g_{1}, \ldots, g_{n-1}$, such that $g_{i}^{a_{i}} \equiv a_{i+1} \pmod{n}$ for all $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,n-1\}$, with $a_{n} = a_{1}$.

negatives.text: Let $k$ be a positive integer and define $n = 2^k + 1$. Prove that $n$ is prime if and only if there exists a permutation $a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1}$ of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n-1\}$ and a sequence $g_1, \ldots, g_{n-1}$ such that $n$ divides $g_i^{a_i} + a_{i+1}$ for all $i$, with $a_n = a_1$.

Let $k$ be a positive integer and define $n = 2^k + 1$. Prove that $n$ is prime if and only if there exists a permutation $a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1}$ of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n-1\}$ and a sequence $g_1, \ldots, g_{n-1}$ such that $n$ divides $g_i^{a_{i+1}} - a_i$ for all $i$, with $a_n = a_1$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a right triangle with $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$, and let $C_0$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. Let $X$ lie in the interior of segment $CC_0$, and let $K, L$ be points on segments $AX, BX$ such that $BK = BC$ and $AL = AC$, respectively. Let $M$ be the intersection of $AL$ and $BK$. Prove that $MK = ML$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, and let $C_0$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Choose a point $X$ in the interior of the segment $CC_0$, and let $K, L$ be the points on the segments $AX, BX$ for which $BK = BC$ and $AL = AC$ respectively. Denote by $M$ the intersection of $AL$ and $BK$. Show that $MK = KL$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, and let $C_0$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Choose a point $X$ in the interior of the segment $CC_0$, and let $K, L$ be the points on the segments $AX, BX$ for which $BK = BC$ and $AL = AB$ respectively. Denote by $M$ the intersection of $AL$ and $BK$. Show that $MK = ML$.

positive_text:
Let $S$ be a set of $2000$ distinct real numbers. Show that there are two distinct pairs $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ with $a > b$ and $c > d$ such that
$$
\left|\frac{a-b}{c-d}-1\right|<\frac{1}{100000}
$$

negatives.text:
Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a > b$ and $c > d$ with $a \neq c$ or $b \neq d$, such that
$$
\left|\frac{a-b}{c-d}+1\right|<\frac{1}{100000}
$$

Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a > b$ and $c > d$ with $a \neq c$ or $b \neq d$, such that
$$
\left|\frac{a-b}{c-d}-1\right|<\frac{1}{1000}
$$

Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a > b$ and $c > d$ with $a \neq c$ or $b \neq d$, such that
$$
\left|\frac{a-b}{c-d}-\frac{1}{2}\right|<\frac{1}{100000}
$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An $A$-partition of $n$ into $k$ parts is a representation of $n$ as $n = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_k$, where each $a_i \in A$. The number of different parts in the partition is the number of distinct elements in $\{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k\}$. An $A$-partition is called optimal if no $A$-partition of $n$ has fewer than $k$ parts. Prove that any optimal $A$-partition of $n$ has at most $\sqrt[3]{6n}$ distinct parts.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer and $A$ a subset of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. An $A$-partition of $n$ into $k$ parts is a decomposition $n = a_1 + \cdots + a_k$ with $a_i \in A$. The number of distinct parts is the size of $\{a_1, \dots, a_k\}$. An optimal $A$-partition is one with the fewest parts. Prove that any optimal $A$-partition of $n$ has at most $\sqrt{6n}$ distinct parts.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and $A$ a subset of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. An $A$-partition of $n$ into $k$ parts is a decomposition $n = a_1 + \cdots + a_k$ with $a_i \in A$. The number of distinct parts is the size of $\{a_1, \dots, a_k\}$. An optimal $A$-partition is one with the fewest parts. Prove that any optimal $A$-partition of $n$ has at least $\sqrt[3]{6n}$ distinct parts.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and $A$ a subset of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. An $A$-partition of $n$ into $k$ parts is a decomposition $n = a_1 + \cdots + a_k$ with $a_i \in A$. The number of distinct parts is the size of $\{a_1, \dots, a_k\}$. An optimal $A$-partition is one with the fewest parts. Prove that any optimal $A$-partition of $n$ has at most $\sqrt[3]{6n^2}$ distinct parts.

positive_text: Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular arrangements of the numbers $0,1, \ldots, n$, identifying arrangements that are rotations of each other. An arrangement is called beautiful if, for any four distinct numbers $0 \leqslant a, b, c, d \leqslant n$ such that $a + c = b + d$, the chords connecting $a$ and $c$ and $b$ and $d$ do not intersect. Let $M$ be the number of beautiful arrangements of $0,1, \ldots, n$. Let $N$ be the number of coprime pairs ($x, y$) of positive integers with $x + y \leqslant n$. Prove that $$ M = N + 1. $$

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular arrangements of the numbers $0,1, \ldots, n$, identifying rotations. An arrangement is called beautiful if for any four distinct numbers $0 \leqslant a, b, c, d \leqslant n$ with $a + c = b + d$, the chords joining $a$ and $c$ and $b$ and $d$ do not cross. Let $M$ be the number of beautiful arrangements. Let $N$ be the number of pairs ($x, y$) of positive integers such that $x + y \leqslant n$ and $\operatorname{gcd}(x, y) = 1$. Prove that $$ M = N. $$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular arrangements of the numbers $0,1, \ldots, n$, up to rotation. An arrangement is called beautiful if for any four distinct numbers $0 \leqslant a, b, c, d \leqslant n$ with $a + c = b + d$, the chords joining $a$ and $c$ and $b$ and $d$ intersect. Let $M$ be the number of beautiful arrangements. Let $N$ be the number of pairs ($x, y$) of positive integers such that $x + y \leqslant n$ and $\operatorname{gcd}(x, y) = 1$. Prove that $$ M = N + 1. $$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular arrangements of the numbers $0,1, \ldots, n$, where rotations are considered equal. An arrangement is called beautiful if for any four distinct numbers $0 \leqslant a, b, c, d \leqslant n$ with $a + c = b + d$, the chords joining $a$ and $c$ and $b$ and $d$ do not intersect. Let $M$ be the number of beautiful arrangements. Let $N$ be the number of pairs ($x, y$) of positive integers such that $x + y = n$ and $\operatorname{gcd}(x, y) = 1$. Prove that $$ M = N + 1. $$

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ satisfy $\angle B > \angle C$. Place points $P$ and $Q$ on the line $AC$ such that $\angle PBA = \angle QBA = \angle ACB$, with $A$ lying between $P$ and $C$. If there exists a point $D$ on segment $BQ$ such that $\angle PBD = \angle DPB$, and ray $AD$ meets the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ again at $R$, prove that $QR = QB$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle B > \angle C$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on the line $AC$ with $\angle PBA = \angle QBA = \angle ACB$ and $A$ between $P$ and $C$. Suppose $D$ is a point on segment $BQ$ such that $PD = PB$. Let ray $AD$ intersect the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $R$. Prove that $PR = QR$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be such that $\angle B > \angle C$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on the line $AC$ such that $\angle PBA = \angle QBA = \angle ACB$ and $A$ is between $P$ and $C$. Let $D$ be a point on segment $BQ$ such that $PD = QB$. Ray $AD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $R$. Prove that $QR = QB$.

positive_text: Let $PQRSTU$ be a convex hexagon such that $PQ = TU$, $QR = UV$, $RS = VP$, and $\angle P - \angle U = \angle R - \angle V = \angle T - \angle Q$. Prove that the lines $PR$, $QS$, and $RT$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $AB C D E F$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = DE$, $BC = EF$, $CD = FA$, and $\angle A + \angle D = \angle C + \angle F = \angle E + \angle B$. Prove that the diagonals $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are concurrent.

Let $AB C D E F$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = DE$, $BC = EF$, $CD = FA$, and $\angle A - \angle D = \angle C - \angle F = \angle B - \angle E$. Prove that the diagonals $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are concurrent.

Let $AB C D E F$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = DE$, $BC = EF$, $CD = FA$, and $\angle A - \angle D = 2(\angle C - \angle F) = \angle E - \angle B$. Prove that the diagonals $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. On an $n \times n$ board, place $n$ rooks such that each row and each column contains exactly one rook. Such a placement is termed a permutation configuration. Determine the maximum integer $k$ such that every permutation configuration guarantees the existence of an empty $k \times k$ subgrid.

negatives.text: Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. Consider an $n \times n$ chessboard with $n$ rooks placed such that each row and column contains exactly one rook. Find the greatest positive integer $k$ such that there exists a $k \times k$ square with at least one rook in it.

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. Consider an $n \times n$ chessboard with $n$ rooks placed such that each row and column contains exactly one rook. Find the greatest positive integer $k$ such that for every configuration, every $k \times k$ square contains at least one rook.

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer. Consider an $n \times n$ chessboard with $n$ rooks placed such that each row and column contains exactly one rook. Find the greatest positive integer $k$ such that there exists a configuration where no $k \times k$ square is entirely empty.

positive_text: Suppose $n \geq 3$ lines are drawn in the plane, with no two being parallel and no three intersecting at a single point. These lines partition the plane into various regions, and let $\mathcal{F}$ denote the set of regions with finite area. Show that it is possible to select and colour $\lceil\sqrt{n / 2}\rceil$ lines blue such that no bounded region in $\mathcal{F}$ is entirely enclosed by blue lines.

negatives.text: Let $n \geq 3$ be lines in the plane with no two parallel and no three concurrent. These lines form a set of regions, and let $\mathcal{F}$ be the bounded regions. Prove that it is possible to colour $\lfloor\sqrt{n / 2}\rfloor$ of the lines blue such that no region in $\mathcal{F}$ is entirely enclosed by blue lines.

Given $n \geq 3$ lines in the plane such that no two are parallel and no three intersect at a single point, these lines form regions. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of bounded regions. Prove that it is possible to colour $\lceil\sqrt{n / 2}\rceil$ of the lines blue such that no region in $\mathcal{F}$ has a boundary that is completely red.

Let $n \geq 3$ be lines in the plane with no two parallel and no three concurrent. These lines form a set of polygonal regions, among which $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of finite-area regions. Prove that it is possible to colour $\lceil\sqrt{n / 2}\rceil$ of the lines blue such that at least one region in $\mathcal{F}$ has a completely blue boundary.

positive_text: Let $M$ be a set of $n \geqslant 4$ points in the plane, with no three collinear. Initially, $n$ segments are drawn such that every point is an endpoint of exactly two segments. At each step, if two segments $AB$ and $CD$ intersect in their interiors, they can be replaced with $AC$ and $BD$, provided neither is already present. Show that no more than $n^{3} / 4$ such replacements can occur.

negatives.text: Let $M$ be a set of $n \geqslant 4$ points in the plane, no three collinear, connected by $n$ segments such that each point is an endpoint of two segments. If two segments intersect, they can be swapped with a pair of non-present segments. Prove that the number of such swaps cannot exceed $n^{3} / 2$.

Let $M$ be a set of $n \geqslant 4$ points in the plane, no three collinear, connected by $n$ segments such that each point is an endpoint of two segments. If two segments intersect, they can be swapped with a pair of non-present segments. Prove that the number of such swaps cannot exceed $n^{2} / 4$.

Let $M$ be a set of $n \geqslant 4$ points in the plane, no three collinear, connected by $n$ segments such that each point is an endpoint of two segments. If two segments intersect, they can be swapped with a pair of non-present segments. Prove that the number of such swaps is at least $n^{3} / 4$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $BC$ such that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on the extensions of $AP$ and $AQ$ beyond $P$ and $Q$, respectively, so that $PM = AP$ and $QN = AQ$. Show that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ meet on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $\angle PAB = \angle BAC$ and $\angle QAC = \angle ABC$. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on the rays $AP$ and $AQ$, respectively, with $PM = AP$ and $QN = AQ$. Prove that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ intersect on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on the rays $AP$ and $AQ$, respectively, with $PM = 2AP$ and $QN = 2AQ$. Prove that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ intersect on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on the rays $AP$ and $AQ$, respectively, with $PM = AP$ and $QN = AQ$. Prove that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ intersect on the incircle of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $\Omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and circumcenter of triangle $ABC$, where $\angle ABC < 90^\circ$ and $AB > BC$. Let $M$ be the second intersection of the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ with $\Omega$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $R$ lie on $PQ$ such that $BR = MR$. Show that $BR \parallel AC$.

negatives.text: Let $\Omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and circumcenter of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\Omega$ at $M \neq B$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The angle bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The point $R$ is chosen on the line $PQ$ so that $BR = BR'$. Prove that $BR \parallel AC$, where $R'$ is the reflection of $R$ over $B$.

Let $\Omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and circumcenter of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\Omega$ at $M \neq B$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The angle bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The point $R$ is chosen on the line $PQ$ so that $BR = MR$. Prove that $BR$ bisects $\angle ABC$.

positive_text: Along a one-dimensional road in Lineland, there are $n \geqslant 1$ towns positioned from left to right. Each town is equipped with a distinct-sized right-facing and left-facing bulldozer. When two bulldozers face each other (one right-facing, one left-facing), the larger one pushes the smaller one off the road. If a bulldozer reaches the back of another bulldozer, it pushes it off regardless of size. Given two towns $A$ and $B$, with $B$ to the right of $A$, we define that $A$ can sweep $B$ if the right bulldozer of $A$ can reach $B$ and remove all intervening bulldozers. Similarly, $B$ can sweep $A$ if its left bulldozer can reach $A$ and clear the path. Prove that there is a unique town that cannot be swept away by any other.

negatives.text: In Lineland there are $n \geqslant 1$ towns arranged left to right, each with a left and a right bulldozer of distinct size. When a right and a left bulldozer meet, the larger one pushes the smaller one off the road. A bulldozer reaching the rear of another one pushes it off regardless of size. Let $A$ and $B$ be two towns, with $B$ to the right of $A$. $A$ can sweep $B$ if its right bulldozer can reach $B$ and push off all bulldozers it meets. Similarly, $B$ can sweep $A$ if its left bulldozer can reach $A$ and push off all bulldozers. Prove that there is exactly one town which can be swept away by at least one other town.

positive_text:
Let $S$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say $S$ is symmetric if for every pair of points $A, B \in S$ with $A \neq B$, there is a point $C \in S$ such that $AC = BC$. We say $S$ is center-avoiding if for all triples of distinct points $A, B, C \in S$, there is no point $P \in S$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Prove that for all $n \geq 3$, there exists a symmetric set with $n$ points.

b. Determine all $n \geq 3$ for which a symmetric, center-avoiding set of $n$ points exists.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = 2BC$. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points?

Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = BC$. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points with no three points collinear?

Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = BC$. We say that $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points with no point being the midpoint of any two others?

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of $ABC$, $M$ the midpoint of side $BC$, and $F$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$. Suppose points $Q$ and $K$ lie on $\Gamma$ such that $\angle AQH = 90^\circ$ and $\angle KQH = 90^\circ$. Show that the circumcircles of triangles $KQH$ and $KFM$ are tangent.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $H$ be the orthocenter, $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, and $F$ the foot of the altitude from $A$. Suppose $Q$ and $K$ lie on $\Gamma$ such that $\angle AQH = 90^\circ$ and $\angle KQH = 90^\circ$. Prove that the circumcircles of $\triangle KQH$ and $\triangle KFM$ are intersecting at two points.

positive_text:
Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for any real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, there exists a choice of $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ for which
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right| \leqslant 1
$$

negatives.text:
Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for any real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ and $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ with $\left|a_k\right| + \left|b_k\right| = 1$ for all $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, there exists a choice of $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k a_k\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k b_k\right| \leqslant 2
$$

Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for any real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ and $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ with $\left|a_k\right| + \left|b_k\right| = 1$ for all $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, there exists a choice of $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k a_k\right|^2 + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k b_k\right|^2 \leqslant 1
$$

Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for any real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ and $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ with $\left|a_k\right| + \left|b_k\right| = 1$ for all $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, there exists a choice of $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k a_k\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k b_k\right| = 1
$$

positive_text:
Let $k$ be a positive integer greater than or equal to 1. In the plane, there are $2k+1$ segments such that any two intersect at a unique interior point and no three intersect at the same point. Jeff assigns a snail to one endpoint of each segment and claps $2k$ times. Each clap causes the snails to advance to the next intersection point along their respective segments. After $2k$ claps, the snails reach the furthest intersection from their starting point.

a) Prove that Jeff can always choose the starting positions of the snails so that no two snails ever share an intersection point during the claps.

b) Prove that if $k$ is a positive integer such that $2k+1$ is replaced with $2k$, then regardless of Jeff's choices, there will be a clap at which at least two snails share an intersection point.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. There are $n$ segments in the plane such that any two intersect at a unique interior point and no three intersect at the same point. Jeff places a snail at one endpoint of each segment and claps $n-1$ times. At each clap, the snails move to the next intersection point along their segments. After $n-1$ claps, they reach the farthest such point from their starting position.

a) Prove that if $n$ is odd then Jeff can always place the snails so that no two of them ever occupy the same intersection point.

b) Prove that if $n$ is even then there must be a moment when some two snails occupy the same intersection point no matter how Jeff places the snails, but the snails only move to the previous intersection point on each clap.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. There are $n$ segments in the plane such that any two intersect at a unique interior point and no three intersect at the same point. Jeff places a snail at one endpoint of each segment and claps $n-1$ times. At each clap, the snails move to the next intersection point along their segments. After $n-1$ claps, they reach the farthest such point from their starting position.

a) Prove that if $n$ is odd then Jeff can always place the snails so that no two of them ever occupy the same intersection point.

b) Prove that if $n$ is even then there must be a moment when some two snails occupy the same intersection point no matter how Jeff places the snails, but now the snails move to the next intersection point only if it is to the right (in a fixed coordinate system).

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. There are $n$ segments in the plane such that any two intersect at a unique interior point and no three intersect at the same point. Jeff places a snail at one endpoint of each segment and claps $n-1$ times. At each clap, the snails move to the next intersection point along their segments. After $n-1$ claps, they reach the farthest such point from their starting position.

a) Prove that if $n$ is odd then Jeff can always place the snails so that no two of them ever occupy the same intersection point.

b) Prove that if $n$ is even then there must be a moment when some two snails occupy the same intersection point no matter how Jeff places the snails, but now the snails are allowed to skip one intersection point during the movement at each clap.

positive_text: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $(f(a)+b)(f(b)+a)>0$, it follows that $f(a)+b=f(b)+a$. Show that $f(a)+b \leqslant f(b)+a$ for all $a > b$.

negatives.text: Assume that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the following condition: For every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $(f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) < 0$, we have $f(x)+y = f(y)+x$. Prove that $f(x)+y \leqslant f(y)+x$ whenever $x > y$.

Assume that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the following condition: For every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $(f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) > 0$, we have $f(x)+y = f(y)+x$. Prove that $f(x)+y < f(y)+x$ whenever $x > y$.

Assume that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the following condition: For every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $(f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) > 0$, we have $f(x)+y = f(y)+x$. Prove that $f(x)+y \geqslant f(y)+x$ whenever $x > y$.

positive_text:
Let $n$ be an integer greater than or equal to 3. Given two regular polygons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ with $n$ sides in the plane, show that the vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ which are contained within or on the boundary of $\mathcal{B}$ form a connected arc of the polygon $\mathcal{A}$.
(That is, prove that such a set of vertices can be separated from the rest of $\mathcal{A}$'s vertices by a straight line.)

negatives.text:
Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. Two regular $n$-gons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are given in the plane. Prove that the vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ that lie strictly inside $\mathcal{B}$ are consecutive.
(That is, prove that there exists a line separating those vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ that lie strictly inside $\mathcal{B}$ from the other vertices of $\mathcal{A}$.)

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be distinct positive integers with $a_i, b_i \in [1, 5n]$ for all $i$. If the values
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
form an arithmetic progression, show that all the fractions are equal.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms a geometric progression. Prove that the terms of the sequence are equal.

Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms a strictly decreasing arithmetic progression. Prove that the terms of the sequence are equal.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(2x) + 2f(y) = f(f(x+y)).
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) - 2f(b) = f(f(a+b)).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a) + f(b)).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a^2 + b)).
$$

positive_text:
Let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2019}$ be real numbers such that
$$
x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{2019}=0 \quad \text{and} \quad x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\cdots+x_{2019}^{2}=1 .$$
Let $m=\min \left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2019}\right)$ and $M=\max \left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2019}\right)$. Prove that
$$
mM \leqslant-\frac{1}{2019}$$

negatives.text:
Let $u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}$ be real numbers satisfying
$$
u_{1}+u_{2}+\cdots+u_{2019}=0 \quad \text{and} \quad u_{1}^{2}+u_{2}^{2}+\cdots+u_{2019}^{2}=1 .$$
Let $a=\min \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$ and $b=\max \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$. Prove that
$$
ab \geqslant-\frac{1}{2019}$$

Let $u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}$ be real numbers satisfying
$$
u_{1}+u_{2}+\cdots+u_{2019}=1 \quad \text{and} \quad u_{1}^{2}+u_{2}^{2}+\cdots+u_{2019}^{2}=1 .$$
Let $a=\min \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$ and $b=\max \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right)$. Prove that
$$
ab \leqslant-\frac{1}{2019}$$

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
 x_{1} + x_{2} + \cdots + x_{n} = 0 .
$$
Define the set $S$ as
$$
 S = \left\{ (p, q) \mid 1 \leqslant p < q \leqslant n,\ |x_p - x_q| \geqslant 1 \right\} .
$$
Show that if $S$ is non-empty, then
$$
\sum_{(p, q) \in S} x_p x_q < 0 .
$$

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ and $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be real numbers such that
$$
 a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = 0 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
 A = \left\{ (i, j) \mid 1 \leqslant i < j \leqslant n,\ |a_i - a_j| \geqslant 1 \right\} .
$$
Prove that if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_i a_j > 0 .
$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ and $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be real numbers such that
$$
 a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = 0 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
 A = \left\{ (i, j) \mid 1 \leqslant i < j \leqslant n,\ |a_i - a_j| > 1 \right\} .
$$
Prove that if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_i a_j < 0 .
$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ and $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be real numbers such that
$$
 a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = 1 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
 A = \left\{ (i, j) \mid 1 \leqslant i < j \leqslant n,\ |a_i - a_j| \geqslant 1 \right\} .
$$
Prove that if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_i a_j < 0 .
$$

positive_text:
Let $P(x, y, z)$ be a real polynomial in three variables satisfying
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y - z) = P(x, x z - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Show that $P(x, y, z)$ can be written as $F(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} - x y z)$ for some univariate polynomial $F(t)$.

negatives.text:
A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y + z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} - x y z\right)\n$$

A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y - z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} + x y z\right)\n$$

A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y - z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{3} + y^{3} + z^{3} - x y z\right)\n$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Consider a sequence of $n$ bits $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$, where each $b_i$ is either 0 or 1 (representing tails or heads). Repeatedly perform the following: if there are exactly $k$ ones among the bits and $k > 0$, then flip the $k^{	ext{th}}$ bit; otherwise, terminate. For a sequence $C$, define $\ell(C)$ as the number of operations until all bits are zero. Prove that $\ell(C)$ is finite for all $C$, and compute the average of $\ell(C)$ over all $2^n$ sequences.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins lined up on his desk, each showing heads or tails. He repeatedly does the following operation: if there are $k$ coins showing heads and $k>0$, then he flips the $(k+1)^{\text{th}}$ coin over; otherwise he stops the process. Let $\ell(C)$ denote the number of steps before all coins show $T$. Show that this number is finite and determine its average value over all $2^n$ configurations.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins lined up on his desk, each showing heads or tails. He repeatedly does the following operation: if there are $k$ coins showing heads and $k>0$, then he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin over; otherwise he stops the process. Let $\ell(C)$ denote the number of steps before all coins show $H$. Show that this number is finite and determine its average value over all $2^n$ configurations.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins lined up on his desk, each showing heads or tails. He repeatedly does the following operation: if there are at least $k$ coins showing heads and $k>0$, then he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin over; otherwise he stops the process. Let $\ell(C)$ denote the number of steps before all coins show $T$. Show that this number is finite and determine its average value over all $2^n$ configurations.

positive_text: Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Suppose $2n$ distinct points in the plane are given, with no three collinear. Label these points $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{2n}$ in some order. Consider the $2n$ smallest positive angles formed consecutively as $\angle P_{1}P_{2}P_{3}, \angle P_{2}P_{3}P_{4}, \ldots, \angle P_{2n}P_{1}P_{2}$. Prove that there exists a labelling of the points such that the angles can be partitioned into two subsets with equal total angle sum.

negatives.text: Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Given $2n$ points in the plane, no three collinear, label them as $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2n}$. Consider the $2n$ angles $\angle A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}, \angle A_{2}A_{3}A_{4}, \ldots, \angle A_{2n}A_{1}A_{2}$, each measured as the smallest positive value. Prove that there exists a labelling such that the sum of all angles is divisible by $180^\circ$.

Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Suppose we are given $2n$ points in the plane, no three collinear, and label them as $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2n}$. Consider the $2n$ angles $\angle A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}, \angle A_{2}A_{3}A_{4}, \ldots, \angle A_{2n}A_{1}A_{2}$, each measured as the smallest positive value. Prove that the sum of all angles is greater than $360^\circ$.

Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Suppose we are given $2n$ points in the plane such that no three are collinear. Label them as $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2n}$ in some order. Consider the $2n$ angles $\angle A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}, \angle A_{2}A_{3}A_{4}, \ldots, \angle A_{2n}A_{1}A_{2}$, each measured as the smallest positive value. Prove that there exists a labelling such that the sum of all angles is a rational number of degrees.

positive_text: In a land with $n \geqslant 2$ cities, each pair of cities is connected by a one-way road whose direction is unknown to Alice. Alice can ask for the direction of any road between two cities. She needs to determine whether there exists a city with at most one outgoing road. Prove that Alice can determine this with at most $4n$ queries.

negatives.text: Alice wants to determine whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one incoming road instead of outgoing road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4n$ questions.

Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one outgoing road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4n$ questions, assuming that some roads may be two-way instead of one-way.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with orthocenter $H$, and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ onto $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Let $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ be the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, tangent to $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$. Let line $MN$ intersect $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at $P$ and $Q$. Show that $MP = NQ$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to the opposite sides. Let $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ be the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, tangent to $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Suppose line $MN$ intersects $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that $MP = PQ$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to the opposite sides. Let $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ be the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, tangent to $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Suppose line $MN$ intersects $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that $MP = MN$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to the opposite sides. Let $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ be the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, tangent to $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Suppose line $MN$ intersects $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that $MP > NQ$.

positive_text: Let $A B C D E$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. A point $P$ lies in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Show that the condition $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$ is equivalent to $P$ being on the diagonal $CE$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC = 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = 2 \cdot (\operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP))$.

positive_text: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three distinct lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ through $X$, the points $f(\ell_{1}), f(\ell_{2}), f(\ell_{3})$, and $X$ are concyclic. Prove that there exists a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell) = P$ for every line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function assigning to each line $\ell$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f(\ell_{1}), f(\ell_{2}), f(\ell_{3})$ and $X$ lie on a line. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function assigning to each line $\ell$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f(\ell_{1}), f(\ell_{2}), f(\ell_{3})$ and $X$ lie on a circle unless $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ are concurrent. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

positive_text:
Let $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ be positive real numbers such that $p \geqslant q \geqslant r \geqslant s > 0$ and $p + q + r + s = 1$. Prove that
$$
(p + 2q + 3r + 4s) p^{p} q^{q} r^{r} s^{s} < 1
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{b} b^{c} c^{d} d^{a} < 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} d^{d} \leq 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be positive real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} d^{d} < 2
$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geqslant 1$. Consider a grid with $n$ rows and $n$ columns where each entry is $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$ for row $i$ and column $j$. Find all values of $n$ such that the sum of all $n^{2}$ entries is $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n-1)$.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geqslant 1$. Consider an $n \times n$ grid with entries $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$ for $i, j = 1, 2, \ldots, n$. Find all $n$ such that the total sum of the entries is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n+1)$.

Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geqslant 1$. Consider an $n \times n$ grid with entries $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$ for $i, j = 1, 2, \ldots, n$. Find all $n$ such that the total sum of the entries is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{3}(n-1)$.

Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geqslant 1$. Consider an $n \times n$ grid with entries $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$ for $i, j = 1, 2, \ldots, n$. Find all $n$ such that the total sum of the entries is equal to $\frac{1}{2} n^{2}(n-1)$.

positive_text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. Define an integer $m \geqslant n+1$ as $n$-colourful if it is possible to arrange $m$ marbles of $n$ different colours $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{n}$ around a circle such that each block of $n+1$ adjacent marbles contains all $n$ distinct colours. Show that only finitely many positive integers fail to be $n$-colourful and determine the maximum such integer.

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if it is possible to place $m$ marbles of $n$ distinct colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$ around a circle so that in any group of $n$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of each colour. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful and find the largest among them.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if it is possible to place $m$ marbles of $n$ distinct colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$ around a circle so that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of each colour $C_{i}$ for each $i=1, \ldots, n$. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful and find the smallest among them.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if it is possible to place $m$ marbles of $n$ distinct colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$ in a line (not a circle) such that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of each colour. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful and find the largest among them.

positive_text: Find the maximum number $N$ such that there exists an $N \times 100$ matrix $T$ where each row is a permutation of $\{1,2,\ldots,100\}$, and for every pair of distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is at least one column $c$ with $|T(r,c) - T(s,c)| \geq 2$.

negatives.text: Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns such that every row contains the numbers $1,2,\ldots,100$ in some order and for any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ with $|T(r, c)-T(s, c)| < 2$.

Find the maximum number $N$ for which there exists a $100$-column table $T$ with $N$ rows such that each row is a permutation of $\{1,2,\ldots,100\}$ and for any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, all columns $c$ satisfy $|T(r, c)-T(s, c)| < 2$.

Determine the largest $N$ such that there exists an $N \times 100$ matrix $T$ where each row is a permutation of $\{1,2,\ldots,100\}$ and for any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is at least one column $c$ with $T(r, c) = T(s, c)$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram with $AC = BC$. A point $P$ lies on the extension of $AB$ past $B$. The circle passing through $A$, $C$, and $D$ intersects $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circle through $A$, $P$, and $Q$ intersects $PC$ again at $R$. Show that $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ meet at a common point.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram such that $AC = BC$. A point $P$ is chosen on the extension of the segment $BA$ beyond $A$. The circumcircle of triangle $ACD$ meets the segment $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ meets the segment $PC$ again at $R$. Prove that the lines $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ are concurrent.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram such that $AC = BC$. A point $P$ is chosen on the extension of the segment $AB$ beyond $B$. The circumcircle of triangle $ACD$ meets the segment $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ meets the segment $PB$ again at $R$. Prove that the lines $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ are concurrent.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram such that $AC = BC$. A point $P$ is chosen on the extension of the segment $AB$ beyond $B$. The circumcircle of triangle $ACD$ meets the segment $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ meets the segment $PC$ again at $R$. Prove that the lines $CD$, $AP$, and $BR$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Find all integers $n \geq 3$ such that in any convex polygon with $n$ sides, each of length $1$, there exists an equilateral triangle with side length $1$ whose boundary is entirely contained within the polygon.

negatives.text: Determine all integers $n \geq 3$ such that every convex $n$-gon with all sides of length $1$ contains an equilateral triangle of side length $\sqrt{2}$.

Determine all integers $n \geq 3$ such that every convex $n$-gon with all sides of length $1$ contains an equilateral triangle with side length $1$ that lies strictly inside the polygon (not on the boundary).
Determine all integers $n \geq 3$ such that every convex $n$-gon with all sides of length $1$ contains an isosceles triangle with side length $1$.

positive_text: Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients, and define $P^{(1)}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{(k+1)}(x) = P\left(P^{(k)}(x)\right)$ for all $k \geq 1$. Determine all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients for which the set $\{P^{(m)}(1), P^{(m)}(2), \ldots, P^{(m)}(n)\}$ has precisely $\left\lceil n / 2^{m} \right\rceil$ distinct values modulo $n$ for all $m \geq 1$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients, and define $P^{(1)}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{(k+1)}(x) = P\left(P^{(k)}(x)\right)$ for all $k \geq 1$. Determine all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients for which the set $\{P^{(m)}(1), P^{(m)}(2), \ldots, P^{(m)}(n)\}$ has exactly $\left\lceil n / 3^{m} \right\rceil$ distinct values modulo $n$ for all $m \geq 1$.

positive_text: The Bank of Oslo produces coins from two metals: aluminium ($A$) and copper ($C$). Morgane possesses $n$ of each type and arranges them in a row in some arbitrary order. Given a fixed positive integer $k \leqslant 2n$, she performs the following operation repeatedly: find the maximal group of consecutive coins of the same metal that includes the $k$-th coin from the left and move this group to the leftmost position. For instance, if $n=4$ and $k=4$, the configuration $A A C C C A C A$ evolves as $$ A A C C C A C A \rightarrow C C C A A A C A \rightarrow A A A C C C C A \rightarrow C C C C A A A A \rightarrow \cdots . $$ Determine all pairs $(n, k)$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$ such that for any initial configuration, at some point in the process the number of adjacent $A$-$C$ pairs is at most one.

negatives.text: The Bank of Oslo issues coins made out of two types of metal: aluminium ($A$) and copper ($C$). Morgane has $n$ aluminium coins, and $n$ copper coins, and arranges her $2n$ coins in a row in some arbitrary initial order. Given a fixed positive integer $k \leqslant 2n$, she repeatedly performs the following operation: identify the largest subsequence containing the $k$-th coin from the left which consists of consecutive coins made of the same metal, and move all coins in that subsequence to the right end of the row.
