\text{Let } ABC \text{ be an equilateral triangle with side length } 2. \text{ Prove that for any point } P \text{ on the incircle of } ABC, \text{ the sum } PA^2 + PB^2 + PC^2 = 5. \text{ Also, show that the triangle formed by sides } PA, PB, PC \text{ has area } \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be an equilateral triangle with side length } 2. \text{ Prove that for any point } P \text{ on the circumcircle of } ABC, \text{ the sum } PA^2 + PB^2 + PC^2 = 5. \text{ Also, show that the triangle formed by sides } PA, PB, PC \text{ has area } \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.

positive_text: \text{\$ABCD\$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with an incircle centered on side \$AB\$ that is tangent to sides \$BC\$, \$CD\$, and \$DA\$. Prove that \$AB = AD + BC\$. Determine the maximum area of \$ABCD\$ in terms of the lengths \$\|AB\|\$ and \$\|CD\|\$.}

negatives.text: \text{\$ABCD\$ is cyclic with an incircle centered on side \$AB\$ that is tangent to sides \$BC\$, \$CD\$, and \$DA\$. Prove that \$AB = AD - BC\$. What is the maximum possible area of \$ABCD\$ in terms of \$\|AB\|\$ and \$\|CD\|\$?}

\text{\$ABCD\$ is cyclic with a circle centered on side \$AB\$ that is tangent to sides \$BC\$, \$CD\$, and \$DA\$. Prove that \$AB = AD + BC\$. What is the minimum possible area of \$ABCD\$ in terms of \$\|AB\|\$ and \$\|CD\|\$?}

\text{\$ABCD\$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with a circle centered on side \$AB\$ that is tangent to sides \$BC\$, \$CD\$, and \$DA\$. Prove that \$AB = AD + BC\$. What is the maximum possible area of \$ABCD\$ in terms of \$\|AB\|\$ and \$\|BD\|\$?}

positive_text: Let \mathrm{ABC} be a triangle with median \mathrm{AD}, and let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of \mathrm{AD}. If the ray \mathrm{BM} intersects \mathrm{AC} at point N, prove that the tangent from \mathrm{A} to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} is \mathrm{AB} if and only if \mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN} = (\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BN})^{2}.

negatives.text: Let \mathrm{ABC} be a triangle with median \mathrm{AD}, and let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of \mathrm{AD}. The ray \mathrm{BM} meets \mathrm{AC} at N. Show that \mathrm{AB} is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} if and only if \mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN} = (\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BN})^{2} + 1.

Let \mathrm{ABC} be a triangle with median \mathrm{AD}, and let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of \mathrm{AD}. The ray \mathrm{BM} meets \mathrm{AC} at N. Show that \mathrm{AB} is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} if and only if \mathrm{BM}^{2} = \mathrm{BN} \cdot \mathrm{BC}^{2} / \mathrm{BN}^{2} - 1.

Let \mathrm{ABC} be a triangle with median \mathrm{AD}, and let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of \mathrm{AD}. The ray \mathrm{BM} meets \mathrm{AC} at N. Show that \mathrm{AB} is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} if and only if \mathrm{BM}^{2} = \mathrm{BN}^{2} \cdot (\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BN})^{2}.

positive_text: Let $ n > 2 $ be an integer. Define the set $ S $ of pairs $ (a, b) $ of positive integers with $ a < b \leq n $, $ \gcd(a, b) = 1 $, and $ a + b > n $. Prove that $ \sum_{(a, b) \in S} \frac{1}{ab} = \frac{1}{2} $.

negatives.text: Let $ n > 2 $ be an integer. Consider all pairs $ (a, b) $ of relatively prime positive integers such that $ a < b \leq n $ and $ a + b < n $. Prove that the sum of $ \frac{1}{ab} $ over these pairs is $ \frac{1}{2} $.

Let $ n > 2 $ be an integer. Consider all pairs $ (a, b) $ of relatively prime positive integers such that $ a < b \leq n $ and $ a + b > n $. Compute the sum of $ \frac{1}{a^2b} $ over all such pairs and show it equals $ \frac{1}{2} $.

Let $ n > 2 $ be an integer. Consider all pairs $ (a, b) $ of positive integers such that $ a < b \leq n $, $ a + b > n $, and $ \gcd(a, b) = 2 $. Show that the sum of $ \frac{1}{ab} $ over all such pairs is $ \frac{1}{2} $.

positive_text: Let $ n > 1 $ be an integer. Let $ D_n $ be the set of lattice points $ (x, y) $ such that $ x, y $ satisfy $ -n \leq x, y \leq n $. If each point in $ D_n $ is assigned one of three colors, prove that there exist two points of the same color such that the line connecting them contains no other points of $ D_n $. Show that there exists a coloring with four colors such that no line intersects $ D_n $ at exactly two points of the same color.

negatives.text: Let $ n > 1 $ be an integer. Let $ D_n $ be the set of lattice points $ (x, y) $ with $ |x|, |y| \leq n $. If the points of $ D_n $ are colored with three colors (one for each point), show that there are always two points with the same color such that the line containing them does not contain any other points of $ D_n $. Show that it is possible to color the points of $ D_n $ with four colors (one for each point) so that if any line contains two or more points of $ D_n $, then those two points have different colors.

Let $ n > 1 $ be an integer. Let $ D_n $ be the set of lattice points $ (x, y) $ with $ |x|, |y| \leq n $. If the points of $ D_n $ are colored with three colors (one for each point), show that there are always two points with the same color such that the line containing them does not contain any other points of $ D_n $. Show that it is possible to color the points of $ D_n $ with four colors (one for each point) so that if any line contains exactly two points of $ D_n $, then those two points have the same color.

Let $ n > 1 $ be an integer. Let $ D_n $ be the set of lattice points $ (x, y) $ with $ |x|, |y| \leq n $. If the points of $ D_n $ are colored with three colors (one for each point), show that there are always two points with the same color such that the line containing them does not contain any other points of $ D_n $. Show that it is possible to color the points of $ D_n $ with four colors (one for each point) so that if any line contains two points of $ D_n $, then those two points have different colors and are not aligned.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$, and let the incircle touch sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $D$, $E$, and $F$ respectively. Let $AD$ intersect the incircle again at $Q$. Prove that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ if and only if triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AC = BC$.

negatives.text: The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AC = AB$.
The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $FQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AE$ iff $AC = BC$.
The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AB = BC$.

positive_text: Determine all positive integers $n < 1000$ for which $n^2 = \left(\sum_{i=0}^{k} d_i\right)^3$, where $d_i$ are the digits of $n$.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the cube of the product of the digits of $n$ equals $n^{2}$.
Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the cube of the sum of the digits of $n$ is greater than $n^{2}$.
Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the square of the sum of the digits of $n$ equals the cube of $n$.

positive_text: Let $A$ and $B$ be fixed points, and let $C$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of segment $AB$. Construct a sequence $C_1, C_2, C_3, \ldots$ such that $C_1 = C$, and for each $n$, if $C_n$ does not lie on line $AB$, then $C_{n+1}$ is the circumcenter of triangle $ABC_n$. The sequence ends if $C_n$ lies on $AB$. Determine all such points $C$ for which the sequence eventually becomes periodic.

negatives.text: Let $A$ and $B$ be fixed points, and let $C$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of segment $AB$. Define a sequence $C_1, C_2, C_3, \ldots$ such that $C_1 = C$, and for each $n$, if $C_n$ does not lie on line $AB$, then $C_{n+1}$ is the centroid of triangle $ABC_n$. If $C_n$ lies on $AB$, the sequence terminates. Determine all such points $C$ for which the sequence eventually becomes periodic.

Let $A$ and $B$ be fixed points, and let $C$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of segment $AB$. Define a sequence $C_1, C_2, C_3, \ldots$ such that $C_1 = C$, and for each $n$, if $C_n$ does not lie on line $AB$, then $C_{n+1}$ is the midpoint of segment $C_nA$. If $C_n$ lies on $AB$, the sequence terminates. Determine all such points $C$ for which the sequence eventually becomes periodic.

Let $A$ and $B$ be fixed points, and let $C$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of segment $AB$. Define a sequence $C_1, C_2, C_3, \ldots$ such that $C_1 = C$, and for each $n$, if $C_n$ does not lie on line $AB$, then $C_{n+1}$ is the circumcenter of triangle $ABC_n$. If $C_n$ lies on the line $AB$, the sequence terminates. Determine all such points $C$ for which the sequence eventually becomes unbounded.

positive_text: Assign distinct integers $1$ through $n$ to the vertices of a regular $n$-gon with $n > 3$. Connect all non-adjacent vertices with diagonals. Prove that when $n$ is odd, it is possible to assign labels $1$ to $n$ to each side and diagonal such that no label matches its endpoints and all edges incident to a vertex have distinct labels.

negatives.text: Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon from $1$ to $n > 3$. Draw all the diagonals. Show that if $n$ is even then we can label each side and diagonal with a number from $1$ to $n$ different from the labels of its endpoints so that at each vertex the sides and diagonals all have different labels.

Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon from $1$ to $n > 3$. Draw all the diagonals. Show that we can label each side and diagonal with a number from $1$ to $n$ equal to the labels of its endpoints so that at each vertex the sides and diagonals all have different labels.

Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon from $1$ to $n > 3$. Draw all the diagonals. Show that if $n$ is odd then we can label each side and diagonal with a number from $1$ to $n$ such that all edges have distinct labels and at least one edge shares a label with its endpoints.

positive_text: Let $b_{1} = 56$ and define $b_{n+1} = b_{n} - \frac{1}{b_{n}}$. Prove that there exists an integer $k$ with $1 < k < 2002$ such that $b_{k} < 0$.

negatives.text: Let $a_{1} = 56$ and define $a_{n+1} = a_{n} + \frac{1}{a_{n}}$. Show that $a_{n} > 0$ for all $n$ with $0 < n < 2002$.
Let $a_{1} = 56$ and define $a_{n+1} = a_{n} - \frac{1}{a_{n}^2}$. Show that $a_{n} < 0$ for some $n$ such that $0 < n < 2002$.
Let $a_{1} = 56$ and define $a_{n+1} = a_{n} - \frac{1}{a_{n}}$. Show that $a_{n} < 0$ for some $n$ such that $0 < n < 200$.

positive_text: Let $A$, $B$ be sets of $N$ consecutive integers. If $N=2003$, is it possible to match each element of $A$ with one of $B$ to form $N$ pairs $(a,b)$ such that the sum of each pair forms a sequence of $N$ consecutive integers? What if $N=2004$?

negatives.text: Let $A$, $B$ be two sets of $N$ consecutive integers. If $N=2003$, can we form $N$ pairs $(a,b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$ such that the products of the pairs are $N$ consecutive integers? What about $N=2004$?

Let $A$, $B$ be two sets of $N$ consecutive integers. If $N=2003$, can we form $N$ pairs $(a,b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$ such that the sums of the pairs are $N$ consecutive integers, with each sum divisible by $2$? What about $N=2004$?

positive_text: Let $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2003}$ be a sequence with $a_0 = 1$ and $0 \leq a_i \leq 2 a_{i-1}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq 2003$. Suppose $T = \pm a_1 \pm a_2 \pm \ldots \pm a_{2002} + a_{2003}$. Prove that the sequence maximising $T$ can be determined without knowing the signs of the terms.

negatives.text: Let $x_0 = 1$ and $0 \leq x_i \leq 2 x_{i-1}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 2003$. Suppose $S = \pm x_1 \pm x_2 \pm \ldots \pm x_{2002} - x_{2003}$. Show that the sequence maximising $S$ can be determined without knowing the signs.

Let $x_0 = 1$ and $0 \leq x_i \leq 3 x_{i-1}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 2003$. Suppose $S = \pm x_1 \pm x_2 \pm \ldots \pm x_{2002} + x_{2003}$. Show that the sequence maximising $S$ can be determined without knowing the signs.

Let $x_0 = 1$ and $0 \leq x_i \leq 2 x_{i-1}$ for $1 \leq i \leq 2003$. Suppose $S = x_1^2 \pm x_2 \pm \ldots \pm x_{2002} + x_{2003}$. Show that the sequence maximising $S$ can be determined without knowing the signs.

positive_text: Find integer solutions $(x, y, z)$ satisfying $$x+y+z=1, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{2}=1.$$

negatives.text: Solve for integers $x, y, z$ : $$x+y=1-z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1+z^{2}.$$
Find integer solutions $x, y, z$ satisfying $$x+y=1-z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1-z^{3}.$$
Solve for integers $x, y, z$ : $$x+y=1+z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1-z^{2}.$$

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $AB = CD$, $(\sqrt{3}+1)BC = DA$, and $\angle CDA - \angle DAB = 30^\circ$. Show that
$$
\angle ABC - \angle BCD = 90^\circ
$$

negatives.text:
In a convex quadrilateral $PQRS$, $PQ = RS$, $(\sqrt{3}+1)QR = SP$, and $\angle RSP - \angle SPQ = 60^\circ$. Prove that
$$
\angle PQR - \angle QRS = 90^\circ
$$

In a convex quadrilateral $PQRS$, $PQ = RS$, $(\sqrt{3}+1)QR = SP$, and $\angle SPQ - \angle RSP = 30^\circ$. Prove that
$$
\angle PQR - \angle QRS = 90^\circ
$$

positive_text: Let $p, q, r$ be three real numbers such that $1 \geq p \geq q \geq r \geq 0$. Prove that if $\mu$ is a root of the cubic equation $x^{3}+p x^{2}+q x+r=0$ (real or complex), then $|\mu| \leq 1$.

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c$ be real numbers such that $1 \geq a \geq b \geq c \geq 0$. Prove that if $\lambda$ is a root of the cubic equation $x^{3} - a x^{2} + b x + c = 0$ (real or complex), then $|\lambda| \leq 1$.

Let $a, b, c$ be real numbers such that $1 \geq a \geq b \geq c \geq 0$. Prove that if $\lambda$ is a root of the cubic equation $x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x + c = 0$ (real or complex), then $|\lambda| < 1$.

Let $a, b, c$ be real numbers such that $0 \leq a \leq b \leq c \leq 1$. Prove that if $\lambda$ is a root of the cubic equation $x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x + c = 0$ (real or complex), then $|\lambda| \leq 1$.

positive_text: Show that the equation $$ a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a) $$ has infinitely many solutions in integers $a, b, c$.

negatives.text: Show that the equation $$ x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=(x+y)(y+z)(z+x) $$ has infinitely many solutions in integers $x, y, z$.
Show that the equation $$ x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=(x-y)(y-z)(z-x) + 1 $$ has infinitely many solutions in integers $x, y, z$.

positive_text:
Let triangle $PQR$ have side lengths $x, y, z$. Construct a triangle $P_1 Q_1 R_1$ with side lengths $x + \frac{y}{2}$, $y + \frac{z}{2}$, $z + \frac{x}{2}$. Prove that
$$
\left[P_1 Q_1 R_1\right] \geq \frac{9}{4}[PQR].
$$

negatives.text:
Let triangle $ABC$ have sides $a, b, c$. Consider a triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with sides $a - \frac{b}{2}$, $b - \frac{c}{2}$, $c - \frac{a}{2}$. Show that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] \geq \frac{9}{4}[ABC].
$$

Let triangle $ABC$ have sides $a, b, c$. Consider a triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with sides $a + \frac{b^2}{2}$, $b + \frac{c^2}{2}$, $c + \frac{a^2}{2}$. Show that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] \geq \frac{9}{4}[ABC].
$$

Let triangle $ABC$ have sides $a, b, c$. Consider a triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with sides $a + \frac{b}{2}$, $b + \frac{c}{2}$, $c + \frac{a}{2}$. Show that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] \leq \frac{9}{4}[ABC].
$$

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with midpoints $K, L, M, N$ of sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ respectively. Suppose:
(i) $BD$ bisects $KM$ at a point $Q$;
(ii) $Q$ is equidistant from all vertices $A, B, C, D$; and
(iii) the ratio $\frac{LK}{LM} = \frac{CD}{CB}$.
Show that $ABCD$ must be a square.

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with midpoints $K, L, M, N$ of sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Suppose:
(i) $BD$ bisects $KM$ at point $Q$;
(ii) $QA = QB = QC = QD$; and
(iii) $\frac{LK}{LM} = \frac{CB}{CD}$.
Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with midpoints $K, L, M, N$ of sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Suppose:
(i) $BD$ bisects $KM$ at point $Q$;
(ii) $QA = QB = QC = QD$; and
(iii) $\frac{LK}{LM} = 1$.
Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with midpoints $K, L, M, N$ of sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Suppose:
(i) $BD$ bisects $KM$ at point $Q$;
(ii) $QA = QB = QC = QD$; and
(iii) $\frac{LM}{LK} = \frac{CD}{CB}$.
Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

positive_text: Let $\alpha$ be a real solution of the equation $x^{5} - x^{3} + x = 2$. Prove that the floor of $\alpha^{6}$ is equal to 3.

negatives.text: If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5} + x^{3} - x - 2 = 0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{6}\right] = 3$.
If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5} - x^{3} + x - 2 = 0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{7}\right] = 3$.
If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5} - x^{3} + x - 2 = 0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{6}\right] = 4$.

positive_text:
Prove that for each positive integer $n$ there exists a unique pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers satisfying
$$
n = a + \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2)
$$

negatives.text:
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that
$$
n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2) - a
$$

Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that
$$
n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b)(a + b - 1) + a
$$

Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that
$$
n = \frac{1}{2}(a - b - 1)(a - b - 2) + a
$$

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ of triangle $ABC$ slides along the side $BC$ towards $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ from inside, it is also tangent to the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ of triangle $ABC$ slides on $BC$ in the direction of $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ externally, it also touches the altitude through $A$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ of triangle $ABC$ slides on $BC$ in the direction of $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ internally, it also touches the median from $A$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ of triangle $ABC$ slides on $BC$ in the direction of $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ internally, it also touches the angle bisector from $A$.

positive_text:
Determine all real-valued functions $f$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$, the identity
$$
 f(x+y) + f(x)f(y) = f(x)(1+y) + f(y)(1+x) + f(xy)
$$
holds true.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the equation
$$
 f(x+y) - f(x)f(y) = (1+y)f(x) + (1+x)f(y) + f(xy),
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the equation
$$
 f(x+y) + f(x)f(y) = (1+y)f(x) + (1+x)f(y) + f(x)f(y),
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the equation
$$
 f(x+y) + f(x)f(y) = (1+y)f(x) + (1+x)f(y) - f(xy),
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text:
Let $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ be a permutation of the integers $1, 2, \dots, n$ arranged in a circular sequence. Determine
$$
\min \sum_{i=1}^{n} |b_i - b_{i+1}| \quad \text{and} \quad \max \sum_{i=1}^{n} |b_i - b_{i+1}|,
$$
where $b_{n+1} = b_1$ and the minimum and maximum are computed over all such permutations.

negatives.text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be an arbitrary arrangement of numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ on a circle. Find
$$
\min \sum_{j=1}^{n} (a_j - a_{j+1})^2 \quad \text{and} \quad \max \sum_{j=1}^{n} (a_j - a_{j+1})^2,
$$
where $a_{n+1} = a_1$ and the extrema are taken over all such arrangements.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be an arbitrary arrangement of numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ on a circle. Find
$$
\min \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j + a_{j+1}| \quad \text{and} \quad \max \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j + a_{j+1}|,
$$
where $a_{n+1} = a_1$ and the extrema are taken over all such arrangements.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be an arbitrary arrangement of numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ on a line instead of a circle. Find
$$
\min \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j - a_{j+1}| \quad \text{and} \quad \max \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j - a_{j+1}|,
$$
where $a_{n+1}$ is undefined and the extrema are taken over all such linear arrangements.

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $P$ lie on $AD$. Let $E$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AC$. If $\frac{AP}{PD} = \frac{BP}{PE} = \lambda$, $\frac{BD}{AD} = m$, and $z = m^2(1+\lambda)$, prove that
$$
 z^2 - (\lambda^3 - \lambda^2 - 2)z + 1 = 0
$$
Deduce that $\lambda \geq 2$ and equality holds if and only if $ABC$ is equilateral.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $P$ a point on $AD$. Suppose $E$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AC$. If $\frac{AP}{PD} = \frac{BP}{PE} = \lambda$, $\frac{BD}{AD} = m$, and $z = m^2(1+\lambda)$, prove that
$$
 z^2 + (\lambda^3 - \lambda^2 - 2)z + 1 = 0
$$
Hence show that $\lambda \geq 2$ and $\lambda = 2$ if and only if $ABC$ is equilateral.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $P$ a point on $AD$. Suppose $E$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AC$. If $\frac{AP}{PD} = \frac{BP}{PE} = \lambda$, $\frac{BD}{AD} = m$, and $z = m^2(1+\lambda)$, prove that
$$
 z^2 - (\lambda^3 - \lambda^2 - 2)^2 z + 1 = 0
$$
Hence show that $\lambda \geq 2$ and $\lambda = 2$ if and only if $ABC$ is equilateral.

positive_text: Show that there exist infinitely many pairs $(a, b)$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ and $a < b$ such that $\frac{(a + b)(a + b + 1)}{ab}$ is an integer.

negatives.text: Prove that there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers such that $m < n$ and $\frac{(m+n)(m+n-1)}{mn}$ is an integer.
Prove that there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers such that $m < n$ and $\frac{(m+n)(m+n+1)}{m+n}$ is an integer.
Prove that there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers such that $m < n$ and $\frac{(m+n)(m+n+1)}{m+n+1}$ is an integer.

positive_text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle and let } P \text{ be an interior point such that } \angle BPC = 90^{\circ} \text{ and } \angle BAP = \angle BCP. \text{ Let } M, N \text{ be the midpoints of } AC, BC \text{ respectively. If } BP = 2PM, \text{ prove that points } A, P, N \text{ lie on a straight line.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with an interior point } P \text{ such that } \angle BPC = 90^{\circ} \text{ and } \angle BAP = \angle CBP. \text{ Let } M, N \text{ be the midpoints of } AC, BC. \text{ Suppose } BP = 2PM. \text{ Prove that } A, P, N \text{ are collinear.}

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with an interior point } P \text{ such that } \angle BPC = 120^{\circ} \text{ and } \angle BAP = \angle BCP. \text{ Let } M, N \text{ be the midpoints of } AC, BC. \text{ Suppose } BP = 2PM. \text{ Prove that } A, P, N \text{ are collinear.}

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with an interior point } P \text{ such that } \angle BPC = 90^{\circ} \text{ and } \angle BAP = \angle BCP. \text{ Let } M, N \text{ be the midpoints of } AC, BC. \text{ Suppose } BP = 2PM. \text{ Prove that } A, P, N \text{ are not collinear.}

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. If $3^n + 4^n \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$, prove that $7 \mid n$.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. If $n$ divides $3^n - 4^n$, prove that $7$ divides $n$.
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. If $n$ divides $3^n + 4^{n+1}$, prove that $7$ divides $n$.
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. If $n$ divides $3^n + 4^n$, prove that $n$ is a power of $7$.

positive_text: Determine all integers $n \ge 2$ and all primes $p, q, r$ such that for any set of $n$ distinct positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$, if for all $1 \le j < k \le n$, $p \mid (a_j - a_k)$, $q \mid (a_j - a_k)$, or $r \mid (a_j - a_k)$, then it must be the case that one of $p, q, r$ divides every difference $a_j - a_k$ for $1 \le j < k \le n$.

negatives.text: Find all integers $n \ge 2$ and primes $p, q, r$ such that whenever distinct positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ are such that the difference $a_j - a_k$, $1 \le j < k \le n$ is divisible by at least one of $p, q, r$, then the product $pqr$ divides all the differences $a_j - a_k$, $1 \le j < k \le n$.

Find all integers $n \ge 2$ and primes $p, q, r$ such that whenever distinct positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ are such that the difference $a_j - a_k$, $1 \le j < k \le n$ is divisible by at least one of $p, q, r$, then the sum $a_j + a_k$ is divisible by one of $p, q, r$.

Find all integers $n \ge 2$ and primes $p, q, r$ such that whenever distinct positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ are such that the difference $a_j - a_k$, $1 \le j < k \le n$ is divisible by at least one of $p, q, r$, then the maximum of $p, q, r$ divides all the differences $a_j - a_k$, $1 \le j < k \le n$.

positive_text: Let $\{b_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence defined by $b_n = 1 - \left(\left\lfloor \sqrt{n} \right\rfloor^2 = n\right)$, where $\lfloor \cdot \rfloor$ is the floor function. Let $y = 0.b_1 b_2 b_3 \ldots$ be the real number with the $n$-th decimal digit equal to $b_n$. Determine whether $y$ is rational or irrational.

negatives.text: Define a sequence $\{e_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ as follows: $e_n = 1$ if the number of positive divisors of $n$ is odd, and $e_n = 0$ otherwise. Let $u = 0.e_1 e_2 e_3 \ldots$ be the real number with $e_n$ as the $n$-th digit in its decimal expansion. Determine whether $u$ is rational or irrational.

Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be defined by $f_n = 0$ if $n$ is a square of a prime number and $f_n = 1$ otherwise. Let $v = 0.f_1 f_2 f_3 \ldots$ be the real number with $f_n$ as the $n$-th digit in its decimal expansion. Determine whether $v$ is rational or irrational.

Define a sequence $\{g_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ by $g_n = 0$ if the number of prime divisors of $n$ is odd, and $g_n = 1$ otherwise. Let $t = 0.g_1 g_2 g_3 \ldots$ be the real number with $g_n$ as the $n$-th digit in its decimal expansion. Determine whether $t$ is rational or irrational.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$ with $AB > AC$, let $AM$ be the median from $A$ to $BC$, and $AK$ be the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. A point $L$ lies on $AM$ such that $\angle KLC = \angle ACB$. Show that $CL$ is perpendicular to $AK$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB > AC$. Let $AM$ be the median and $AK$ be the angle bisector with $M, K$ on $BC$. Let $L$ be a point on $AM$ such that $KL$ is perpendicular to $AC$. Prove that $CL$ is perpendicular to $AK$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB > AC$. Let $AM$ be the median and $AK$ be the angle bisector with $M, K$ on $BC$. Let $L$ be a point on $AK$ such that $KL$ is parallel to $AC$. Prove that $CL$ is perpendicular to $AK$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB > AC$. Let $AM$ be the median and $AK$ be the angle bisector with $M, K$ on $BC$. Let $L$ be a point on $AM$ such that $KL$ is parallel to $AB$. Prove that $CL$ is perpendicular to $AK$.

positive_text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be an acute triangle with orthocentre } H. \text{ Let } h_{\max} \text{ be the greatest height of the triangle. Show that } \$$ AH + BH + CH \leq 2 h_{\max} \$$

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be an acute-angled triangle with orthocentre } H. \text{ Let } h_{\max} \text{ be the largest altitude. Prove that } \$$ AH + BH + CH \geq 2 h_{\max} \$$
\text{Let } ABC \text{ be an acute-angled triangle with orthocentre } H. \text{ Let } h_{\max} \text{ be the largest altitude. Prove that } \$$ AH^2 + BH^2 + CH^2 \leq 2 h_{\max}^2 \$$
\text{Let } ABC \text{ be an acute-angled triangle with orthocentre } H. \text{ Let } h_{\min} \text{ be the smallest altitude. Prove that } \$$ AH + BH + CH \leq 2 h_{\min} \$$

positive_text: \sum_{k=0}^{n} \left[ \binom{3n+2-k}{k} 2^k - \binom{3n+1-k}{k-1} 2^{k-1} \right] = 2^{3n},\quad\text{where the second term is 0 for } k = 0.

negatives.text: \sum_{j=0}^{n} \left\{ \binom{3n+2-j}{j} 2^j + \binom{3n+1-j}{j-1} 2^{j-1} \right\} = 2^{3n},\quad\text{where the second term is 0 for } j = 0.
\sum_{j=0}^{n} \left\{ \binom{3n+2-j}{j} 2^j - \binom{3n+1-j}{j-1} 2^{j} \right\} = 2^{3n},\quad\text{where the second term is 0 for } j = 0.
\sum_{j=0}^{n} \left\{ \binom{3n+2-j}{j} 2^j - \binom{3n+1-j}{j} 2^{j-1} \right\} = 2^{3n},\quad\text{where the second term is 0 for } j = 0.

positive_text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be integers with $b$ even. Suppose the cubic polynomial $x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c$ has roots $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ satisfying $\alpha^2 = \beta + \gamma$. Prove $\alpha$ is an integer and $\beta \neq \gamma$.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be integers such that $b$ is even. Suppose the equation $x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c = 0$ has roots $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ such that $\alpha^2 = \beta - \gamma$. Prove that $\alpha$ is an integer and $\beta \neq \gamma$.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be integers such that $b$ is odd. Suppose the equation $x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c = 0$ has roots $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ such that $\alpha^2 = \beta + \gamma$. Prove that $\alpha$ is an integer and $\beta \neq \gamma$.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be integers such that $b$ is even. Suppose the equation $x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c = 0$ has roots $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ such that $\alpha = \beta + \gamma$. Prove that $\alpha$ is an integer and $\beta \neq \gamma$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$ such that $BC = 3DC$. Let $P$ be a point on $AD$ such that $\angle BAC = \angle BPD$. Show that $\angle BAC = 2\angle DPC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$ such that $BD = 2DC$. Let $P$ be a point on $AD$ such that $\angle BAC = \angle DPC$. Prove that $\angle BAC = 2\angle BPD$.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$ such that $BD = DC$. Let $P$ be a point on $AD$ such that $\angle BAC = \angle BPD$. Prove that $\angle BAC = 2\angle DPC$.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$ such that $BD = 2DC$. Let $P$ be a point on $AD$ such that $\angle BPD = 2\angle BAC$. Prove that $\angle BAC = 2\angle DPC$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with side $AB = \sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}$, and suppose the central angle subtended by $AB$ is $\frac{3\pi}{4}$. Determine the largest possible area of $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with side $AB = \sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}$ and suppose the central angle subtended by $AB$ is $45^\circ$. Find the maximum possible area of $ABCD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with side $AB = \sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}$ and suppose the central angle subtended by $AB$ is $135^\circ$. Find the minimum possible area of $ABCD$.
Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with side $AB = \sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}$ and suppose the inscribed angle subtended by $AB$ is $135^\circ$. Find the maximum possible area of $ABCD$.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{R}^+$ denote the set of all positive real numbers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^+$, it holds that
$$
 f(a) + f(b) \le \frac{f(a+b)}{2}, \quad \frac{f(a)}{a} + \frac{f(b)}{b} \ge \frac{f(a+b)}{a+b}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{R}^+$ denote the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
 f(x) + f(y) \le \frac{f(x+y)}{2}, \quad \frac{f(x)}{x} + \frac{f(y)}{y} \le \frac{f(x+y)}{x+y},
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+$.

Let $\mathbb{R}^+$ denote the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
 f(x) + f(y) \ge \frac{f(x+y)}{2}, \quad \frac{f(x)}{x} + \frac{f(y)}{y} \ge \frac{f(x+y)}{x+y},
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+$.

Let $\mathbb{R}^+$ denote the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
 f(x) + f(y) \le \frac{f(x+y)}{2}, \quad \frac{f(x)}{x} + \frac{f(y)}{y} \ge \frac{f(x+y)}{x+y} + 1,
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+$.

positive_text: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f(x + y + xy) = f(x) + f(y) + f(xy)$ for all real numbers $x, y$. Prove that $f$ satisfies $f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f(x + y + xy) = f(x) + f(y) - f(xy)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that $f$ satisfies $f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f(x + y + xy) = f(x) + f(y) + f(xy)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that $f$ satisfies $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f(x^2 + y^2) = f(x) + f(y) + f(xy)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that $f$ satisfies $f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text: Let $P(z) = \sum_{k=m}^{n} c_k z^k$ be a polynomial with complex coefficients such that $c_m \neq 0$, $c_n \neq 0$ and $n > m$. Prove that $$\max_{|z|=1}\{|P(z)|\} \ge \sqrt{\sum_{k=m}^{n} |c_k|^2 + 2|c_m c_n|}.$$

negatives.text: Let $P(z) = a_n z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \dots + a_m z^m$ be a polynomial with complex coefficients such that $a_m \neq 0$, $a_n \neq 0$ and $n > m$. Prove that $$\max_{|z|=1}\{|P(z)|\} \ge \sqrt{\sum_{k=m}^{n} |a_k|^2 - 2|a_m a_n|}.$$

Let $P(z) = a_n z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \dots + a_m z^m$ be a polynomial with complex coefficients such that $a_m \neq 0$, $a_n \neq 0$ and $n > m$. Prove that $$\max_{|z| < 1}\{|P(z)|\} \ge \sqrt{\sum_{k=m}^{n} |a_k|^2 + 2|a_m a_n|}.$$

Let $P(z) = a_n z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \dots + a_m z^m$ be a polynomial with complex coefficients such that $a_m \neq 0$, $a_n \neq 0$ and $n > m$. Prove that $$\max_{|z|=1}\{|P(z)|\} \le \sqrt{\sum_{k=m}^{n} |a_k|^2 + 2|a_m a_n|}.$$

positive_text: Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $a$ and $b$, with $b > 1$ and $a > b\sqrt{3} - 1$, such that $ab + 1$ is divisible by $a + b$ and $ab - 1$ is divisible by $a - b$.

negatives.text: Show that there exist infinitely many pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers with the property that $a + b$ divides $ab + 1$, $a - b$ divides $ab + 1$, $b > 1$ and $a > b\sqrt{3} - 1$.

positive_text: A positive integer $n$ admits a unique decomposition into a non-decreasing sequence of odd positive integers $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k)$ such that $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_k = n$ and for every integer $m$ in $[1, n]$, $m$ has a unique representation as a subsum of the $a_i$. The sequence $(1, 1, 3, 3)$ is an example for $n = 8$. How many such sequences exist for $n = 9999$?

negatives.text: For a positive integer $n$, a sum-friendly odd partition of $n$ is a sequence $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k)$ of odd positive integers with $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_k = n$ such that for all positive integers $m \le n$, $m$ can be written as a subsum $m = a_{i_1} + a_{i_2} + \dots + a_{i_r}$ in at least one way. How many such sequences exist for $n = 9999$?

For a positive integer $n$, a sum-friendly odd partition of $n$ is a sequence $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k)$ of odd positive integers with $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_k = n$ such that for all positive integers $m \le n$, $m$ can be uniquely written as a subsum $m = a_{i_1} + a_{i_2} + \dots + a_{i_r}$. However, the sequence is now allowed to contain repeated subsums that differ in indices. For example, $(1, 1, 3, 3)$ is a sum-friendly odd partition of $8$. How many such sequences exist for $n = 9999$?

For a positive integer $n$, a sum-friendly odd partition of $n$ is a sequence $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k)$ of odd positive integers with $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_k = n$ such that for all positive integers $m \le n$, $m$ can be uniquely written as a subsum $m = a_{i_1} + a_{i_2} + \dots + a_{i_r}$, where the sequence is allowed to be in any order. How many such sequences exist for $n = 9999$?

positive_text:
Let $ h $ be an integer such that $ h \ge 3 $, and define $ X = \{ n \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \mid n \ge 2h \} $. Suppose $ S $ is a nonempty subset of $ X $ satisfying: 
* For all $ a, b \ge h $, if $ a + b \in S $, then $ ab \in S $;
* For all $ a, b \ge h $, if $ ab \in S $, then $ a + b \in S $. 
Prove that $ S = X $.

negatives.text:
Let $ h \ge 3 $ be an integer and $ X $ the set of all positive integers that are greater than or equal to $ 2h $. Let $ S $ be a nonempty subset of $ X $ such that the following two conditions hold: 
* if $ a + b \in S $ with $ a \ge h, b \ge h $, then $ ab \notin S $;
* if $ ab \in S $ with $ a \ge h, b \ge h $, then $ a + b \in S $. 
Prove that $ S = X $.

Let $ h \ge 3 $ be an integer and $ X $ the set of all positive integers that are greater than or equal to $ 2h $. Let $ S $ be a nonempty subset of $ X $ such that the following two conditions hold: 
* if $ a + b \in S $ with $ a \ge h, b \ge h $, then $ ab^2 \in S $;
* if $ ab^2 \in S $ with $ a \ge h, b \ge h $, then $ a + b \in S $. 
Prove that $ S = X $.

Let $ h \ge 3 $ be an integer and $ X $ the set of all positive integers that are greater than or equal to $ 2h $. Let $ S $ be a nonempty subset of $ X $ such that the following two conditions hold: 
* if $ a + b \in S $ with $ a \ge h, b \ge h $, then $ ab \in S $;
* if $ ab \in S $ with $ a \ge h, b \ge h $, then $ a + b \notin S $. 
Prove that $ S = X $.

positive_text: Two circles $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ touch externally at point $R$. A line $l_{1}$ is tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $P$ and passes through the center $O_{1}$ of $\Gamma_{1}$. Another line $l_{2}$ is tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $Q$ and passes through the center $O_{2}$ of $\Gamma_{2}$. Let $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ intersect at a point $K$ such that $KP = KQ$. Show that triangle $PQR$ is equilateral.

negatives.text: Let $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ be two circles touching externally at $R$. A line $l_{1}$, passing through the center $O_{1}$ of $\Gamma_{1}$, is tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $P$. A line $l_{2}$, passing through the center $O_{2}$ of $\Gamma_{2}$, is tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $Q$. Suppose $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ intersect at $K$ such that $KP = 2KQ$. Prove that triangle $PQR$ is equilateral.

Let $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ be two circles touching externally at $R$. A line $l_{1}$, passing through the center $O_{1}$ of $\Gamma_{1}$, is tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $P$. A line $l_{2}$, passing through the center $O_{2}$ of $\Gamma_{2}$, is tangent to $\Gamma_{1}$ at $Q$. Suppose $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ intersect at $K$ such that $KP = KQ$. Prove that triangle $PQR$ is equilateral.

Let $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ be two circles touching externally at $R$. A line $l_{1}$, passing through the center $O_{1}$ of $\Gamma_{1}$, is tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $P$. A line $l_{2}$, passing through the center $O_{2}$ of $\Gamma_{2}$, is tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $Q$. Suppose $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ intersect at $K$ such that $KP = KQ$. Prove that triangle $PQR$ is isosceles.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meeting at $P$. Let $PE$, $PF$, $PG$, and $PH$ be the perpendiculars from $P$ to the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Prove that $ABCD$ is tangential (i.e., has an incircle) if and only if $$\frac{1}{PE} + \frac{1}{PG} = \frac{1}{PF} + \frac{1}{PH}$$

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersecting at $P$. Let $PE$, $PF$, $PG$, and $PH$ be the perpendiculars from $P$ to sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Prove that $ABCD$ is tangential if and only if $$\frac{1}{PE} + \frac{1}{PG} = \frac{1}{PF} - \frac{1}{PH}$$

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersecting at $P$. Let $PE$, $PF$, $PG$, and $PH$ be the perpendiculars from $P$ to sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Prove that $ABCD$ is tangential if and only if $$\frac{1}{PE^2} + \frac{1}{PG^2} = \frac{1}{PF^2} + \frac{1}{PH^2}$$

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersecting at $P$. Let $PE$, $PF$, $PG$, and $PH$ be the perpendiculars from $P$ to sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Prove that $ABCD$ is tangential if and only if $$\frac{1}{PE} + \frac{1}{PF} = \frac{1}{PG} + \frac{1}{PH}$$

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. If the orthocenter of the triangle lies on its incircle, determine the value of $AB/BC$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle in which $AB = AC$. Suppose the centroid of the triangle lies on the in-circle. Find the ratio $AB/BC$.
Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle in which $AB = AC$. Suppose the orthocenter of the triangle lies on the circumcircle. Find the ratio $AB/BC$.
Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle in which $AB = AC$. Suppose the orthocenter of the triangle lies on the incircle and $\angle BAC = 90^\circ$. Find the ratio $AB/BC$.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{N}$ be the set of positive integers. Define a function $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ by $f(2m) = m$ and $f(2m + 1) = 2m + 2$. Let $f^r(n) = f(f^{r-1}(n))$ for $r > 1$. 
(i) Prove that for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists $r$ such that $f^r(n) = 1$.
(ii) For each $r \in \mathbb{N}$, let $d_r$ be the number of $n$ such that $f^r(n) = 1$. Show that $d_{r+2} = d_{r+1} + d_r$ for $r \ge 1$.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{N}$ be the set of natural numbers. Define $T: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ by $T(2k) = k$ and $T(2k + 1) = 2k - 1$. Let $T^k(n)$ denote the $k$-fold composition of $T$.
(i) Show that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists $k$ such that $T^k(n) = 1$.
(ii) Let $c_k$ be the number of $n$ such that $T^k(n) = 1$. Prove that $c_{k+2} = c_{k+1} + c_k$ for $k \ge 1$.

Let $\mathbb{N}$ be the set of natural numbers. Define $T: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ by $T(2k) = k$ and $T(2k + 1) = 2k + 1$. Let $T^k(n)$ denote the $k$-fold composition of $T$.
(i) Show that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists $k$ such that $T^k(n) = 1$.
(ii) Let $c_k$ be the number of $n$ such that $T^k(n) = 1$. Prove that $c_{k+2} = c_{k+1} + c_k$ for $k \ge 1$.

Let $\mathbb{N}$ be the set of natural numbers. Define $T: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ by $T(2k) = k$ and $T(2k + 1) = 2k + 2$. Let $T^k(n)$ denote the $k$-fold composition of $T$.
(i) Show that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists $k$ such that $T^k(n) = 1$.
(ii) Let $c_k$ be the number of $n$ such that $T^k(n) = 1$. Prove that $c_{k+2} = 2c_{k+1}$ for $k \ge 1$.

positive_text: Given that $2016$ distinct points on a circle are painted red and all other points are blue, show that for every integer $n \ge 3$, there exists a regular $n$-gon with all vertices in the blue set.

negatives.text: Suppose $2016$ points of the circumference of a circle are coloured red and the remaining points are coloured blue. Given any natural number $n \ge 3$, prove that there is a regular $n$-sided polygon with at least one vertex red.

Suppose $2016$ points of the circumference of a circle are coloured red and the remaining points are coloured blue. Given any natural number $n \ge 3$, prove that there is a regular $n$-sided polygon with all of its vertices red.

Suppose $2016$ points of the circumference of a circle are coloured red and the remaining points are coloured blue. Given any natural number $n \ge 3$, prove that there is a regular $n$-sided polygon with exactly one vertex red.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a right-angled triangle at $B$. A point $D$ lies on $AC$ such that the in-radii of triangles $ABD$ and $CBD$ are equal, both equal to $r'$. If $r$ is the in-radius of triangle $ABC$, prove that $$\frac{1}{r'} = \frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{BD}.$$

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B = 90^\circ$. Let $D$ be a point on side $AC$ such that the in-radii of $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CBD$ are equal to $r'$. If $r$ is the in-radius of $\triangle ABC$, prove that $$\frac{1}{r'} = \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{BD}.$$

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B = 90^\circ$. Let $D$ be a point on side $AC$ such that the in-radii of $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CBD$ are equal to $r'$. If $r$ is the in-radius of $\triangle ABC$, prove that $$\frac{1}{r'} = \frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{CD}.$$

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B = 90^\circ$. Let $D$ be a point on side $AC$ such that the in-radii of $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CBD$ are equal to $r'$. If $r$ is the in-radius of $\triangle ABC$, prove that $$\frac{1}{r'} = \frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{AD}.$$

positive_text: Let $a_1, a_2, \dots$ be a non-constant arithmetic progression. Suppose $p > 1$ and $q > 1$ are relatively prime integers such that $a_1^2$, $a_{p+1}^2$, and $a_{q+1}^2$ lie on the same arithmetic progression. Prove that every term in the progression is an integer.

negatives.text: Consider a non-constant arithmetic progression $a_1, a_2, \dots$. Suppose there exist relatively prime positive integers $p > 1$ and $q > 1$ such that $a_1^2$, $a_{p+1}^2$, and $a_{q+1}^2$ are terms in the same geometric progression. Prove that the terms of the arithmetic progression are all integers.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots$ be a non-constant arithmetic progression. Suppose there exist relatively prime positive integers $p > 1$ and $q > 1$ such that $a_1^2$, $a_{p+1}^2$, and $a_{q+1}^2$ are all rational numbers. Prove that the terms of the arithmetic progression are all integers.

Consider a non-constant arithmetic progression $a_1, a_2, \dots$. Suppose there exist relatively prime positive integers $p > 1$ and $q > 1$ such that $a_1^2$, $a_{p+1}^2$, and $a_{q+1}^2$ are all terms in the same arithmetic progression. Prove that the terms of the arithmetic progression are all rational numbers.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a non-negative integer such that all the integer roots of the cubic equation $x^3 + \alpha x + 4 - 2 \cdot 2016^n = 0$ exist. Determine all possible values of $\alpha$.

negatives.text: Suppose $n \ge 0$ is an integer and all the roots of $x^3 + \alpha x^2 + 4 - (2 \times 2016^n) = 0$ are integers. Find all possible values of $\alpha$.
Suppose $n \ge 0$ is an integer and all the roots of $x^3 + \alpha x + 4 + (2 \times 2016^n) = 0$ are integers. Find all possible values of $\alpha$.
Suppose $n \ge 0$ is an integer and all the roots of $x^3 + \alpha x + 4 - (2 \times 2016^{2n}) = 0$ are integers. Find all possible values of $\alpha$.

positive_text: Let a polynomial $p(x)$ with real coefficients be defined as a square if it is non-constant and there exists a polynomial $q(x)$ with real coefficients such that $p(x) = q(x)^2$. Suppose that $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are non-constant polynomials over $\mathbb{R}$ with $f(x) \ne q(x)^2$ and $g(x) \ne r(x)^2$ for any polynomials $q(x), r(x)$, yet $f(g(x))$ is a square. Prove that $g(f(x))$ cannot be a square.

negatives.text: A polynomial $p(x)$ with real coefficients is called a square if and only if it is not a constant and there exists a polynomial $q(x)$ with real coefficients such that $p(x) = q(x)^2$. Suppose that $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are non-constant polynomials with real coefficients such that neither of them is a square, but $f(g(x))$ is. Show that $g(f(x))$ is a square.

A polynomial $p(x)$ with real coefficients is called a square if and only if it is not a constant and there exists a polynomial $q(x)$ with real coefficients such that $p(x) = q(x)^2$. Suppose that $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are non-constant polynomials with real coefficients such that neither of them is a square, but $f(g(x))$ is. Show that $f(f(x))$ is not a square.

A polynomial $p(x)$ with real coefficients is called a square if and only if it is not a constant and there exists a polynomial $q(x)$ with real coefficients such that $p(x) = q(x)^2$. Suppose that $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are non-constant polynomials with real coefficients such that neither of them is a square, but $f(g(x))$ is. Show that $g(g(x))$ is not a square.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with incenter $I$. A line is drawn perpendicular to $BI$ at $I$, intersecting side $BC$ at $D$ and side $BA$ at $E$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the incenters of triangles $BIA$ and $BIC$, respectively. If points $D, E, P, Q$ lie on a circle, show that $AB = CB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with incenter $I$. A line is drawn perpendicular to $CI$ at $I$, intersecting $BC$ at $D$ and $BA$ at $E$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the incenters of triangles $BIA$ and $BIC$. Suppose the points $D, E, P, Q$ are concyclic. Prove that $BA = BC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with incenter $I$. A line is drawn perpendicular to $BI$ at $I$, intersecting $BC$ at $D$ and $BA$ at $E$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the incenters of triangles $BIA$ and $BIC$. Suppose the points $D, E, P, Q$ are collinear. Prove that $BA = BC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with incenter $I$. A line is drawn perpendicular to $BI$ at $I$, intersecting $BC$ at $D$ and $BA$ at $E$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the incenters of triangles $BIA$ and $BIC$. Suppose the points $D, E, P, Q$ form a cyclic quadrilateral with $PQ$ as diameter. Prove that $BA = BC$.

positive_text: Let $n$ and $M$ be positive integers with $M > n^{n-1}$. Show that one can find $n$ distinct primes $q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, \ldots, q_{n}$ satisfying the condition $q_{k} \mid M + k$ for all $k$ in $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$.

negatives.text: Let $n$ and $M$ be positive integers with $M > n^{n-1}$. Prove that there are $n$ distinct primes $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{n}$ such that $p_{j}$ divides $M - j$ for $1 \leq j \leq n$.
Let $n$ and $M$ be positive integers with $M > n^{n-1}$. Prove that there are $n$ distinct primes $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{n}$ such that $p_{j}^2$ divides $M + j$ for $1 \leq j \leq n$.
Let $n$ and $M$ be positive integers with $M > n^{n-1}$. Prove that there are $n$ distinct primes $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{n}$ such that $p_{j} + j$ divides $M$ for $1 \leq j \leq n$.

positive_text: Given a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $\angle ABD = 30^\circ$, $\angle BCA = 75^\circ$, $\angle ACD = 25^\circ$ and $CD = CB$. Let $E$ be the second point of intersection of the line $CB$ extended with the circumcircle of triangle $DAC$. Show that $CE = BD$.

negatives.text: In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\angle ABD = 30^\circ$, $\angle BCA = 75^\circ$, $\angle ACD = 25^\circ$ and $CD = CB$. Extend $CB$ to meet the circumcircle of triangle $DAC$ at $E$. Prove that $CE = 2BD$.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\angle ABD = 30^\circ$, $\angle BCA = 75^\circ$, $\angle ACD = 25^\circ$ and $CD = 2CB$. Extend $CB$ to meet the circumcircle of triangle $DAC$ at $E$. Prove that $CE = BD$.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\angle ABD = 30^\circ$, $\angle BCA = 75^\circ$, $\angle ACD = 25^\circ$ and $CD = CB$. Extend $AD$ to meet the circumcircle of triangle $DAC$ at $E$. Prove that $CE = BD$.

positive_text:
Suppose $r > 0$ and the interior of a disc $D(r)$ is colored with two colors. 
1. If $r > \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$, prove that there exist two points $A, B$ inside $D(r)$ with $AB = \pi$ and the same color.
2. Is the result from (1) still valid if $r > \frac{\pi}{2}$?

negatives.text:
Let $r > 0$ and the interior of the disc $D(r)$ be two-colored. 
1. If $r > \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$, show that there are two points $A, B$ in the interior of $D(r)$ with $AB = 2\pi$ and the same color.
2. Does the result in (1) hold if $r > \frac{\pi}{2}$?

Let $r > 0$ and the interior of the disc $D(r)$ be two-colored. 
1. If $r > \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$, prove that there are two points $A, B$ in the interior of $D(r)$ such that $AB < \pi$ and the same color.
2. Does the conclusion in (1) hold if $r > \frac{\pi}{2}$?

Let $r > 0$ and the interior of the disc $D(r)$ be two-colored. 
1. If $r > \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$, prove that there are two points $A, B$ in the interior of $D(r)$ with $AB = \pi$ and opposite colors.
2. Does the result in (1) hold if $r > \frac{\pi}{2}$?

positive_text:
Let $r > 0$ be a real number. Suppose that all points in the open disk $D(r)$ are assigned one of two colors, red or blue.

1. If $r > \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$, prove that there exist two points $A$ and $B$ inside the disk such that the Euclidean distance $AB = \pi$ and both points have the same color.

2. Does the result in (1) remain valid if $r > \frac{\pi}{2}$?

negatives.text:
Let $r > 0$ be a real number. All the interior points of the disc $D(r)$ of radius $r$ are colored with one of two colors, red or blue.

1. If $r > \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$, show that we can find two points $A$ and $B$ in the interior of the disc such that the distance $AB = \pi$ and $A$ and $B$ have different colors.

2. Does the conclusion in (1) hold if $r > \frac{\pi}{2}$?

Let $r > 0$ be a real number. All the interior points of the disc $D(r)$ of radius $r$ are colored with one of two colors, red or blue.

1. If $r > \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$, show that we can find two points $A$ and $B$ in the interior of the disc such that the distance $AB = 1$ and $A$ and $B$ have the same color.

2. Does the conclusion in (1) hold if $r > \frac{\pi}{2}$?

Let $r > 0$ be a real number. All the interior points of the disc $D(r)$ of radius $r$ are colored with one of two colors, red or blue.

1. If $r > \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$, show that we can find two points $A$ and $B$ on the boundary of the disc such that the distance $AB = \pi$ and $A$ and $B$ have the same color.

2. Does the conclusion in (1) hold if $r > \frac{\pi}{2}$?

positive_text: Alice starts with an integer $ N > 1 $ on a blackboard. Every minute, she replaces the number $ x $ with $ 2x + 1 $ if $ x $ is not a perfect cube, or with $ \sqrt[3]{x} $ if it is. Prove that eventually, the number on the blackboard exceeds $ 10^{100} $.

negatives.text: Alice has an integer $ N > 1 $ on a blackboard. Each minute, she replaces the number $ x $ with $ 2x - 1 $ if $ x $ is not a cube, or the cube root of $ x $ otherwise. Prove that eventually, the number on the blackboard exceeds $ 10^{100} $.

Alice starts with an integer $ N > 1 $ on a blackboard. Each minute, she replaces the number $ x $ with $ 2x + 1 $ if $ x $ is not a cube, or $ x^2 $ otherwise. Prove that eventually, the number on the blackboard exceeds $ 10^{100} $.

positive_text: Let $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ be $n$ distinct points in the plane. For each pair $(P_i, P_j)$, define $f(P_i, P_j) = \lfloor \log_2 \|P_i - P_j\| \rfloor$. Prove that the number of distinct values of $f$ is strictly less than $2n$.

negatives.text: Euler marks $n$ different points in the Euclidean plane. For each pair of marked points, Gauss writes down the number $\lfloor \log_2 d^2 \rfloor$ where $d$ is the distance between the two points. Prove that Gauss writes down less than $2n$ distinct values.

Euler marks $n$ different points in the Euclidean plane. For each pair of marked points, Gauss writes down the number $\lceil \log_2 d \rceil$ where $d$ is the distance between the two points. Prove that Gauss writes down less than $2n$ distinct values.

Euler marks $n$ different points in the Euclidean plane. For each pair of marked points, Gauss writes down the number $\lfloor \log_2 (1/d) \rfloor$ where $d$ is the distance between the two points. Prove that Gauss writes down less than $2n$ distinct values.

positive_text: In an acute scalene triangle $ABC$, the incircle touches $BC$ at $D$, and $I$ is the incentre. Let $Z$ be the point diametrically opposite to $A$ on the circumcircle of $ABC$. Point $L$ lies on the internal bisector of $\angle BZC$ such that $LI = AL$. Let $M$ be the arc midpoint of $BZC$, and let $V$ be the midpoint of segment $ID$. Prove that $\angle IML = \angle DVM$.

negatives.text: Suppose an acute scalene triangle $ABC$ has incentre $I$ and incircle touching $BC$ at $D$. Let $Z$ be the antipode of $A$ in the circumcircle of $ABC$. Point $L$ is chosen on the external angle bisector of $\angle BZC$ such that $AL = LI$. Let $M$ be midpoint of arc $BZC$, and let $V$ be the midpoint of $ID$. Prove that $\angle IML = \angle DVM$.

Suppose an acute scalene triangle $ABC$ has incentre $I$ and incircle touching $BC$ at $D$. Let $Z$ be the antipode of $A$ in the circumcircle of $ABC$. Point $L$ is chosen on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BZC$ such that $AL = 2LI$. Let $M$ be midpoint of arc $BZC$, and let $V$ be the midpoint of $ID$. Prove that $\angle IML = \angle DVM$.

Suppose an acute scalene triangle $ABC$ has incentre $I$ and incircle touching $BC$ at $D$. Let $Z$ be the antipode of $A$ in the circumcircle of $ABC$. Point $L$ is chosen on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BZC$ such that $AL = LI$. Let $M$ be midpoint of arc $BZC$, and let $V$ be the midpoint of $ID$. Prove that $\angle IML = \angle VDM$.

positive_text: Let $f(k)$ represent the sum of the decimal digits of a positive integer $k$. Is there a positive integer $M$ such that $f(2^n) \le f(2^{n+1})$ holds for all $n > M$?

negatives.text: Let $S(k)$ denote the sum of digits (in base 10) of any positive integer $k$. Does there exist a positive integer $N$ so that $S(2^n) > S(2^{n+1})$ for all integers $n > N$?
Let $S(k)$ denote the sum of digits (in base 10) of any positive integer $k$. Does there exist a positive integer $N$ so that $S(2^n) \le S(2^{n+1})$ for all integers $n < N$?
Let $S(k)$ denote the sum of digits (in base 10) of any positive integer $k$. Does there exist a positive integer $N$ so that $S(2^n) \le S(2^{n+1})$ for all even integers $n > N$?

positive_text: Suppose $P(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ is a polynomial of degree $d \ge 2$. Show that there cannot exist an infinite sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of rational numbers satisfying $P(a_n) = a_{n-1} + n$ for all $n \ge 1$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $d \ge 2$. Prove there is no infinite sequence $a_0, a_1, \dots$ of rational numbers such that $P(a_i) = a_{i-1} - i$ for all $i \ge 1$.
Let $P(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $d \ge 2$. Prove there is no infinite sequence $a_0, a_1, \dots$ of rational numbers such that $P(a_i) = a_{i-1} + 2^i$ for all $i \ge 1$.
Let $P(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $d = 1$. Prove there is no infinite sequence $a_0, a_1, \dots$ of rational numbers such that $P(a_i) = a_{i-1} + i$ for all $i \ge 1$.

positive_text:
Let two circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ intersect at points $P$ and $K$. A common tangent $XY$ is drawn near $P$, with $X$ lying on $\omega_1$ and $Y$ on $\omega_2$. The line $XP$ intersects $\omega_2$ again at $C$, and the line $YP$ intersects $\omega_1$ again at $B$. The lines $BX$ and $CY$ intersect at point $A$. Let $Q$ be the second point of intersection of the circumcircles of $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle AXY$. Show that
$$
\angle QXA = \angle QKP
$$
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ be natural numbers such that for all $i \ne j$, $a_j - a_i$ divides $a_i$. Prove that for all $i < j$, $\frac{a_j}{j} \le \frac{a_i}{i}$.

negatives.text: Let $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ be natural numbers such that for all $i \ne j$, $a_i$ is divisible by $a_i + a_j$. Prove that for all $i < j$, $i a_j \le j a_i$.
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ be natural numbers such that for all $i \ne j$, $a_i$ divides $a_j + a_i$. Prove that for all $i < j$, $i a_j \le j a_i$.

positive_text: Let $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{1389}$ be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers satisfying $2a_i \ge a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$ for all $1 \le i \le 1388$. Determine the largest constant $c$ such that $$ \sum_{k=0}^{1389} k a_k^2 \ge c \sum_{k=0}^{1389} a_k^2 $$ for all such sequences.

negatives.text: Let $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{1389}$ be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers satisfying $a_i \ge \frac{a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}}{2}$ for all $1 < i < 1389$. Find the largest constant $c$ such that $$ \sum_{i=0}^{1389} i a_i^2 \le c \sum_{i=0}^{1389} a_i^2 $$ holds for all such sequences.

Let $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{1389}$ be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers satisfying $a_i \ge \frac{a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}}{2}$ for all $1 < i < 1389$. Find the largest constant $c$ such that $$ \sum_{i=0}^{1389} i a_i^3 \ge c \sum_{i=0}^{1389} a_i^2 $$ holds for all such sequences.

positive_text: Determine all integers $n \ge 2$ for which the condition $\text{parity}(i + j) = \text{parity}\left(\binom{n}{i} + \binom{n}{j}\right)$ holds for all $i, j$ with $0 \le i, j \le n$.

negatives.text: Find all $n \ge 2$ such that for all $0 \le i, j \le n$, $i \cdot j$ and $\binom{n}{i} + \binom{n}{j}$ have the same parity.
Find all $n \ge 2$ such that for all $0 \le i, j \le n$, $\binom{n}{i} + \binom{n}{j} + i$ and $j$ have the same parity.

positive_text: Let $Q$ be the collection of all contiguous intervals of natural numbers. For any subset $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_k\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, define $g(A)$ as the length of the largest interval in $A$, and $f(A)$ as the largest gap between consecutive elements in $A$. Set $G(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} g(A)$ and $F(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} f(A)$. Show there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n > m$, $F(n) > G(n)$.

negatives.text: Let $Q$ be the set of all subsets of natural numbers that form an interval $[i, j]$, for $i < j$. For any subset $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_k\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, define $g(A) = \max \{ |B| \mid B \subset A, B \in Q \}$ and $f(A) = \min_{1 \le i \le k-1} (a_{i+1} - a_i)$. Define $G(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} g(A)$ and $F(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} f(A)$. Prove there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n > m$, $F(n) > G(n)$.

Let $Q$ be the family of all subsets of natural numbers that form an interval $[i, j]$, for $i < j$. For any subset $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_k\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, define $g(A) = \max \{ |B| \mid B \subset A, B \in Q \}$ and $f(A) = \max_{1 \le i \le k-1} (a_{i+1} - a_i)$. Define $G(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} g(A)^2$ and $F(n) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}} f(A)$. Prove there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n > m$, $F(n) > G(n)$.

positive_text: Let a polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ be called cyclic if $P(x, y, z) = P(y, z, x)$. Show that there exist four cyclic polynomials $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4$ such that any cyclic polynomial $P$ can be expressed as $$P(x, y, z) = Q(P_1(x, y, z), P_2(x, y, z), P_3(x, y, z), P_4(x, y, z))$$ for some four-variable polynomial $Q$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x, y, z)$ be a cyclic polynomial, i.e., $P(x, y, z) = P(y, z, x)$. Prove there exist cyclic polynomials $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4$ such that for any cyclic polynomial $P$, there exists a polynomial $Q$ in four variables satisfying $$P(x, y, z) = Q(P_1(x, y, z), P_2(x, y, z), P_3(x, y, z), P_4(x, y, z)).$$ Additionally, assume that $Q$ must be symmetric in all its variables.

Let $P(x, y, z)$ be a cyclic polynomial, i.e., $P(x, y, z) = P(y, z, x)$. Prove there exist cyclic polynomials $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4$ such that for any cyclic polynomial $P$, there exists a polynomial $Q$ in four variables satisfying $$P(x, y, z) = Q(P_1(x, y, z), P_2(y, x, z), P_3(x, z, y), P_4(z, y, x)).$$

Let $P(x, y, z)$ be a cyclic polynomial, i.e., $P(x, y, z) = P(y, z, x)$. Prove there exist cyclic polynomials $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4$ such that for any cyclic polynomial $P$, there exists a polynomial $Q$ in four variables satisfying $$P(x, y, z) = Q(P_1(x, y, z), P_2(x, y, z)^2, P_3(x, y, z), P_4(x, y, z)).$$

positive_text: Determine all pairs of coprime positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that the decimal $b.a$ equals $\frac{a}{b}$. For example, if $a = 92$ and $b = 13$, then $b.a = 13.92$.

negatives.text: Find all coprime natural numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $b + a = \frac{a}{b}$.
Find all coprime positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $b.a = \frac{b}{a}$. (Note: $13.92 = 13.92$ if $a = 92$ and $b = 13$.)
Find all coprime natural numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $b.a = a + \frac{1}{b}$.

positive_text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. A point $X$ lies on the arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ not containing $A$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the projections of $X$ onto $BI$ and $CI$, respectively, and let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $EF$. Suppose that $MB = MC$. If $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to side $BC$, prove that $\angle BAD = \angle CAX$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. A point $X$ is on the arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ not containing $A$. If $E$ and $F$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $X$ to $BI$ and $CI$, respectively, and $M$ is the midpoint of $EF$, then $MB > MC$. If $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$, show that $\angle BAD = \angle CAX$.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. A point $X$ is on the arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ not containing $A$. If $E$ and $F$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $X$ to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, and $M$ is the midpoint of $EF$, then $MB = MC$. If $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$, show that $\angle BAD = \angle CAX$.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. A point $X$ is on the arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ not containing $A$. If $E$ and $F$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $X$ to $BI$ and $CI$, respectively, and $M$ is the midpoint of $EF$, then $MB = MC$. If $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to $AB$, show that $\angle BAD = \angle CAX$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have circumcircle $\omega$ and circumcenter $O$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of arc $BC$ of $\omega$ not containing $A$. Draw lines through $O$ parallel to $MB$ and $MC$; let these lines intersect $AB$ and $AC$ at $K$ and $L$, respectively. Let $N$ be the second intersection of the altitude from $A$ to $BC$ with $\omega$. Prove that $NK = NL$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ with circumcenter $O$ and circumcircle $\omega$ be given. Let $M$ be the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Lines through $O$ parallel to $MB$ and $MC$ intersect $AB$ and $AC$ at $K$ and $L$, respectively. Let $N$ be the point where the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ meets $\omega$ again. Prove that $NK = NL$.

Let triangle $ABC$ with circumcenter $O$ and circumcircle $\omega$ be given. Let $M$ be the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Lines through $O$ perpendicular to $MB$ and $MC$ intersect $AB$ and $AC$ at $K$ and $L$, respectively. Let $N$ be the point where the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ meets $\omega$ again. Prove that $NK = NL$.

positive_text:
Let $P(x) = Q(y)$ be an **interesting equation** with integer coefficients and degree $\geq 1$, and infinitely many natural number solutions. We define $F(x) = G(y)$ as a **resulting equation** from $P(x) = Q(y)$ if there exists a rational-coefficient polynomial $R$ such that $F(x) = R(P(x))$ and $G(y) = R(Q(y))$.

a) Suppose that $S$ is an infinite subset of $\mathbb{N}^2$. If all elements of $S$ satisfy some interesting equation, show that there exists an interesting equation $P_0(x) = Q_0(y)$ such that all such equations satisfied by $S$ are resulting from $P_0(x) = Q_0(y)$.

b) Let the **degree** of an interesting equation be the maximum of the degrees of $P$ and $Q$. An equation is **primitive** if it cannot be derived from a lower-degree interesting equation. If $P(x) = Q(y)$ is primitive and both $P$ and $Q$ are monic, prove that $\deg P$ and $\deg Q$ are coprime.

negatives.text:

We define $F(x) = G(y)$ as a **resulting equation** from $P(x) = Q(y)$ if there exists a rational-coefficient polynomial $R$ such that $F(x) = R(P(x))$ and $G(y) = R(Q(y))$.

a) Let $S$ be an infinite subset of $\mathbb{N}^2$. Prove that there exists an interesting equation $P_0(x) = Q_0(y)$ such that all equations satisfied by $S$ are resulting from $P_0(x) = Q_0(y)$.

b) The **degree** of an interesting equation is the maximum of the degrees of $P$ and $Q$. An equation is **primitive** if it is not derived from any lower-degree interesting equation. If $P(x) = Q(y)$ is primitive and both $P$ and $Q$ are monic, prove that $\deg P$ and $\deg Q$ are coprime.

positive_text: Let $P_1P_2P_3P_4P_5$ be a convex pentagon in the Cartesian plane with all vertices having rational coordinates. For each $1 \le i \le 5$, let $Q_i$ be the point of intersection of the lines $P_{i+1}P_{i+2}$ and $P_{i+3}P_{i+4}$, where indices are taken modulo 5. Prove that at most three of the lines $P_iQ_i$, for $1 \le i \le 5$, can meet at a common point.

negatives.text: Suppose that $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ is a convex pentagon in the Cartesian plane with all its vertices having rational coordinates. For each $1 \le i \le 5$, define $B_i$ as the intersection point of the extensions of the sides $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ and $A_{i+3}A_{i+4}$, with indices taken modulo 5. Prove that at most two of the lines $A_iB_i$ are concurrent.

Suppose that $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ is a convex pentagon in the Cartesian plane with all its vertices having rational coordinates. For each $1 \le i \le 5$, define $B_i$ as the intersection point of the lines $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ and $A_{i+3}A_{i+4}$, with indices taken modulo 5. Suppose that $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ is a convex pentagon in the Cartesian plane with all its vertices having rational coordinates. positive_text: Let $I_b$ be the $B$-excenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ in the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ not containing $A$. Suppose the line $MI_b$ meets the circumcircle again at point $T$. Prove that $TI_b^2 = TB \times TC$.

negatives.text: Let $I_b$ be the $B$-excenter of triangle $ABC$, and $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ in the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ not containing $A$. Let $T$ be the second intersection of the line $MI_b$ with the circumcircle. Prove that $TI_b^2 = TA \times TC$.

Let $I_b$ be the $B$-excenter of triangle $ABC$, and $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ in the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ not containing $A$. Let $T$ be the second intersection of the line $MI_b$ with the circumcircle. Prove that $TI_b^2 = TB + TC$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a square with points $N$ on $AB$ and $P$ on $AD$ such that $PN = NC$. Let $Q$ be a point on $AN$ with $\angle QPN = \angle NCB$. Show that $\angle BCQ = \frac{1}{2} \angle PQA$.

negatives.text: Square $ABCD$ is given. Points $N$ and $P$ are selected on sides $AB$ and $AD$, respectively, such that $PN = NC$, and point $Q$ is selected on segment $AN$ such that $\angle NCB = \angle QPN$. Prove that $\angle BCQ = 2 \angle PQA$.

positive_text:
Let $p(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ be a polynomial of odd degree $m > 1$, and define a function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{Z}$ such that $p(f(x)) = f(p(x))$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

a) Show that the image of $f$ is finite.

b) If $f$ is non-constant, show that the equation $p(x) = x$ has at least two distinct real roots.

c) Prove that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $n > 1$, there exists a function $f$ with an image of size $n$ and a polynomial $p(x)$ satisfying the given condition.

negatives.text:
Let $p(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ be a polynomial of odd degree $m > 1$, and define $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{Z}$ such that $p(f(x)) = f(p(x))$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

a) Prove that the image of $f$ is a countable set.

b) If $f$ is non-constant, prove that the equation $p(x) = x$ has exactly one real solution.

c) Prove that for each natural number $n > 1$, there exists a function $f$ with an image of size $n$ and a polynomial $p(x)$ such that $p(f(x)) = f(p(x))$ fails to hold for at least one real $x$.

Let $p(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ be a polynomial of odd degree $m > 1$, and define $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{Z}$ such that $p(f(x)) = f(p(x))$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

a) Prove that the image of $f$ is infinite.

b) If $f$ is non-constant, prove that the equation $p(x) = x$ has no real solutions.

c) Prove that for each natural number $n > 1$, there exists a function $f$ with an image of size $n$ and a polynomial $p(x)$ such that $p(f(x)) = f(p(x))$ fails to hold for some $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Let $p(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ be a polynomial of even degree $m > 1$, and define $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{Z}$ such that $p(f(x)) = f(p(x))$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

a) Prove that the image of $f$ is finite.

b) If $f$ is non-constant, prove that the equation $p(x) = x$ has at least two distinct real solutions.

c) Prove that for each natural number $n > 1$, there exists a function $f$ with an image of size $n$ and a polynomial $p(x)$ such that $p(f(x)) = f(p(x))$ holds for all real $x$.

positive_text:
Let $x = \frac{1}{ab}$, $y = \frac{1}{bc}$, $z = \frac{1}{cd}$, $w = \frac{1}{da}$ be positive real numbers such that $x + y + z + w = 1$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{xyzw} + 16 \geq 8\sqrt{(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{z})\left(x + z\right)} + 8\sqrt{(\frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{w})\left(y + w\right)}.
$$

negatives.text:
For positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ such that $\sum_{cyc} \frac{1}{ab} = 1$, prove that
$$
abcd + 16 \geq 8\sqrt{(a - c)\left(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{c}\right)} + 8\sqrt{(b - d)\left(\frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{d}\right)}.
$$

For positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ such that $\sum_{cyc} \frac{1}{ab} = 1$, prove that
$$
abcd + 16 \geq 8\sqrt{(a^2 + c^2)\left(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{c}\right)} + 8\sqrt{(b^2 + d^2)\left(\frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{d}\right)}.
$$

For positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ such that $\sum_{cyc} \frac{1}{ab} = 1$, prove that
$$
abcd + 16 \geq 8\sqrt{(a + c)\left(\frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{c}\right)} + 8\sqrt{(b + d)\left(\frac{1}{b} - \frac{1}{d}\right)}.
$$

positive_text:
a) Let $ m $ be a natural number. Define $ (a_n) $ as the sequence where $ a_n $ is the remainder of $ n $ modulo $ m $. Show that for every base $ k > 1 $, the sequence $ (a_n) $ is $ k $-Computable.

b) If $ (a_n) $ is $ k $-Computable, prove that the shifted sequence $ (b_n) $ with $ b_n = a_{n+1} $ and the doubled index sequence $ (c_n) $ with $ c_n = a_{2n} $ are also $ k $-Computable.

c) Define $ a_n = 1 $ if $ n $ is a perfect square and $ a_n = 0 $ otherwise. Determine whether this sequence is 3-Computable.

d) A modified definition of $ k $-Computable sequences considers input digits provided from left to right. These sequences are termed $ k $-Left Computable. Prove that the original and modified definitions are equivalent.

negatives.text:
a) Suppose $ m $ is a natural number. For each natural number $ n $, define $ (a_n) $ as the remainder of $ n $ when divided by $ m $. Prove that for each natural number $ k $, this sequence is $ k $-Computable.

b) Prove that if sequence $ (a_n) $ is $ k $-Computable, so are sequences $ (b_n) $ and $ (c_n) $ that are defined as $ b_n = a_{n+1} $ and $ c_n = a_{2n+1} $.

c) Define sequence $ (a_n) $ to be 1 for perfect square natural numbers and 0 for the rest. Is this sequence 3-Computable?

d) The definition of Computable sequences can be altered by assuming that the digits are given to the Machine from left to right. These sequences are called $ k $-Left Computable. Prove that this definition is equivalent to the previous one, i.e. a sequence is $ k $-Computable if and only if it is $ k $-Left Computable.

a) Suppose $ m $ is a natural number. For each natural number $ n $, define $ (a_n) $ as the remainder of $ n $ when divided by $ m $. Prove that for each natural number $ k $, this sequence is $ k $-Computable.

b) Prove that if sequence $ (a_n) $ is $ k $-Computable, so are sequences $ (b_n) $ and $ (c_n) $ that are defined as $ b_n = a_{n-1} $ and $ c_n = a_{2n} $.

c) Define sequence $ (a_n) $ to be 1 for perfect square natural numbers and 0 for the rest. Is this sequence 3-Computable?

d) The definition of Computable sequences can be altered by assuming that the digits are given to the Machine from left to right. These sequences are called $ k $-Left Computable. Prove that this definition is equivalent to the previous one, i.e. a sequence is $ k $-Computable if and only if it is $ k $-Left Computable.

a) Suppose $ m $ is a natural number. For each natural number $ n $, define $ (a_n) $ as the remainder of $ n $ when divided by $ m $. Prove that for each natural number $ k $, this sequence is $ k $-Computable.

b) Prove that if sequence $ (a_n) $ is $ k $-Computable, so are sequences $ (b_n) $ and $ (c_n) $ that are defined as $ b_n = a_{n+1} $ and $ c_n = a_{2n} $.

c) Define sequence $ (a_n) $ to be 1 for perfect square natural numbers and 0 for the rest. Is this sequence 3-Computable?

d) The definition of Computable sequences can be altered by assuming that the digits are given to the Machine from left to right, but the Machine only processes the first digit. These sequences are called $ k $-Left Computable. Prove that this definition is equivalent to the previous one, i.e. a sequence is $ k $-Computable if and only if it is $ k $-Left Computable.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with altitudes $AD$, $BF$, and $CE$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on line $EF$ such that $EP = DF$ (with $E$ between $P$ and $F$) and $QF = DE$ (with $F$ between $E$ and $Q$). Let the perpendicular bisector of $DQ$ meet $AB$ at $X$ and the perpendicular bisector of $DP$ meet $AC$ at $Y$. Prove that the midpoint of side $BC$ lies on line $XY$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with altitudes $AD$, $BF$, and $CE$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be points on line $EF$ such that $EP = DF$ (with $E$ between $P$ and $F$) and $QF = DE$ (with $F$ between $E$ and $Q$). Suppose the perpendicular bisector of $DQ$ intersects $AB$ at $X$ and the perpendicular bisector of $DP$ intersects $AC$ at $Y$. Prove that the midpoint of segment $AB$ lies on line $XY$.

Suppose the perpendicular bisector of $DQ$ intersects $AB$ at $X$, and the perpendicular bisector of $DP$ intersects $AC$ at $Y$. Prove that the midpoint of $AC$ lies on line $XY$.

Suppose the perpendicular bisector of $DQ$ intersects $AB$ at $X$, and the perpendicular bisector of $DP$ intersects $AC$ at $Y$. Prove that the centroid of triangle $ABC$ lies on line $XY$.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, $z$ and $w$ be positive real numbers such that $x + y + z + w = 2$. Prove that
$$
\frac{(x+z)^2}{xw+yz} + \frac{(y+w)^2}{xz+yw} + 4 \ge 4 \left( \frac{x+y+1}{z+w+1} + \frac{z+w+1}{x+y+1} \right).
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers with $a + b + c + d = 2$. Prove that
$$
\frac{(a+c)^2}{ad+bc} + \frac{(b+d)^2}{ac+bd} + 4 \le 4 \left( \frac{a+b+1}{c+d+1} + \frac{c+d+1}{a+b+1} \right).
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers with $a + b + c + d = 2$. Prove that
$$
\frac{(a+c)^2}{ad+bc} + \frac{(b+d)^2}{ac+bd} + 4 \ge 4 \left( \frac{a+b+1}{c+d+1} + \frac{c+d+1}{a+b+1} \right)^2.
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be positive real numbers with $a + b + c + d = 3$. Prove that
$$
\frac{(a+c)^2}{ad+bc} + \frac{(b+d)^2}{ac+bd} + 4 \ge 4 \left( \frac{a+b+1}{c+d+1} + \frac{c+d+1}{a+b+1} \right).
$$

positive_text:
Let $(h_1, h_2, \dots, h_{n+1})$ be a $(n+1)$-tuple of $n$-variable polynomials with real coefficients. Define it as **good** if the following holds: whenever $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $h_i(f_1(x), f_2(x), \dots, f_n(x))$ being a polynomial in $x$ for each $1 \le i \le n+1$, then all $f_j(x)$ are themselves polynomials.

a) Show that for each positive integer $n$, one can construct a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple where each $h_i$ has degree strictly greater than one.

b) Demonstrate that for no $n > 1$ is there a **good** $(n+1)$-tuple in which all $h_i$ are symmetric in their variables.

negatives.text:
