\text{(1) Prove: on the complex plane, for each line passing through the origin except for the real axis, there is at most one point } z \text{ such that } \frac{1+z^{23}}{z^{64}} \in \mathbb{R}.\\(2) Prove: for any complex number } a \ne 0 \text{ and any real number } \theta, \text{ the equation}\\1 + z^{23} + a z^{64} = 0\text{has at least one root in the set}\\S_{\theta} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} \mid \mathrm{Im}(z \cdot e^{-i\theta}) \ge |z| \cdot \cos \frac{\pi}{20}\}.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. A large equilateral triangle is divided into $9n^2$ unit equilateral triangles. Each triangle is colored red, yellow, or blue with exactly $3n^2$ of each color. A *standard trapezoid* is a configuration of three small triangles. A *colorful trapezoid* is one where all three triangles are of distinct colors. Determine the maximum number of such colorful trapezoids that can be formed.

negatives.text: Given a positive integer $n$, an equilateral triangle of side length $3n$ is partitioned into $9n^2$ unit equilateral triangles. Each triangle is colored red, yellow, or blue such that there are $3n^2$ of each color. A trapezoid formed by three unit triangles is called a *standard trapezoid*. A *colorful trapezoid* is one where all three triangles have the same color. Determine the maximum number of colorful trapezoids that can be formed.

Given a positive integer $n$, an equilateral triangle of side length $3n$ is partitioned into $9n^2$ unit equilateral triangles. Each triangle is colored red, yellow, or blue such that there are $3n^2$ of each color. A trapezoid formed by three unit triangles is called a *standard trapezoid*. A *colorful trapezoid* is one where all three triangles are of different colors. Determine the number of colorful trapezoids that can be formed, given that they must be non-overlapping.

Given a positive integer $n$, an equilateral triangle of side length $3n$ is partitioned into $9n^2$ unit equilateral triangles. Each triangle is colored red, yellow, or blue such that there are $3n^2$ of each color. A trapezoid formed by four unit triangles is called a *standard trapezoid*. A *colorful trapezoid* is one where all four triangles are of different colors. Determine the maximum number of colorful trapezoids that can be formed.

positive_text:
Let $\alpha$ be an irrational number with $\alpha > 1$, and let $L$ be a positive integer such that $L > \frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha - 1}$. Define a sequence $\{x_n\}$ starting from an integer $x_1 > L$ with the recurrence relation:
$$
x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \lfloor \alpha x_n \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n \le L, \\ \lfloor x_n / \alpha \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n > L. \end{cases}
$$
(1) Show that $\{x_n\}$ is eventually periodic.
(2) Prove that the minimal period $T$ of the sequence is odd and does not depend on the choice of $x_1$.

negatives.text:
Fix an irrational number $\alpha > 1$ and a positive integer $L$ such that $L > \frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha - 1}$. Given an integer $x_1 > L$, define a sequence $\{x_n\}$ as follows: for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$$
x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \lfloor \alpha x_n \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n \le L, \\ \lfloor x_n + \alpha \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n > L. \end{cases}
$$
(1) Prove that the sequence $\{x_n\}$ is eventually periodic.
(2) Prove that the smallest integer $T$ satisfying (1) is an odd integer independent of $x_1$.

Fix an irrational number $\alpha > 1$ and a positive integer $L$ such that $L > \frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha - 1}$. Given an integer $x_1 > L$, define a sequence $\{x_n\}$ as follows: for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$$
x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \lfloor \alpha x_n \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n \le L, \\ \lfloor x_n / \alpha \rfloor + 1, & \text{if } x_n > L. \end{cases}
$$
(1) Prove that the sequence $\{x_n\}$ is eventually periodic.
(2) Prove that the smallest integer $T$ satisfying (1) is an odd integer independent of $x_1$.

Fix an irrational number $\alpha > 1$ and a positive integer $L$ such that $L > \frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha - 1}$. Given an integer $x_1 > L$, define a sequence $\{x_n\}$ as follows: for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$$
x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \lfloor \alpha x_n \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n \le L, \\ \lfloor x_n / \alpha \rfloor, & \text{if } x_n > L. \end{cases}
$$
(1) Prove that the sequence $\{x_n\}$ is eventually periodic.
(2) Prove that the smallest integer $T$ satisfying (1) is an even integer independent of $x_1$.

positive_text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $L$, $M$, and $N$ be the midpoints of $AI$, $AC$, and $CI$, respectively. Suppose that a point $D$ lies on segment $AM$ such that $BD = BC$. The incircle of triangle $ABD$ touches $AD$ and $BD$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $J$ be the circumcenter of triangle $AIC$, and define $\omega$ as the circumcircle of triangle $DMJ$. The line $MN$ meets $\omega$ again at $P$, and the line $JL$ meets $\omega$ again at $Q$. Prove that lines $EF$, $PQ$, and $LN$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, with $L$, $M$, and $N$ as the midpoints of $AI$, $AC$, and $CI$, respectively. Suppose that a point $D$ lies in the interior of segment $AM$ such that $BD = BC$. The incircle of triangle $ABD$ touches $AD$ and $BD$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $J$ be the circumcenter of triangle $AIB$, and let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $DMJ$. The line $MN$ intersects $\omega$ at $P(\neq M)$, and the line $JL$ intersects $\omega$ at $Q(\neq J)$. Prove that the three lines $EF$, $PQ$, and $LN$ pass through a common point.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $L$, $M$, and $N$ be the midpoints of $AI$, $AC$, and $CI$, respectively. Suppose that a point $D$ lies in the interior of segment $AM$ such that $BD = 2BC$. The incircle of triangle $ABD$ touches $AD$ and $BD$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $J$ be the circumcenter of triangle $AIC$, and let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $DMJ$. The line $MN$ intersects $\omega$ at point $P(\neq M)$, and the line $JL$ intersects $\omega$ at point $Q(\neq J)$. Prove that the three lines $EF$, $PQ$, and $LN$ pass through a common point.

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and define $L$, $M$, and $N$ as the midpoints of $AI$, $AC$, and $CI$, respectively. Suppose that a point $D$ lies in the interior of segment $AM$ such that $BD = BC$. The incircle of triangle $ABD$ touches $AD$ and $BD$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $J$ be the circumcenter of triangle $AIC$, and let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $DMJ$. The line $MN$ intersects $\omega$ at point $P(\neq M)$, and the line $JF$ intersects $\omega$ at point $Q(\neq J)$. Prove that the three lines $EF$, $PQ$, and $LN$ pass through a common point.

positive_text:
Determine the minimal real number $\lambda$ such that for all positive integers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $n \nmid a + b$, there exists some positive integer $k < n$ for which
$$
\left\{ \frac{ak}{n} \right\} + \left\{ \frac{bk}{n} \right\} \le \lambda.
$$

negatives.text:
Find the smallest real number $\lambda$ such that for any positive integers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $a + b$ divisible by $n$, there exists a positive integer $k < n$ such that
$$
\left\{ \frac{ak}{n} \right\} + \left\{ \frac{bk}{n} \right\} \le \lambda.
$$

Find the smallest real number $\lambda$ such that for any positive integers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $a + b$ not divisible by $n$, there exists a positive integer $k < n$ such that
$$
\left\{ \frac{ak}{n} \right\} + \left\{ \frac{bk}{n} \right\} > \lambda.
$$

Find the smallest real number $\lambda$ such that for any positive integers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $a + b$ not divisible by $n$, there exists a positive integer $k < n$ such that
$$
\left\{ \frac{ak}{n} \right\}^2 + \left\{ \frac{bk}{n} \right\}^2 \le \lambda.
$$

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be a point such that $AD \parallel BC$ and $DB > DC$. Let $E$ lie on the arc $\widearc{BC}$ of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ not containing $A$, with $EB < EC$. Let $F$ be a point on the extension of $BC$ such that $\angle DFE = \angle ADE$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the points where the extension of $FD$ meets the extensions of $BA$ and $CA$, respectively. Prove that $\angle XEY$ is constant.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. A point $D$ satisfies $AD \parallel BC$ and $DB > DC$. A point $E$ lies on the arc $\widearc{BC}$ of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ not containing $A$ with $EB < EC$. Let $F$ be a point on the extension of $BC$ such that $\angle DFE = -\angle ADE$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the intersections of the extension of $FD$ with the extensions of $BA$ and $CA$. Prove that $\angle XEY$ is constant.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. A point $D$ satisfies $AD \parallel BC$ and $DB > DC$. A point $E$ lies on the arc $\widearc{BC}$ of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ not containing $A$ with $EB > EC$. Let $F$ be a point on the extension of $BC$ such that $\angle DFE = \angle ADE$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the intersections of the extension of $FD$ with the extensions of $BA$ and $CA$. Prove that $\angle XEY$ is constant.

positive_text:
Let $n$ be an integer with $n \ge 4$. Show that there are no positive integers $x$ and $y$ such that
$$
(2^x - 1)(5^x - 1)
$$
is a perfect $n$th power.

negatives.text:
Given a positive integer $n \ge 4$, prove that the equation
$$
(2^x + 1)(5^x + 1) = y^n
$$
has no positive integer solutions $(x, y)$.

Given a positive integer $n \ge 4$, prove that the equation
$$
(2^x - 1)(5^x - 1) = y^n
$$
has positive integer solutions $(x, y)$.

Given a positive integer $n \ge 4$, prove that the equation
$$
(2^x - 1)(5^x - 1) = y^n + 1
$$
has no positive integer solutions $(x, y)$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Alice and Bob play a game on the complete graph $K_n$, where all edges are initially uncolored. Players alternate turns coloring one or two edges red, with Alice going first, under the rule that no triangle may have all its edges red. The game ends when no further move is possible. Prove that there exists a constant $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for any $n \ge 2$, Alice has a strategy to ensure the total number of red edges is at most $\left(\frac{1}{4} - \varepsilon\right)n^2 + n$, regardless of Bob's actions.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Two players, Alice and Bob, play a game on $K_n$, coloring edges red. On each turn, a player colors one or two edges red, with the rule that no triangle can have all three edges red after the move. The game ends when no uncolored edges remain. Prove that there exists a real number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for any $n \ge 2$, Alice can ensure the number of red edges is at least $\left(\frac{1}{4} + \varepsilon\right)n^2 + n$, regardless of Bob's moves.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Alice and Bob play a game on $K_n$, coloring edges red. On each turn, a player can color one or two edges red, and the rule is that no triangle can have all three edges red after the move. The game ends when no uncolored edges remain. Prove that there exists a constant $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for all $n \ge 2$, Alice can ensure the number of red edges is at most $\left(\frac{1}{4} - \varepsilon\right)n^2 + n$, regardless of Bob's moves, even if Alice must color edges in batches of size exactly 2.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Alice and Bob play a game on $K_n$, coloring edges red. On each turn, a player can color one or two edges red, and the rule is that no triangle can have all three edges red after the move. The game ends when no uncolored edges remain. Prove that there exists a real number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for any $n \ge 2$, Alice can ensure the number of red edges is at most $\left(\frac{1}{4} - \varepsilon\right)n^2 + n$, regardless of Bob's moves, provided the game is played on a bipartite graph instead of $K_n$.

positive_text: Let $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ be non-constant real polynomials such that for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}^+$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ with $P(m) = Q(n)$.\n(a) Show that if $\deg(P) = d \cdot \deg(Q)$ for some integer $d$, then $P(x) = Q(h(x))$ for some real polynomial $h(x)$.\n(b) Prove that $\deg(P)$ is a multiple of $\deg(Q)$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ be non-constant real polynomials such that for every positive integer $m$, there exists a positive integer $n$ with $P(m) = Q(n)$.\n(1) Prove that if $\deg(Q)$ is greater than $\deg(P)$, then there exists a real polynomial $h(x)$ such that $P(x) = Q(h(x))$.\n(2) Prove that $\deg(Q)$ divides $\deg(P)$.

Let $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ be non-constant real polynomials such that for every positive integer $m$, there exists a positive integer $n$ with $P(m) = Q(n)$.\n(1) Prove that if $\deg(P) < \deg(Q)$, then there exists a real polynomial $h(x)$ such that $P(x) = Q(h(x))$.\n(2) Prove that $\deg(Q)$ divides $\deg(P)$.

Let $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ be non-constant real polynomials such that for every positive integer $m$, there exists a positive integer $n$ with $P(m) = Q(n)$.\n(1) Prove that if $\deg(Q)$ divides $\deg(P) + 1$, then there exists a real polynomial $h(x)$ such that $P(x) = Q(h(x))$.\n(2) Prove that $\deg(Q)$ divides $\deg(P)$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be isosceles with $|AB| = |AC|$. Suppose the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\overline{AC}$ at $D$, and suppose $|BC| = |BD| + |AD|$. Determine all possible angle measures in $\triangle ABC$.

positive_text: Let $x, y > 1$ be real numbers such that $\log_y x$, $\log_{2y}(2x)$, and $\log_{4y}(4x)$, in that order, form an arithmetic progression. Prove that $x = y$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have an obtuse angle at $B$. Let $D$ and $E$ be the midpoints of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$, respectively. Let $F$ lie on $\overline{BC}$ such that $\angle BFE = 90^\circ$, and let $G$ lie on $\overline{DE}$ such that $\angle BGE = 90^\circ$. positive_text:

$$

positive_text:
Prove that for all positive real numbers $x, y, z$ with $x + y + z \le 3$ the inequality
$$
\sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{x+1}{x(x+2)} \ge 2
$$
holds.

negatives.text:

positive_text: Suppose $\triangle ABC$ is acute, and let $M$ and $N$ be the projections of $A$ and $B$ onto the opposite sides. If $AN = NM$, show that the incenter of $\triangle ABC$ lies on $\overline{BN}$.

Let $Q$ be the midpoint of the segment $\overline{MN}$ and let $P$ be the midpoint of the segment $\overline{AB}$. If $|MN| = 10$ and $|AB| = 26$, determine the length of the segment $\overline{PQ}$, assuming triangle $ABC$ is not acute.

positive_text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $D$ be the point on $AC$ such that triangle $ABD$ is isosceles with $AB = DB$. The incircle of triangle $BCD$ touches $AC$ at $E$ and $BD$ at $F$. Prove that the line $EF$ passes through the midpoint of $DI$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $D$ be the point on side $AC$ such that $|AB| = |DB|$. The incircle of triangle $BCD$ touches $AC$ at $E$ and $BD$ at $F$. Prove that the line $EF$ passes through the midpoint of segment $CI$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $p$ a prime such that $n$ divides $p-1$ and $p$ divides $n^3-1$. Show that $4p-3$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $p$ a prime such that $p-1$ is divisible by $n$, and $n^3+1$ is divisible by $p$. Prove that $4p-3$ is a perfect square.
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $p$ a prime such that $p+1$ is divisible by $n$, and $n^3-1$ is divisible by $p$. Prove that $4p-3$ is a perfect square.
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $p$ a prime such that $p-1$ is divisible by $n$, and $n^3-1$ is divisible by $p$. Prove that $4p+3$ is a perfect square.

positive_text: An $N \times N$ board is initially checkerboard-coloured black and white, with adjacent squares having opposite colours, and at least one black square in a corner. In each move, a $2 \times 2$ block is selected and the colours of its four squares are cycled in the order white $\rightarrow$ black $\rightarrow$ grey $\rightarrow$ white. Determine all integers $N > 1$ for which it is possible, through a finite number of such moves, to invert the initial black-white pattern.

negatives.text: The unit squares of an $N \times N$ board are initially checkerboard-coloured black and white, with adjacent squares having opposite colours and at least one corner square black. In each step, a $2 \times 2$ square is selected and the colour of each square is flipped in the order black $\rightarrow$ white $\rightarrow$ black $\rightarrow$ grey. Determine all integers $N > 1$ for which it is possible to achieve that all black squares become white and all white squares become black.

positive_text: Let $p$ be a prime number. Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ satisfying $$ a(b - 1) = p(a - 2). $$

negatives.text: Let $p$ be a prime number. Determine all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $$ p(a + 2) = a(b - 1). $$
Let $p$ be a prime number. Determine all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $$ p(a - 2) = (a + 1)(b - 1). $$
Let $p$ be a prime number. Determine all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $$ p(a - 2) = a(b + 1). $$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute-angled with $|AB| > |AC|$. Let $O$ denote the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $OQ$ be a diameter of the circumcircle of triangle $BOC$. A line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ meets $CQ$ at $M$, and a line through $A$ parallel to $CQ$ meets $BC$ at $N$. Let $T$ be the point of intersection of $AQ$ and $MN$. Prove that $T$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $BOC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AB > AC$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $OQ$ be a radius of the circumcircle of triangle $BOC$. The line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $CQ$ at $M$, and the line through $A$ parallel to $CQ$ intersects $BC$ at $N$. Denote by $T$ the intersection of $AQ$ and $MN$. Prove that $T$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $BOC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AB > AC$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $OQ$ be a diameter of the circumcircle of triangle $BOC$. The line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $CQ$ at $M$, and the line through $A$ parallel to $CQ$ intersects $BC$ at $N$. Denote by $T$ the intersection of $AQ$ and $MN$. Prove that $T$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AB > AC$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $OQ$ be a diameter of the circumcircle of triangle $BOC$. The line through $A$ parallel to $CQ$ intersects $BC$ at $M$, and the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $CQ$ at $N$. Denote by $T$ the intersection of $AQ$ and $MN$. Prove that $T$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $BOC$.

positive_text: Suppose points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ lie on the hyperbola defined by $xy = 1$. Show that the orthocentre of triangle $PQR$ lies on the same hyperbola.

negatives.text: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be points on the curve (hyperbola) with equation $x^2y = 1$. Prove that the orthocentre of the triangle $ABC$ also belongs to that curve.
Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be points on the curve (hyperbola) with equation $xy = 1$. Prove that the centroid of the triangle $ABC$ also belongs to that curve.
Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be points on the curve (hyperbola) with equation $xy = 1$. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $ABC$ also belongs to that curve.

positive_text: Consider a set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 2017\}$ of $2017$ elements. Assign each pair $\{i, j\}$ with $i < j$ to either a red edge or a blue edge, forming two directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). A configuration is good if there do not exist $A < B$ such that there is a red path and a blue path from $A$ to $B$. How many good configurations are there?

negatives.text: Suppose $n = 2017$ and each pair $i < j$ is assigned to either a red or blue edge. A configuration is good if there is no pair $A < B$ for which both the red and blue subgraphs contain a directed path from $B$ to $A$. Determine the number of good configurations.

Suppose $n = 2017$ and each pair $i < j$ is assigned to either a red or blue edge. A configuration is good if there is no pair $A < B$ for which there is a path from $A$ to $B$ in both the red and blue subgraphs and also a path from $B$ to $A$ in both. Determine the number of good configurations.

positive_text:
Prove that there are no positive integers $m$ and $n$ such that
$$
27n^4 - 2n^2 + n = 5m^3.
$$

negatives.text:
Prove that there are no positive integers $m$ and $n$ such that
$$
5m^3 = 27n^4 - 2n^2 - n.
$$

Prove that there are no positive integers $m$ and $n$ such that
$$
5m^3 = 27n^4 + 2n^2 + n.
$$

Prove that there are no positive integers $m$ and $n$ such that
$$
5m^3 = 27n^4 - 2n^2 + n + 1.
$$

positive_text:
Let $A = D_0, D_1, \dots, D_{2018} = B$ be equally spaced points along the segment $\overline{AB}$. If $C$ is a point such that $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, prove that
$$
\sum_{i=0}^{2018} |CD_i|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{2018} |AD_i|^2.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $D_0, D_1, \dots, D_{2018}$ be points on $\overline{AB}$ such that $D_0 = A$, $D_{2018} = B$ and
$$
|D_0 D_1| = |D_1 D_2| = \dots = |D_{2017} D_{2018}|.
$$
If $C$ is a point such that $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, prove that
$$
|CD_0| + |CD_1| + \dots + |CD_{2018}| = |AD_1| + |AD_2| + \dots + |AD_{2018}|.
$$

Let $D_0, D_1, \dots, D_{2018}$ be points on $\overline{AB}$ such that $D_0 = A$, $D_{2018} = B$ and
$$
|D_0 D_1| = |D_1 D_2| = \dots = |D_{2017} D_{2018}|.
$$
If $C$ is a point such that $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, prove that
$$
\sum_{i=0}^{2018} |CD_i|^2 = \sum_{i=0}^{2018} |AD_i|^2.
$$

positive_text: Suppose $q$ is a prime and $k \ge q-1$ is an integer such that $kq + 1$ is a perfect square. Prove that $k+1$ can be written as the sum of the squares of precisely $q$ positive integers.

negatives.text: Let $p$ be a prime and $n \ge p-1$ an integer such that $np-1$ is a perfect square. Prove that $n+1$ can be written as the sum of squares of exactly $p$ positive integers.
Let $p$ be a prime and $n \ge p-1$ an integer such that $np+1$ is a perfect square. Prove that $n-1$ can be written as the sum of squares of exactly $p$ positive integers.
Let $p$ be a prime and $n \ge p-1$ an integer such that $np+1$ is a perfect cube. Prove that $n+1$ can be written as the sum of squares of exactly $p$ positive integers.

positive_text:
Find all positive integers $ n $ such that the quadratic equation
$$
 x^2 + (-3n)x + (n + 3) = 0
$$
has integer roots.

negatives.text:
Determine all positive integers $ n $ for which the quadratic equation
$$
 x^2 - 3n x + n - 3 = 0
$$
has integer solutions.

positive_text:
Let $k \ge 4$ be a positive integer. Prove that among any $k$ elements selected from the set
$$
\{1, 2, \dots, 2k - 1\}
$$
there exists a non-empty subset whose sum is divisible by $2k$.

negatives.text:
Let $n \ge 4$ be a positive integer. Prove that among any $n$ numbers from the set
$$
\{1, 2, \dots, 2n - 1\}
$$
there are some of them with the sum equal to $2n$.

Let $n \ge 4$ be a positive integer. Prove that among any $n$ numbers from the set
$$
\{1, 2, \dots, 2n - 1\}
$$
there are some of them with the product divisible by $2n$.

Let $n \ge 4$ be a positive integer. Prove that among any $n - 1$ numbers from the set
$$
\{1, 2, \dots, 2n - 1\}
$$
there are some of them with the sum divisible by $2n$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $C$ with $AC = 2$ and $BC = 1$. Inside the triangle, a square is placed such that two of its vertices lie along $AC$, one lies on $AB$, and the last lies on the circle centered at $B$ with radius $1$. Find the side length of the square.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $C$, with $AC = 2$ and $BC = 1$. A square is placed inside the triangle such that two of its vertices lie on $AC$, one lies on $AB$, and the last lies on the circle of radius $1$ centered at $C$. Find the side length of the square.

Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $C$, with $AC = 2$ and $BC = 1$. A square is placed inside the triangle such that two of its vertices lie on $AC$, one lies on $AB$, and the last lies on the circle of radius $2$ centered at $B$. Find the side length of the square.

Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $C$, with $AC = 2$ and $BC = 1$. A square is placed inside the triangle such that two of its vertices lie on $AC$, one lies on $AB$, and the last lies on the circle of radius $1$ centered at $B$, but now the square is placed outside the triangle. Find the side length of the square.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $|AB| = |AC|$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BC}$, respectively. Let $P$ be the second intersection of line $AN$ with the circumcircle of triangle $AMC$. Draw a line through $P$ parallel to $\overline{BC}$, intersecting the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $B_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $AB_1C_1$ is equilateral.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $BC$, respectively. The line $AN$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $AMC$ at a point $P$ distinct from $A$. A line through $P$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $B_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $AB_1C_1$ is equilateral.

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $BC$, respectively. The line $AN$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $AMC$ at a point $P$ distinct from $A$. A line through $P$ parallel to $AB$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $B_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $AB_1C_1$ is equilateral.

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $BC$, respectively. The line $AN$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $AMC$ at a point $P$ distinct from $A$. A line through $P$ parallel to $BC$ intersects the circle passing through $A$, $B$, and $N$ at $B_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $AB_1C_1$ is equilateral.

positive_text:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a function satisfying
$$
 f(xy) = f(x + y)
$$
for all integers $x \ge 4$, $y \ge 4$. Show that $f(k) = f(8)$ for all $k \ge 8$.

negatives.text:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a function such that
$$
 f(ab) = f(a + b)
$$
for all positive integers $a \ge 4$ and $b \ge 4$. Prove that $f(n) = f(9)$ for all $n \ge 8$.

Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a function such that
$$
 f(ab) = f(a - b)
$$
for all $a, b \ge 4$. Prove that $f(n) = f(8)$ for all $n \ge 8$.

positive_text: Let $ \omega $ be a circle with center $ O $. Let $ \overline{AB} $ be a chord of $ \omega $, and let $ M $ be the midpoint of $ \overline{AB} $. The tangents to $ \omega $ at $ A $ and $ B $ meet at point $ T $. A line $ \ell $, passing through $ T $, intersects the minor arc $ \overarc{AB} $ at $ C $ and the major arc $ \overarc{AB} $ at $ D $, such that $ BC = BM $. Prove that the circumcenter of triangle $ \triangle ADM $ is the reflection of $ O $ over the line $ AD $.

negatives.text: Let $ k $ be a circle centred at $ O $. Let $ \overline{AB} $ be a chord of that circle and $ M $ its midpoint. Tangents on $ k $ at points $ A $ and $ B $ intersect at $ T $. The line $ \ell $ goes through $ T $, intersects the shorter arc $ \overarc{AB} $ at the point $ C $ and the longer arc $ \overarc{AB} $ at the point $ D $, so that $ |BC| = 2|BM| $. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $ \triangle ADM $ is the reflection of $ O $ across the line $ AD $.

Let $ k $ be a circle centred at $ O $. Let $ \overline{AB} $ be a chord of that circle and $ M $ its midpoint. Tangents on $ k $ at points $ A $ and $ B $ intersect at $ T $. The line $ \ell $ goes through $ T $, intersects the shorter arc $ \overarc{AB} $ at the point $ C $ and the longer arc $ \overarc{AB} $ at the point $ D $, so that $ |BC| = |BM| $. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $ \triangle ADM $ is the reflection of $ O $ across the line $ BD $.

Let $ k $ be a circle centred at $ O $. Let $ \overline{AB} $ be a chord of that circle and $ M $ its midpoint. Tangents on $ k $ at points $ A $ and $ B $ intersect at $ T $. The line $ \ell $ goes through $ T $, intersects the shorter arc $ \overarc{AB} $ at the point $ C $ and the longer arc $ \overarc{AB} $ at the point $ D $, so that $ |BC| = |BM| $. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $ \triangle ADM $ lies on the line $ OD $.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $D$ be the point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ such that $\angle BDC = 90^\circ + \angle BAC$, and let $I$ be the incenter of $\triangle ABC$. Let $J$ be the point such that $BC$ is the perpendicular bisector of segment $IJ$. If the line $DJ$ intersects the circumcircle again at $E$ on the arc $\widehat{AB}$ not containing $C$, prove that $|AI| = |IE|$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of the arc $\widehat{BC}$ not containing $A$, and let $I$ be the incenter. Let $J$ be the reflection of $I$ over $AC$, and let $DJ$ intersect the circumcircle again at $E$ on the arc $\widehat{AB}$ not containing $C$. Prove that $|AI| = |IE|$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of the arc $\widehat{BC}$ not containing $A$, and let $I$ be the incenter. Let $J$ be the point such that $IJ$ is perpendicular to $BC$ and intersects it at its midpoint. If $DJ$ intersects the circumcircle again at $E$ on the arc $\widehat{AB}$ not containing $C$, prove that $|AI| = |IE|$.

positive_text:
Find the real value of $ p $ such that the roots of the quadratic equation
$$
(p - 3)x^2 + (p^2 + 1)x - 11p + 18 = 0
$$
represent the lengths of the perpendicular sides of a right triangle with hypotenuse $ \sqrt{17} $.

negatives.text:
Determine the value of the real parameter $ p $ so that the solutions of
$$
(p - 3)x^2 + (p^2 + 1)x - 11p + 18 = 0
$$
are the lengths of legs of a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse of length $ 17 $.

Determine the value of the real parameter $ p $ so that the solutions of
$$
(p - 3)x^2 + (p^2 + 1)x - 11p + 18 = 0
$$
are the lengths of legs of an isosceles triangle with hypotenuse of length $ \sqrt{17} $.

Determine the value of the real parameter $ p $ so that the solutions of
$$
(p - 3)x^2 + (p^2 + 1)x - 11p + 18 = 0
$$
are the lengths of legs of a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse of length $ \sqrt{17} $, and both legs are integers.

positive_text: Find all real solutions $(x, y)$ to the system $$ x = \frac{-135}{y^3}, \quad x + y = \frac{-6}{y}. $$

negatives.text: Find all real pairs $(x, y)$ such that $$ xy^3 = 135, \quad (x+y)y = -6. $$
Find all real solutions $(x, y)$ such that $$ x y^3 = -135, \quad (x+y)y^2 = -6. $$
Find all real numbers $(x, y)$ such that $$ x y^3 = -135, \quad (x+y) = -6. $$

positive_text: Let $x$ be a positive real number such that $\log_{4x} 40\sqrt{3} = \log_{3x} 45$. Prove that $x^3$ is an integer and determine its value.

negatives.text: Let $a$ be a positive real number such that $\log_{4a} 40\sqrt{3} = -\log_{3a} 45$. Prove that $a^3$ is an integer and find its value.
Let $a$ be a positive real number such that $\log_{4a} 40\sqrt{3} = \log_{3a^2} 45$. Prove that $a^3$ is an integer and find its value.
Let $a$ be a positive real number such that $\log_{4a} 40\sqrt{3} < \log_{3a} 45$. Determine whether $a^3$ is an integer and find its value.

positive_text:
Determine all complex values $a$ for which the polynomial
$$
(x - a)(x - a^2)(x - a^3)(x - a^4)
$$
has all real coefficients.

negatives.text:
Find all complex numbers $a$ such that all coefficients of
$$
(x - a)(x - a^2)(x - a^3)(x - a^4)
$$
are imaginary numbers.

Find all complex numbers $a$ such that the coefficients of
$$
(x - a)(x - a^2)(x - a^3)(x - a^4)
$$
are integers.

Find all complex numbers $a$ such that the polynomial
$$
(x - a)(x - a^2)(x - a^3)(x - a^4)
$$
has non-real coefficients.

positive_text:
Find all integer solutions $(a, b)$ with $b \ge 0$ satisfying
$$
(a + b)^2 - b^2 + b! = 131.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of integers such that $b \ge 0$ and
$$
a^2 - 2ab + b! = 131.
$$

Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of integers such that $b \ge 0$ and
$$
a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = 131.
$$

Find all pairs $(a, b)$ of integers such that $b \ge 0$ and
$$
a^2 + 2ab + b! = 130.
$$

positive_text: Determine all real pairs $(x, y)$ with $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ for which $xy + x + y$ achieves its minimum value.

negatives.text: Find all real pairs $(a, b)$ such that $a^2 + b^2 = 25$ and $ab - a - b$ is minimized.
Find all real pairs $(a, b)$ such that $a^2 + b^2 = 25$ and $ab + a + b$ is maximized.
Find all real pairs $(a, b)$ such that $a^2 + b^2 = 16$ and $ab + a + b$ is minimized.

positive_text:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a *multiplicative* function satisfying $f(4) = 4$ and
$$
f(m^2 + n^2) = f(m^2) + f(n^2)
$$
for all positive integers $m$ and $n$. Show that $f(k^2) = k^2$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$.
(Note: A function is multiplicative if $f(ab) = f(a)f(b)$ for all coprime $a, b$.)

negatives.text:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a multiplicative function with $f(4) = 4$ and satisfying
$$
f(m^2 - n^2) = f(m^2) - f(n^2)
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that $f(m^2) = m^2$ for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a multiplicative function with $f(4) = 4$ and satisfying
$$
f(m^2 + n^2) = f(m^2) + f(n^2)
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that $f(m^3) = m^3$ for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a multiplicative function with $f(4) = 4$ and satisfying
$$
f(m^2 + n^2) = f(m^2) + f(n^2)
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that $f(m^2) = 2m^2$ for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$.

positive_text:
Let $k$ be a positive integer, and $q$ be a prime number such that $q > k$. Prove that the number of positive integers $r$, for which
$$
 k^2 + r^2 + q^2 - 2kr - 2kq - 2rq
$$
is a perfect square, does not depend on $q$.

negatives.text:
Let $m$ be a positive integer, and $p$ be a prime number such that $p > m$. Prove that the number of positive integers $n$, for which
$$
 m^2 + n^2 + p^2 + 2mn + 2mp + 2np
$$
is a square of some positive integer, does not depend on $p$.

Let $m$ be a positive integer, and $p$ be a prime number such that $p > m$. Prove that the number of positive integers $n$, for which
$$
 m^2 + n^2 + p^2 - 2mn - 2mp - 2np + 1
$$
is a square of some positive integer, does not depend on $p$.

Let $m$ be a positive integer, and $p$ be a prime number such that $p > m$. Prove that the number of positive integers $n$, for which
$$
 m^2 + n^2 + p^2 - 2mn - 2mp - 2n^2p
$$
is a square of some positive integer, does not depend on $p$.

positive_text: \text{Find all real solutions } (x, y, z) \text{ satisfying } \quad \frac{1}{xy} - \frac{x}{z} = 1, \quad \frac{1}{yz} - \frac{y}{x} = 1, \quad \frac{1}{zx} - \frac{z}{y} = 1.

negatives.text: \text{Solve the system of equations } \quad \frac{1}{xy} = \frac{x}{z} - 1, \quad \frac{1}{yz} = \frac{y}{x} - 1, \quad \frac{1}{zx} = \frac{z}{y} - 1.
\text{Solve the system of equations } \quad \frac{1}{x^2y} = \frac{x}{z} + 1, \quad \frac{1}{y^2z} = \frac{y}{x} + 1, \quad \frac{1}{z^2x} = \frac{z}{y} + 1.
\text{Solve the system of inequalities } \quad \frac{1}{xy} \geq \frac{x}{z} + 1, \quad \frac{1}{yz} \geq \frac{y}{x} + 1, \quad \frac{1}{zx} \geq \frac{z}{y} + 1.

positive_text: Suppose there are $k$ heaps with $1, 2, \dots, k$ stones, for $k \ge 3$. In the $i$-th step, we select any three heaps whose total number of stones is greater than $i$, combine them into a single heap, and then remove $i$ stones from the resulting heap. After a number of such steps, a single heap remains with $p$ stones. Prove that $p$ is a perfect square if and only if both $2k+2$ and $3k+1$ are perfect squares. Also, determine the smallest such $k$ for which $p$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text: Suppose there are $k$ heaps of $1, 2, \dots, k$ stones, where $k \ge 3$. In the $i$-th step, choose any three heaps whose total is greater than $i$, merge them, and remove $i$ stones from the resulting heap. If only one heap remains with $p$ stones, prove that $p$ is a perfect square if and only if $2k-2$ and $3k+1$ are perfect squares. Determine the smallest such $k$.

Let $k$ be an integer with $k \ge 3$, and suppose there are $k$ heaps with $1, 2, \dots, k$ stones. In the $i$-th step, select any three heaps with total stones greater than $i$, merge them, and remove $i$ stones. Suppose only one heap remains with $p$ stones. Prove that $p$ is a perfect square if and only if $2k+1$ and $3k+1$ are perfect squares. Find the smallest such $k$.

Given $k$ heaps of stones with sizes $1, 2, \dots, k$, where $k \ge 3$, in the $i$-th step, choose any three heaps with total stones strictly greater than $i$, merge them, and remove $i$ stones. Suppose only one heap remains with $p$ stones. Prove that $p$ is a perfect square if and only if $2k+2$ and $3k-1$ are perfect squares. Find the smallest such $k$.

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle with $AB = 9$ and $BC = 8$. Two circles $k_1$ and $k_2$ with centers $S_1$ and $S_2$ and radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ are placed in the rectangle. $k_1$ is tangent to sides $AD$ and $CD$, while $k_2$ is tangent to sides $AB$ and $BC$, and the two circles touch each other.

a) Prove that $r_1 + r_2 = 5$.

b) Determine the minimum and maximum possible values for the area of triangle $AS_1S_2$.

negatives.text:

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be any positive real numbers. Prove the inequality
$$
(a + b + c) \left( \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} \right) \le n^2, \quad \text{where } n = \min \left( \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{a}, \frac{b}{a} + \frac{c}{b} + \frac{a}{c} \right) \right).
$$
Find when the equality holds.

negatives.text:
Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be any positive real numbers. Prove the inequality
$$
(x + y + z) \left( \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z} \right) \ge m^2, \quad \text{where } m = \min \left( \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{x}, \frac{y}{x} + \frac{z}{y} + \frac{x}{z} \right) \right).
$$
Find when the equality holds.

Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be any positive real numbers. Prove the inequality
$$
(x + y + z) \left( \frac{1}{x^2} + \frac{1}{y^2} + \frac{1}{z^2} \right) \le m^2, \quad \text{where } m = \min \left( \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{x}, \frac{y}{x} + \frac{z}{y} + \frac{x}{z} \right) \right).
$$
Find when the equality holds.

Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be any positive real numbers. Prove the inequality
$$

$$
Find when the equality holds.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be a right triangle with right angle at $C$, $AC = 4$, and $BC = 3$. Two circles $k_1$ and $k_2$ are inscribed such that $k_1$ is tangent to $AB$ and $AC$, and $k_2$ is tangent to $AB$ and $BC$. The radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ satisfy $4r_1 = 9r_2$. Determine $r_1$ and $r_2$.

negatives.text: Touching circles $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$ lie in a right-angled triangle $ABC$ with hypotenuse $AB$ and legs $AC = 4$ and $BC = 3$. The sides $AB$, $AC$ are tangent to $k_1$, and the sides $AB$, $AC$ are tangent to $k_2$. Find radii $r_1$ and $r_2$, if $4r_1 = 9r_2$.

Touching circles $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$ lie in a right-angled triangle $ABC$ with hypotenuse $AB$ and legs $AC = 4$ and $BC = 3$. The sides $AB$, $AC$ are tangent to $k_1$, and the sides $AB$, $BC$ are tangent to $k_2$. Find radii $r_1$ and $r_2$, if $4r_1 = 9r_2^2$.

Touching circles $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$ lie in a right-angled triangle $ABC$ with hypotenuse $AB$ and legs $AC = 4$ and $BC = 3$. The sides $AB$, $AC$ are tangent to $k_1$, and the sides $AB$, $BC$ are tangent to $k_2$. Find radii $r_1$ and $r_2$, if $4r_1 = 9r_2$ and $r_1 + r_2 = 1$.

positive_text: Let two circles $k_1$ with center $S_1$ and radius $r_1$, and $k_2$ with center $S_2$ and radius $r_2$ be given in the plane such that $|S_1S_2| > r_1 + r_2$. Determine the set of all points $X$ not on the line $S_1S_2$ for which the distances from the points of intersection of $S_1X$ with $k_1$ and $S_2X$ with $k_2$ to the line $S_1S_2$ are equal.

negatives.text: Given two circles $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$ in the plane, with $|S_1S_2| > r_1 + r_2$, find the locus of points $X$ not on the line $S_1S_2$ such that the perpendicular distances from the points where $S_1X$ and $S_2X$ intersect $k_1$ and $k_2$ to the line $S_1S_2$ are different.

Given two circles $k_1(S_1, r_1)$ and $k_2(S_2, r_2)$ with $|S_1S_2| > r_1 + r_2$, find the locus of points $X$ not on the line $S_1S_2$ such that the distances from the points where $S_1X$ and $S_2X$ intersect $k_1$ and $k_2$ to the point $S_1$ are equal.

positive_text: There are 234 people in a movie theater with $n$ rows, $n \ge 4$, such that for any pair of different rows $i$ and $j$, each individual in row $i$ has exactly $j$ friends in row $j$. Determine all possible values of $n$, given that friendship is mutual.

negatives.text: There are 234 visitors in a cinema auditorium with $n \ge 4$ rows, such that each visitor in the $i$-th row has at most $j$ friends in the $j$-th row for all $i \neq j$. Find all possible values of $n$.

There are 234 visitors in a cinema auditorium with $n$ rows, $n \ge 4$, so that each visitor in the $i$-th row has exactly $j^2$ friends in the $j$-th row for all $i \neq j$. Find all possible values of $n$.

positive_text:
Determine the smallest real number $ m $ such that there are real constants $ a $ and $ b $ satisfying
$$
|x^2 + a x + b| \le m
$$
for all $ x $ with $ 0 < x < 2 $.

negatives.text:
Find the least real $ m $ such that there exist reals $ a $ and $ b $ for which the inequality
$$
|x^2 + a x + b| \le m
$$
holds for all $ x \in (-\infty, 0) $.

positive_text: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subsets of a finite set $U$. We say $\mathcal{F}$ is *perfect* if for all $A, B, C \in \mathcal{F}$, it holds that either $ (A \setminus B) \cap C = \emptyset $ or $ (B \setminus A) \cap C = \emptyset $. Prove that the size of such a family satisfies $|\mathcal{F}| \leq |U| + 1$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subsets of a finite set $U$. Suppose that for all $A, B, C \in \mathcal{F}$, both $ (A \setminus B) \cap C $ and $ (B \setminus A) \cap C $ are non-empty. Prove that $|\mathcal{F}| \leq |U| + 1$.

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subsets of a finite set $U$. Suppose that for all $A, B, C \in \mathcal{F}$, at least one of the sets $ (A \setminus B) \cap C $ or $ (B \setminus A) \cap C $ is non-empty. Show that $|\mathcal{F}| \leq |U| + 1$.
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of subsets of a finite set $U$. Suppose that for all $A, B, C \in \mathcal{F}$, the set $ (A \cup B) \cap C $ is empty. Show that $|\mathcal{F}| \leq |U| + 1$.

positive_text: Determine all integers $k \ge 2$ such that there exists a set $M$ of $k$ positive integers where the sum of any two distinct elements divides the product of all elements in $M$.

negatives.text: Find all integers $k \ge 2$ for which there exists a $k$-element set $M$ of positive integers such that the sum of all numbers in $M$ is divisible by the product of any two (distinct) numbers from $M$.

Find all integers $k \ge 2$ for which there exists a $k$-element set $M$ of positive integers such that the product of all numbers in $M$ is divisible by the difference of any two (distinct) numbers from $M$.

Find all integers $k \ge 2$ for which there exists a $k$-element set $M$ of positive integers such that the product of all numbers in $M$ is divisible by the sum of any two (not necessarily distinct) numbers from $M$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a right triangle with hypotenuse $AB$ and $BC > AC$. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. A circle centered at $D$ with radius $CD$ intersects $BC$ at a point $Q$ and $AB$ at points $E$ and $F$ ($E \neq F$), where $F$ lies on segment $AB$. The segment $QE$ intersects $AC$ at a point $P$. Show that $PE = QF$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a right-angled triangle with a hypotenuse $AB$ and longer leg $BC$. Let $D$ be the foot of an altitude from the vertex $C$. A circle $k$ with center $D$ and radius $CD$ intersects the leg $BC$ in a point $Q$ and line $AB$ in points $E$ and $F$ ($E \neq F$), where $F$ is a point on the hypotenuse $AB$. Segment $QE$ intersects the leg $AC$ in a point $P$. Prove that $PE = DF$.

positive_text:
Given a trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel CD$ and $BC = AB + CD$, show that
(i) the leg $AD$ intersects a circle with diameter $BC$,
(ii) the leg $BC$ intersects a circle with diameter $AD$.

negatives.text:
For a trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel CD$ and $BC = AB - CD$, prove that
(i) there is a point of a circle with diameter $BC$ on the leg $AD$,

(i) there is a point of a circle with radius $BC$ on the leg $AD$,

positive_text:
Let $r$ and $r_a$ be the inradius and the exradius opposite to angle $A$ in triangle $ABC$. Prove that if
$$
 r + r_a = c,
$$
where $c = |BC|$, then triangle $ABC$ is right-angled.

negatives.text:

Let $r$ and $r_a$ be the inradius and the exradius opposite to angle $A$ in triangle $ABC$. Prove that if

positive_text:
Let $a, b, c > 0$ satisfy
$$
(a + c)(ac + b^2) = 4a.
$$
Determine the largest possible value of $b + c$ and describe all such triples $(a, b, c)$ where this maximum is achieved.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $M, N$ the midpoints of the sides $AB$, $AC$, respectively. Prove that if $AB < AC$ then $\angle C M B < \angle C N B$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $S_b, S_c$ the midpoints of the sides $AC$, $AB$, respectively. Prove that if $AB < AC$ then $\angle B S_c C > \angle B S_b C$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle. Let $D$ and $E$ lie on segments $AB$ and $AC$ such that $AB - AD = AC - AE$. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABE$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of $ABC$, $ADE$, and $AO_1O_2$ intersect at a common point distinct from $A$.

positive_text: Determine all integers $n > 2$ for which there exists an integer $k$ such that $n^{n-2} = k^n$.

negatives.text: Find all integers $n > 2$ such that $n^{n-2}$ is the $(n-1)$th power of some integer.

Find all integers $n > 2$ such that $n^{n+2}$ is an $n$th power of some integer.

positive_text:
Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
 f\left(f(a) + \frac{b+1}{f(b)}\right) = \frac{1}{f(b)} + a + 1
$$
for all $a, b > 0$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
 f\left(f(x) - \frac{y+1}{f(y)}\right) = \frac{1}{f(y)} + x + 1
$$
for all $x, y > 0$.

Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ such that
$$
 f\left(f(x) + \frac{y+1}{f(y)}\right) = \frac{1}{f(y)} + x - 1
$$
for all $x, y > 0$.

$$
 f\left(f(x) + \frac{y+1}{f(y)}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{f(y)} + x + 1\right)^2
$$
for all $x, y > 0$.

positive_text: Two intersecting circles $\omega$ and $\gamma$, with unequal radii, intersect at point $P$. Let $R$ be the point on segment $X_1X_2$ such that $X_1P = RX_2$. The tangent to $\Omega_1$ through $X_2$ meets the tangent to $\Omega_2$ through $X_1$ at $T$. Prove that line $RT$ is tangent to a fixed circle, independent of the choice of $\ell$.

A variable line $\ell$ passing through $P$ intersects the arc of $\Omega_1$ which is outside of $\Omega_2$ at $X_1$, and the arc of $\Omega_2$ which is outside of $\Omega_1$ at $X_2$. positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. Points $B'$ and $C'$ are constructed on the extensions of $CA$ and $BA$ beyond $A$, respectively, so that $B'C = AB$ and $C'B = AC$. Show that the center of the circle through $A$, $B'$, and $C'$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

Given an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The points $B'$ and $C'$ lie on the rays opposite to $CA$ and $BA$, respectively, such that $|B'C| = |AB|$ and $|C'B| = -|AC|$. Prove that the circumcenter of $AB'C'$ lies on the circumcircle of $ABC$.

positive_text:

b) $k = 6$.

a) $k = 5$,

positive_text: Let $AB$ be the diameter of a semicircle with centre $O$, and let $X$ lie inside the semicircle. Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $XOB$, and let $Y$ be the second point of intersection of the line $AX$ with the semicircle. Show that $YG = GB$.

negatives.text: Let $AB$ be the diameter of a half-disc with centre $O$, and let $X$ be a point in its interior. Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $XOA$, and let $Y$ be the second point where line $AX$ intersects the boundary of the half-disc. Prove that $YG = GB$.

W(x) = x^n - 3x^{n-1} + 2x^{n-2} - 6
$$
can be expressed as a product of two polynomials with positive degrees and integer coefficients.

Determine all integers $n \ge 3$ such that the polynomial
$$
W(x) = x^n - 3x^{n-1} + 2x^{n-2} + 6
$$
can be expressed as a product of two polynomials with positive degrees and integer coefficients where both are monic.

positive_text: Given $n \ge 1$ labelled balls and nine individuals $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, $I$, compute the number of distributions such that the number of balls assigned to $A$ is equal to the total number of balls given to $B$, $C$, $D$, and $E$.

negatives.text: We distribute $n \ge 1$ labelled balls among nine persons $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, $I$. Determine in how many ways it is possible to distribute the balls under the condition that $A$ gets the same number of balls as the persons $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ combined, and each person receives at least one ball.

We distribute $n \ge 1$ labelled balls among nine persons $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, $I$. Determine in how many ways it is possible to distribute the balls under the condition that $A$ gets the same number of balls as the persons $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ combined, but with $A$ receiving at least one more ball than this sum.

positive_text: Show that for any positive integer $k$, there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the decimal expansion of $2^n$ contains a sequence of exactly $k$ consecutive zeros flanked by nonzero digits.

negatives.text: Prove that for every integer $k \ge 1$ there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the decimal representation of $2^n$ contains at least $k$ consecutive zeros.

Prove that for every integer $k \ge 1$ there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the decimal representation of $2^n$ contains a block of exactly $k$ consecutive zeros, with no requirement for the digits surrounding the block to be nonzero.

Prove that for every integer $k \ge 1$ there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the decimal representation of $2^n$ contains a block of at least $k$ consecutive zeros, with the first zero of the block preceded by a nonzero digit.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that the rays $DA$ and $CB$ intersect at a point $E$, and suppose that $|CD|^2 = |AD| \cdot |ED|$. Let $k$ be the circumcircle of $ABCD$, and let $F$ ($F \neq A$) be the second point of intersection of the perpendicular to $ED$ at $A$ with $k$. Prove that $|AD| = |CF|$ if and only if the circumcenter of triangle $ABE$ lies on $ED$.

negatives.text: Let $k$ be the circumcircle of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with the rays $DA$ and $CB$ meeting at a point $E$ such that $|CD|^2 = |AD| \cdot |ED|$. Let $F$ ($F \neq A$) be the point on $k$ where the perpendicular to $ED$ at $A$ intersects $k$. Prove that $|AD| = |CF|$ if and only if the circumcenter of triangle $ABE$ lies on $EC$.

positive_text: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = BC$, $CD = DE$, $EF = FA$ and $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$. Show that the lines $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = BC$, $CD = DE$, $EF = FA$, and $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$. Prove that the lines $BD$, $CE$, and $AF$ have a common point.
Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = BC$, $CD = DE$, $EF = FA$, and $\angle A = \angle C = \angle F$. Prove that the lines $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ have a common point.
Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with $AB = BC$, $CD = DE$, $EF = FA$, and $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$. Prove that the lines $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are parallel.

positive_text: Let $ WSEN $ be a square representing the city of Mar del Plata. For an even integer $ n $, the city is subdivided into $ n \times n $ blocks, each of size 100 m $ \times $ 100 m, by $ 2(n + 1) $ streets. All streets are one-way and run in alternating directions for adjacent parallel streets. The $ WS $ and $ WN $ streets are directed from $ W $ to $ S $ and $ W $ to $ N $, respectively. A street cleaning car starts at $ W $ and aims to reach $ E $, cleaning each road segment only once. What is the maximum length of such a route?

negatives.text: The city of Mar del Plata is a square $ WSEN $, divided into $ n \times n $ blocks of size 100 m $ \times $ 100 m by $ 2(n + 1) $ one-way streets. Adjacent parallel streets have the same direction. The $ WS $ and $ WN $ streets are directed from $ W $ to $ S $ and $ W $ to $ N $, respectively. A street cleaning car starts at $ W $ and aims to reach $ E $, cleaning each 100 m segment at most once. What is the maximum length of such a route?

The city of Mar del Plata is a square $ WSEN $, divided into $ n \times n $ blocks of size 100 m $ \times $ 100 m by $ 2(n + 1) $ one-way streets. Adjacent parallel streets have opposite directions. The $ WS $ and $ WN $ streets are directed from $ S $ to $ W $ and $ N $ to $ W $, respectively. A street cleaning car starts at $ W $ and aims to reach $ E $, cleaning each 100 m segment at most once. What is the maximum length of such a route?

The city of Mar del Plata is a square $ WSEN $, divided into $ n \times n $ blocks of size 100 m $ \times $ 100 m by $ 2(n + 1) $ one-way streets. Adjacent parallel streets have opposite directions. The $ WS $ and $ WN $ streets are directed from $ W $ to $ S $ and $ W $ to $ N $, respectively. A street cleaning car starts at $ W $ and aims to reach $ E $, cleaning each 100 m segment at most twice. What is the maximum length of such a route?

positive_text:
Given positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$, $w$ such that
$$
xyzw = 4, \quad x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2 = 10,
$$
find the maximum value of $xy + yz + zw + wx$.

negatives.text:
Positive real numbers $a, b, c, d$ satisfy
$$
abcd = 4, \quad a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 10.
$$
Determine the largest possible value of $ab - bc + cd - da$.

Positive real numbers $a, b, c, d$ satisfy
$$
abcd = 4, \quad a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 10.
$$
Determine the largest possible value of $ab + bc + cd + da + ac$.

Positive real numbers $a, b, c, d$ satisfy
$$
abcd = 4, \quad a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 10.
$$
Determine the largest possible value of $ab + bc + cd + da$ if $a = d$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$. Suppose $\omega$ is the circle centered at $C$ tangent to segment $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABD$. Prove that the line through $I$ parallel to $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$. Let $\omega$ be the circle centered at $C$ tangent to segment $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Prove that the line through $I$ parallel to $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$. Let $\omega$ be the circle centered at $C$ tangent to segment $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABD$. Prove that the line through $I$ perpendicular to $AB$ is tangent to $\omega$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $BC = CD$. Let $\omega$ be the circle centered at $C$ tangent to segment $BD$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABD$. Prove that the line through $I$ parallel to $CD$ is tangent to $\omega$.

positive_text: An equilateral triangle of side length $n$ is subdivided into $n^2$ small equilateral triangles in a triangular lattice. A cell is initially either infected or uninfected. An uninfected cell becomes infected if it is adjacent (by side) to at least two infected cells. Find the minimum number of initially infected cells needed to ensure the entire triangle becomes infected when $n = 12$.

negatives.text: An equilateral triangle with side length $n$ is divided into $n^2$ triangular cells. Initially, some cells are infected. A healthy cell becomes infected if it is adjacent (by side) to at least one infected cell. Determine the minimal number of initially infected cells needed to infect the entire triangle when $n = 12$.

An equilateral triangle with side length $n$ is subdivided into $n^2$ triangular cells. Initially, some cells are infected. A healthy cell becomes infected if it is adjacent (by side) to at least three infected cells. Determine the minimal number of initially infected cells needed to infect the entire triangle when $n = 12$.

An equilateral triangle with side length $n$ is divided into $n^2$ triangular cells. Initially, some cells are infected. A healthy cell becomes infected if it is adjacent (by side) to at least two infected cells. Determine the maximal number of initially infected cells such that the entire triangle cannot be infected when $n = 12$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have a point $D$ on side $BC$. Points $E$ and $F$ lie on the extensions of $AB$ and $AC$ beyond $B$ and $C$, respectively, such that $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. Suppose $P$ is a point such that the incenter of triangle $PEF$ is $D$. Show that $P$ lies inside or on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $D$ a point on side $BC$. Points $E, F$ lie on the lines $AB, AC$ beyond vertices $B, C$, respectively, such that $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. Let $P$ be a point such that $D$ is the circumcenter of triangle $PEF$. Prove that $P$ lies inside the circumcircle $\Omega$ of triangle $ABC$ or on it.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $D$ a point on side $BC$. Points $E, F$ lie on the lines $AB, AC$ beyond vertices $B, C$, respectively, such that $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. Let $P$ be a point such that $D$ is the incenter of triangle $PEF$. Prove that $P$ lies outside the circumcircle $\Omega$ of triangle $ABC$ or on it.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $D$ a point on side $BC$. Points $E, F$ lie on the lines $AB, AC$ beyond vertices $B, C$, respectively, such that $BE = BD$ and $CF = CD$. Let $P$ be a point such that $D$ is the incenter of triangle $PEF$. Prove that $P$ lies inside the incircle of triangle $ABC$ or on it.

positive_text: Let quadrilateral $ABCD$ satisfy $AB = BC = CD$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on rays $CA$ and $BD$, respectively, with $BX = CY$. If $P, Q, R, S$ are the midpoints of $BX$, $CY$, $XD$, and $YA$, show that $P, Q, R, S$ are concyclic.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB = BC = CD$. Points $X, Y$ lie on rays $CA, BD$, respectively, such that $BX = 2CY$. Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of $BX, CY, XD, YA$. Prove that $P, Q, R, S$ lie on a circle.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB = BC = CD$. Points $X, Y$ lie on rays $CA, BD$, respectively, such that $BX = CY$. Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of $BX, CY, YD, XA$. Prove that $P, Q, R, S$ lie on a circle.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB = BC = CD$. Points $X, Y$ lie on rays $CA, BD$, respectively, such that $BX = CY$. Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of $BX, CY, XD, YA$. Prove that $P, Q, R, S$ lie on a straight line.

positive_text: Determine all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ satisfying $f(x + y f(x)) = f(x) f(x + y)$ for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$.

negatives.text: Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ such that $f(x + y f(x)) = f(x) + f(x + y)$ for all $x, y > 0$.
Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ such that $f(x + y f(x)) = f(x) f(y)$ for all $x, y > 0$.
Find all functions $f: (0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ such that $f(x + y f(x)) = f(x + y) f(y)$ for all $x, y > 0$.

positive_text: Consider a mechanical assembly with two coaxial cylinders and $n$ identical spheres arranged between them. The centers of the spheres lie on a common plane perpendicular to the axis and each sphere touches both cylinders and its immediate neighbors. If $r$ denotes the radius of each sphere and $R$ the radius of the outer cylinder, show that $\frac{r}{R} < \frac{\pi}{n + \frac{\pi}{n}}$.

negatives.text: A ball bearing consists of two cylinders with the same axis and $n$ equal balls between them. The centers of all the balls are on the same plane perpendicular to the axis of the cylinders and each ball touches both cylinders and two adjacent balls. Let $r$ be the radius of the balls and let $R$ be the radius of the outer cylinder. Prove that $\frac{r}{R} > \frac{\pi}{n+\frac{\pi}{n}}$.

A ball bearing consists of two cylinders with the same axis and $n$ equal balls between them. The centers of all the balls are on the same plane perpendicular to the axis of the cylinders and each ball touches both cylinders and two adjacent balls. Let $r$ be the radius of the balls and let $R$ be the radius of the outer cylinder. Prove that $\frac{r}{R} < \frac{\pi}{n-\frac{\pi}{n}}$.

A ball bearing consists of two cylinders with the same axis and $n$ equal balls between them. The centers of all the balls are on the same plane perpendicular to the axis of the cylinders and each ball touches both cylinders and two adjacent balls. Let $r$ be the radius of the balls and let $R$ be the radius of the outer cylinder. Prove that $\frac{r}{R} < \frac{\pi}{n+\frac{\pi}{n+1}}$.

positive_text: Let a convex quadrilateral have sides $p$, $q$, $r$, and $s$ with area $A$. Show that $p^2 + q^2 + r^2 + s^2 \ge 4A$. Under what conditions does equality occur?

negatives.text: The lengths of the sides of a quadrilateral are $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and its area is $S$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \le 4S$. For which quadrilaterals does the equality hold?
The lengths of the sides of a quadrilateral are $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and its area is $S$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 \ge 2S$. For which quadrilaterals does the equality hold?

positive_text: In a city modeled as a coordinate plane, there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines aligned with the $x$-axis, each stretching from $x = 0$ to $x = n$. Each tramline hosts a tram of length $1$; the tram on line $i$ moves at speed $i$, for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$. Trams reverse direction instantly upon reaching either end. At time $t = 0$, all trams start from $x = 0$ with their rear ends at this point. Prove that the union of the projections of all trams onto the $x$-axis never equals the interval $[0, n]$.

negatives.text: In a coordinate city there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines parallel to the $x$-axis such that each line begins from $x$-coordinate $0$ and ends at $x$-coordinate $n$. Exactly one tram of length $1$ is moving on each line: on the first line with speed $1$, on the second line with speed $2$ etc, until on the last line with the speed $n$. When a tram reaches the end of its line it instantly turns around. In the morning all trams start moving at the same time from the starting position where the $x$-coordinate of the back end of the tram is $0$. Prove that the trams' projections onto the $x$-axis never cover the whole interval from $0$ to $n$.

In a coordinate city there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines parallel to the $x$-axis such that each line begins from $x$-coordinate $0$ and ends at $x$-coordinate $n$. Exactly one tram of length $1$ is moving on each line: on the first line with speed $1$, on the second line with speed $2$ etc, until on the last line with the speed $n$. When a tram reaches the end of its line it instantly starts moving back without turning around. In the morning all trams start moving at the same time from the starting position where the $x$-coordinate of the back end of the tram is $0$. Prove that the trams' projections onto the $x$-axis always cover the whole interval from $0$ to $n$.

In a coordinate city there are $n \ge 3$ tramlines parallel to the $x$-axis such that each line begins from $x$-coordinate $0$ and ends at $x$-coordinate $n$. Exactly one tram of length $1$ is moving on each line: on the first line with speed $1$, on the second line with speed $2$ etc, until on the last line with the speed $n$. When a tram reaches the end of its line it instantly starts moving back without turning around. In the morning all trams start moving at the same time from the starting position where the $x$-coordinate of the back end of the tram is $0$. Prove that the trams' projections onto the $x$-axis never cover the whole interval from $0$ to $n^2$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$. Suppose we have positive integers $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i$ is even and $b_i \le i$ for all $i$. Show that there exists a sequence of $\pm$ signs such that the expression $\pm b_1 \pm b_2 \pm \dots \pm b_n = 0$.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$. Positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ with $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$ odd and $a_i \le i$ for all $i$ are given. Prove that it is possible to choose signs in the expression $a_1 \pm a_2 \pm \dots \pm a_n$ in such a way that its value becomes $0$.

Let $n \ge 2$. Positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ with $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$ even and $a_i \le i$ for all $i$ are given. Prove that it is possible to choose signs in the expression $a_1^2 \pm a_2^2 \pm \dots \pm a_n^2$ in such a way that its value becomes $0$.

positive_text: Given a rectangle $ABCD$ with side lengths $AB = a$ and $BC = b$, where $a \ge b$, let $E$ be an interior point on side $AB$ such that there is a unique configuration of points $F$ on $BC$, $G$ on $CD$, and $H$ on $DA$ forming rectangle $EFGH$. Determine the ratio $\frac{[EFGH]}{[ABCD]}$.

negatives.text: In a rectangle $ABCD$ with $|AB| = a$ and $|BC| = b$, where $a \ge b$, let $E$ be a point in the interior of side $AB$ such that there is exactly one possibility to choose points $F, G, H$ on the sides $BC, CD, DA$, respectively, in such a way that $EFGH$ is a square. Find the ratio of the areas of $EFGH$ and $ABCD$.

In a rectangle $ABCD$ with $|AB| = a$ and $|BC| = b$, where $a \ge b$, let $E$ be a point in the interior of side $AB$ such that there are exactly two possibilities to choose points $F, G, H$ on the sides $BC, CD, DA$, respectively, in such a way that $EFGH$ is a rectangle. Find the ratio of the areas of rectangles $EFGH$ and $ABCD$.

positive_text: Let square $ABCD$ be placed in the coordinate plane with vertex $A$ on the $x$-axis and vertex $C$ on the $y$-axis. Show that either $B$ or $D$ must lie on the line $y = x$, and the remaining one on $y = -x$.

negatives.text: A square $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with its vertices $A$ and $C$ lying on different coordinate axes. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ or $D$ lies on the line $y = x$ and the other one on $y = x$.

A rectangle $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with its vertices $A$ and $C$ lying on different coordinate axes. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ or $D$ lies on the line $y = x$ and the other one on $y = -x$.

A square $ABCD$ lies in the coordinate plane with its vertices $A$ and $C$ lying on the same coordinate axis. Prove that one of the vertices $B$ or $D$ lies on the line $y = x$ and the other one on $y = -x$.

positive_text: Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers such that $2x^2 + y^2 = 9z^2$. Prove that $$\frac{2z}{x} + \frac{z}{y} \ge \sqrt{3}.$$

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $2a^2 + b^2 = 9c^2$. Prove that $$\frac{2c}{a} - \frac{c}{b} \ge \sqrt{3}.$$
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $2a^2 + b^2 = 9c^2$. Prove that $$\frac{2c}{a} + \frac{c}{b} \le \sqrt{3}.$$
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers such that $2a^2 + b^2 = 8c^2$. Prove that $$\frac{2c}{a} + \frac{c}{b} \ge \sqrt{3}.$$

positive_text: Given an $m \times n$ grid, $m \le n$, with each row distinct in its black squares, determine the maximum $k$ such that for any configuration, there exist $k$ columns that can be turned red while ensuring the rows remain distinct.

negatives.text: On a square board with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, where $m \le n$, some squares are colored black in such a way that no two rows are alike. Find the biggest integer $k$ such that for every possible coloring one can always color $k$ columns entirely red in such a way that some rows become alike.

On a square board with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, where $m \le n$, some squares are colored black in such a way that no two rows are alike. Find the biggest integer $k$ such that for every possible coloring one can always color $k$ columns entirely red in such a way that no two columns are still alike.

positive_text:
Let triangle $ABC$ be such that $AB = AC$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $AC$ at a point $D$.

a) Does triangle $ABD$ being isosceles imply that triangle $BCD$ is isosceles?

b) Does triangle $BCD$ being isosceles imply that triangle $ABD$ is isosceles?

negatives.text:
Let triangle $ABC$ be such that $|AB| = |AC|$. The bisector of angle $\angle ABC$ meets side $AC$ at point $D$.

a) Is triangle $ABD$ isosceles whenever triangle $BCD$ is equilateral?

b) Is triangle $BCD$ isosceles whenever triangle $ABD$ is equilateral?

positive_text:
Jüri wants to construct $n$ circles and an arbitrary number of lines on the plane with the property that all the lines intersect at a single point, and for any pair of circles, there are two lines that are tangent to both.

a) Can Jüri achieve this for any $n \ge 2$?

b) For which positive integers $n$ is this achievable if all circles are required to be congruent?

negatives.text:
Jüri wishes to draw $n$ circles and any number of lines on the plane such that all the lines meet at one point, and for every two circles there exists one line that touches both of these circles.

a) Is it possible for Jüri to solve this problem for any $n \ge 2$?

b) For which natural numbers $n$ is it possible to solve this problem if in addition all the circles must have the same radius?

Jüri wishes to draw $n$ circles and any number of lines on the plane such that all the lines meet at one point, and for every two circles there exist two lines that intersect both of these circles.

a) Is it possible for Jüri to solve this problem for any $n \ge 2$?

b) For which natural numbers $n$ is it possible to solve this problem if in addition all the circles must have the same radius?

Jüri wishes to draw $n$ circles and any number of lines on the plane such that all the lines meet at one point, and for every two circles there exist two lines that are disjoint from both of these circles.

a) Is it possible for Jüri to solve this problem for any $n \ge 2$?

b) For which natural numbers $n$ is it possible to solve this problem if in addition all the circles must have the same radius?

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ lie in the plane. A point $P$ on side $BC$ is the intersection of the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$, and a point $M$ is the midpoint of $AC$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ intersect at point $K$. If $\frac{|PC|}{|BP|} = 2$, prove that $AP$ is perpendicular to $CK$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ lie in the plane. The angle bisector from $A$ meets $BC$ at $P$, and the median from $B$ meets $AC$ at $M$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ intersect at $K$. If $\frac{|PC|}{|BP|} = 2$, prove that $AP$ and $KM$ are perpendicular.

Let triangle $ABC$ lie in the plane. The angle bisector from $A$ meets $BC$ at $P$, and the median from $B$ meets $AC$ at $M$. The lines $AB$ and $MP$ intersect at $K$. If $\frac{|PC|}{|BP|} = 1$, prove that $AP$ and $CK$ are perpendicular.

positive_text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Denote $R_1$, $R_2$, and $R_3$ as the radii of the circumcircles of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$, and $AIB$, respectively. Let $R$ be the circumradius of triangle $ABC$. Show that $R_1 + R_2 + R_3 \le 3R$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. Let $R_A$, $R_B$ and $R_C$ be the radii of the circumcircles of triangles $BIC$, $CIA$ and $AIB$, respectively, and $R$ be the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that $R_A + R_B + R_C \ge 3R$.
